53f74f7a-da43-4d66-96fa-89203b589fc1: 250 Years, Indigenous Futures Presented By Haines Gallery As the U.S. marks its 250th anniversary, Haines Gallery presents 250 Years, Indigenous Futures , a group exhibition centering the work of leading Native American artists. While occasioned by this anniversary, 250 Years, Indigenous Futures does not commemorate it. ABOVE: Haines Gallery is in Building C (far right). TOP OF PAGE: Bra d Kahlhamer , “ Pima Air + Space , ” 2025 (detail). Acrylic, ink, pencil on bedsheet, 69.25 x 53.5 inches, framed. Courtesy of the artist and Haines Gallery, San Francisco. Photo: Shaun Roberts EVENT DETAILS 250 Years, Indigenous Futures takes its title from the writings of Standing Rock Sioux historian Philip J. Deloria and his colleagues, who argue that Native peoples should be understood not primarily through the past, but “through the lens of futurity.” Indigenous knowledge, they write, is not peripheral to contemporary life but generative of new ways of understanding it. In this spirit, the exhibition considers Native presence and creativity as powerful forces shaping our collective future. The artists in the exhibition are: Victoria Grace Canby (Diné [Navaho]); Jordan Ann Craig (Northern Cheyenne); Sky Hopinka (Ho-Chunk Nation / Pechanga Band of Luiseño Indians); Brad Kahlhamer (Indigenous ancestry); Terran Last Gun (Piikani / Blackfoot); Jamie Okuma (Luiseño, Shoshone-Bannock, Wailaki, Okinawan, and La Jolla); Wendy Red Star (Apsáalooke [Crow]); and Keith Secola (Northern Ute / Anishinaabe). Working across painting, drawing, sculpture, film, and photography, these artists engage contemporary culture, Nation-specific visual traditions, and personal histories in distinct and expansive ways. Rather than commemorating the 250th U.S. anniversary, the exhibition recognizes 1776 as only one moment within much longer histories of Indigenous presence, adaptation, and sovereignty. Creating space for artists to define their own terms of engagement, the exhibition aims to bring forward concerns central to their practices. The works on view draw inspiration from a vivid range of sources: boldly painted Piikani lodges; the precise geometry of Northern Cheyenne beadwork; the Indians of All Tribes’ occupation of Alcatraz; cars adorned with blankets and regalia for the annual Crow Fair; blood-soaked horror films; and archival photographs whose subjects meet the visitor’s gaze. The exhibition is informed by Apsáalooke artist Wendy Red Star’s caution against a “foe-based” framing of Native art – one that risks tethering meaning to resistance alone and obscuring the specificity of Nations, histories, and individual practices. Here, each artist’s work emerges from particular relationships to language, land, and material culture. No single framework can contain these worlds. About the Artists Victoria Grace Canby (Diné, b. 1978, Albuquerque, NM). Marin-based artist Victoria Grace Canby’s new works on paper, created for the exhibition, depict the Three Sisters – corn, beans, and squash – as a living model of resilience, healing, and collective care that connects Indigenous Peoples throughout the Americas. “Through fostering our connection to these plants’ powers,” Canby notes, “we can overcome the impacts of colonization.” Jordan Ann Craig (Northern Cheyenne, b. 1992, San Jose, CA). Jordan Ann Craig’s paintings draw from references ranging from Northern Cheyenne beadwork and quillwork to the postwar abstraction of Agnes Martin, all of which she translates into exacting, poetic fields of color and form. In works such as “ Miss Your Musk ” (2024), Craig foregrounds Indigenous abstraction as a living and evolving practice – one capable of holding personal narrative, formal experimentation, and cultural continuity without being reduced to any single source or meaning. Sky Hopinka (Ho-Chunk Nation/Pechanga Band of Luiseño Indians; b. 1984, Ferndale, WA). Sky Hopinka’s film Sunflower Siege Engine (2022) brings together distinct Indigenous sites and histories, connecting the Indians of All Tribes’ occupation of nearby Alcatraz Island (1969–1971) with Illinois’ Cahokia Mounds , one of the largest pre-contact urban centers in North America and a site from which ancestral remains continue to be repatriated. Brad Kahlhamer (Native American ancestry; b. 1956, Tucson, AZ). Painted in acrylic, ink, and pencil on a bedsheet, “ Pima Air + Space ” (2025) belongs to Kahlhamer’s recent “dream sheet” paintings. Its title recalls Arizona’s Pima Air & Space Museum, while birds, horses, masked figures, and a spectral presence drift through an aurora borealis of saturated color. Terran Last Gun , Saakwaynaamah’kaa (Last Gun) (Piikani / Blackfoot; b. 1989, Browning, MT on the Blackfeet Nation Reservation). Inspired by the bold geometric designs of Piikani painted lodges, Terran Last Gun has created a suite of works for the exhibition: precise compositions on vintage ledger paper that bring ancestral forms, colonial records, and the ongoing vitality of Indigenous abstraction into charged relation. Jamie Okuma (Luiseño, Shoshone-Bannock, Wailaki, Okinawan, and La Jolla; b. 1977, Glendale, CA). In “Of Love and Sacrifice: Motherhood” (2026), Jamie Okuma deploys her signature single-stitch beadwork to transform a brain-tanned deerskin handbag into a dazzling portrayal of two figures from Luca Guadagnino’s horror film Suspiria (2018). Drawing bracing cinematic imagery into dialogue with exacting Payómkawichum (Luiseño) beadwork techniques, Okuma conjures the selfless and steadfast power of maternal love. Wendy Red Star (Apsáalooke; b. 1981, Billings, MT). Wendy Red Star’s works from “ The (HUD) ” series focus on the colorful facades of houses built through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development on Montana’s Apsáalooke (Crow) reservation, where the artist was raised. Though their hues were chosen not by residents but by a government agency, Red Star’s images reveal signs of domestic beauty that exceed the mandates of bureaucracy. Keith Secola (Northern Ute / Anishinaabe; b. 1988, Randlett, UT on the Uintah and Ouray Reservation) Keith Secola screen-prints archival portraits of Native Americans onto the covers of vintage books, placing Indigenous presence in direct tension with exclusionary narratives of America’s past. Secola’s images depict subjects who often look directly back at the camera, meeting its gaze with a quiet intensity that transcends time and negates erasure. 2253dbe6-0e6a-4dd9-9468-de8740632969: In this deeply experiential yoga practice, we will explore the dynamic interplay between stability and mobility, strength and relaxation, movement and stillness. Through mindful movement, standing and seated practices, breath, and attention to the subtle ways we organize ourselves in space, we'll investigate what allows us to feel both grounded and free. This event happens each week at the Alembic. Rather than striving for perfect alignment or mastering difficult poses, we'll approach the practice as an exploration. We'll slow down enough to notice, experiment with different possibilities, and discover how the balance between effort and ease can change our experience of movement — and of ourselves.. Teacher Bio: Vickie Russell Bell has been teaching yoga for more than 30 years, bringing together the precision of alignment-based yoga with a deep curiosity about how we inhabit our bodies, regulate our nervous systems, and move through the world. She is an E-RYT 500 and Certified Yoga Therapist (C-IAYT), and has studied with some of the most respected teachers in the Iyengar-influenced yoga tradition. Her teaching is grounded in the belief that yoga is less about mastering poses than developing a more intimate relationship with ourselves. Her classes invite students to slow down, pay attention, and explore the constantly shifting relationships between stability and mobility, strength and softness, effort and ease. She teaches students of all ages and abilities, with a particular interest in yoga as a practice for living fully and well over time.
5e4a11eb-604f-4367-9286-58a8eef6ca01: Every Tuesday morning, the Alembic opens for a half-day of silent meditation practice. This is an unguided silent retreat consisting of three 40-minute meditation periods. There will be no teacher-led instruction during the meditation periods. Participants are invited to bring and engage in their own silent meditation practice. Whether you practice mindfulness, Zen, Vipassana, contemplation, prayer, or another silent form of meditation, all are welcome. The retreat begins promptly at 9:30 AM and concludes at 11:50 AM. Please arrive between 9:15 AM and 9:25 AM to remove your shoes, settle in, and find a seat before the first bell. The morning is divided into three periods of silent meditation: 9:30 AM – 10:10 AM 10:20 AM – 11:00 AM 11:10 AM – 11:50 AM A bell will signal the beginning and end of each meditation period. The meditation hall (Sol) is reserved for silent practice during sitting periods. Between sits, participants may quietly stretch, visit the restroom, or spend time in the tearoom. Conversation is permitted during breaks; however, we encourage participants to keep voices low, as some attendees choose to observe silence throughout the entire morning. You are welcome to leave the meditation hall at any time if needed. If you leave during a meditation period, please wait until the next break before re-entering. We ask that all entrances and exits be as quiet and unobtrusive as possible. This is a “Bring Your Own Silent Meditation” retreat. We provide the structure and the space; you provide your own silent practice. Participants may choose to sit in Sol or engage in quiet movement practice in the tearoom during meditation periods. To minimize disruption, please enter Sol only during the transition periods between sits. If you arrive after a meditation period has begun, you are welcome to practice elsewhere in the Alembic until the next bell. The suggested donation is $10. No one will be turned away for lack of funds. We do ask that all attendees register through the Momence app or via the registration link on the Alembic website. Please note that the retreat ends at 11:50 AM, and we ask all participants to depart by 12:00 PM so that our volunteer teacher and staff may close the space in a timely manner. Thank you for helping us maintain a quiet and supportive environment for practice.

eafa3d97-927a-448b-bd65-4580032a8f65: We are honored to welcome Erin French to Calvary Presbyterian for an afternoon celebrating the release of The Lost Kitchen Volume 3: Seize the Supper. The stunning third volume in The Lost Kitchen cookbook series from Erin French, award-winning restaurant founder and New York Times -bestselling author of Finding Freedom, The Lost Kitchen, and Big Heart Little Stove Erin will be joined in conversation by Tanya Holland, the author of Tanya Holland's California Soul: Recipes from a Culinary Journey West [A Cookbook]. Presented in partnership with Calvary Presbyterian San Francisco Erin French brings you perfectly crafted meals for dining outside the box and living in the moment in her latest cookbook, Seize the Supper . From her beloved home and restaurant, the Lost Kitchen in Freedom, Maine, come hearty main dishes balanced with crisp, bright salads and sweet and spiced desserts. Her well-rounded meals are made with true comfort and seasonal nourishment that are perfect for carrying you from shorter days and late-afternoon feasts to snowy winter nights sitting by the fire to picnics that welcome the blooming of spring. In simple yet rewarding steps, French shares delicious recipes that will foster connection and inspiration around the table. From flavorful salads and sides such as Soft Polenta with Honey & Ricotta, Roasted Asparagus with Tarragon Vinaigrette, and Pear, Walnut & Blue Cheese Waldorf to rich mains including Provençal Roasted Chicken, Fried Halibut, and Buttermilk Leg of Lamb with Fennel & Orange to irresistible desserts like Baked Vanilla Spice Puddings with Cherry Compote and Rosemary Maple Ice Cream, French’s recipes are filled with warmth, heart, and meaningful tips for embracing the joy of now. Erin French , a born-and-raised Mainer, is the owner and chef of the Lost Kitchen, a fifty-seat restaurant in Freedom, Maine, listed among Time ’s World’s Greatest Places to visit and Bloomberg ’s " 12 Restaurants Worth Traveling Across the World to Experience.” With two New York Times bestsellers to her name, Finding Freedom and Big Heart Little Stove , Erin is featured in three seasons of the Magnolia Network series The Lost Kitchen and Getting Lost with Erin French, where she travels the country searching for new experiences and culinary inspiration, streaming on HBO Max. Erin knows the importance of simple pleasures found in gathering for thoughtfully prepared meals. Her love of Maine and sharing its delicious heritage with dinner guests has garnered several James Beard nominations and the attention of The New York Times , Martha Stewart Living, The Wall Street Journal, The Boston Globe, and Food & Wine, as well as NPR’s All Things Considered, CBS News Sunday Morning, and Today. After more than a decade in business, the Lost Kitchen has become so much more than a restaurant, now boasting a farmer’s market, overnight cabins, a retail shop, and a café called the Little Lost Kitchen. Tanya Holland is an award-winning chef, restaurateur, cookbook author, educator, media personality, wine professional, and U.S. State Department Culinary Diplomat. A French-trained chef with more than four decades of experience, she is best known as the founder and executive chef of Oakland’s Brown Sugar Kitchen, where she earned national recognition for modern African American cuisine and thoughtful, inclusive hospitality. Holland is the author of Brown Sugar Kitchen and Tanya Holland’s California Soul and has appeared on Food Network’s Melting Pot, Bravo’s Top Chef, and other programs. Her work has been featured in The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, Bon Appétit, Gourmet, House Beautiful, and O, The Oprah Magazine. She serves on the James Beard Foundation Board of Trustees and, in 2026, joined the University of Virginia as a Senior Lecturer. Across food, wine, teaching, media, and diplomacy, Holland creates memorable experiences that bring people together around the table. Tucked into the northeastern corner of the state, this rural enclave is home to the Nelson brothers — four young, ambitious, fourth-generation commodity farmers who dream of becoming the biggest farmers in the United States. We meet them in the midst of fall harvest. It has been a brutal year: drought has decimated the soybean crop, equipment breakdowns have caused repeated setbacks, and the Nelsons are nearly out of funds. After a second straight year of poor returns, and with neighboring farms shuttering around them, the Nelsons know they cannot afford a third. Then, as the new year begins, an unexpected opportunity arrives: the local school board offers to lease them 1,200 additional acres. Combined with their existing 2,800 acres, it is more land than they have ever farmed. But with climate change, equipment failures, rising costs, biblical flooding, and mounting tensions between the brothers, the stakes have never been higher. For the Nelsons, this season will be make-or-break: will their determination carry them through, or will their ambition undo them? Directed by an award winning mother, Natalie Baszile (author of "Queen Sugar") and daughter (Hyacinth Parker) team. Q&A with filmmaker expected after the screening. Co-presented by SFFILM. We've ditched the doom-and-gloom documentaries that make you want to crawl under a (sustainably sourced) blanket and never come out. Whether you’re an eco-curious cinephile or a die-hard activist, come join in the fun because if we're going to talk about the end of the world as we know it, we might as well laugh, gasp, and maybe even dance a little on the way there. 7d6e2486-480b-4c7e-a1ac-1947fd73c06d: A taut, emotionally gripping, and surprisingly funny novel about a father and daughter stranded in an airport at the end of the world, Passengers is a story of loving across gaps—between parent and child, between things said and unsaid—and what happens when the outside world finally mirrors the chaos within. ​This is Maksik’s most timely and accomplished novel yet! Ivan is a solitary man in his seventies, set in his ways and haunted by the failures of his past. His smart and cynical daughter, Nina, is in the twilight of her twenties and has long kept a distance from her sentimental father. But when Ivan proposes a trip to Europe in hopes that it will bring them closer together, Nina reluctantly agrees. They meet at LAX, where their departure is delayed. And delayed again. And again. As the hours drag on, their sharp, caustic and wide-ranging conversation reveals a lifetime of misunderstandings, unhealed wounds, and stubborn love. Soon more flights are canceled, security tightens, airport staff grow evasive, and it becomes clear to Ivan and Nina that something is wrong. They begin to suspect that they’re being held prisoner—sequestered from the world without explanation. At last, the surreal starts to overtake the mundane, and their need to escape—and to protect each other—turns increasingly urgent. What begins as a piercing portrait of a father and daughter becomes a novel of eerie suspense, as Nina and Ivan navigate not only their fractured bond but also a world teetering on the brink of collapse. A story of loving across gaps—between parent and child, between things said and unsaid—and about what happens when the outside world finally mirrors the chaos within, Passengers is Maksik’s most timely and accomplished novel yet. “A beautiful, unsettling novel about the depths of love, the burden of nostalgia and the maddening impossibility of translating feeling into language.”—Imbolo Mbue, author of Behold the Dreamers “A novel of surpassing beauty and among the most moving portraits of parenthood I’ve ever read. It also happens to be exceptionally funny, propulsive and wise—an example of the alchemy that occurs when a writer finds the work he was born to pursue. Passengers is Alexander Maksik’s masterpiece.”—Anthony Marra, author of Mercury Pictures Presents "Maksik's best to date. Passengers is really about how we're all trying to get somewhere different, somewhere better--to a place where we can be closer to those we love, during this one precious life we have. I could not put it down."—Adam Ross “This is the stuff we live for—a spinning dream of a book, pure heart-in-your-throat magic. I can’t say this enough: read it, today, now.”—Paul Yoon, author of The Hive and the Honey , winner of The Story Prize “ Passengers is a tour de force that reveals just how deeply two ordinary people can love one another…This superb novel takes on the very hardest stuff of life and never looks away.”—Ben Fountain, author of Billy Lynn’s Long Halftime Walk “Maksik’s latest, Passengers, is propulsive and fierce and uncompromising in its humanity. And funny too, in often unexpected ways. Also, my kind of book in that it doesn’t waste a single word. It's kept me intensely good company these past few weeks. Seems to me: A necessary book for these batshit times.”—Peter Orner Alexander Maksik is the author of You Deserve Nothing , a New York Times and IndieBound bestseller; A Marker to Measure Drift , which was a New York Times Notable Book, as well as a finalist for the William Saroyan Prize and Le Prix du Meilleur Livre Étranger, and the basis of the 2023 motion picture Drift ; Shelter in Place , named one of the best books of the year by the Guardian and the San Francisco Chronicle; and The Long Corner , a New York Times Book Review Editor’s Choice, and named one of the best books of the year by The Australian . 20074eee-84d2-4e76-aeea-26881d8e8c4b: 🌊 What if the boundaries we impose on nature prevent us from seeing how it actually works? Scientists often divide the natural world into neat categories: ocean and seafloor, land and water, surface and subsurface. But nature rarely follows those boundaries, and the categories we create can shape what we notice, what we miss, and what we choose to protect. Geological oceanographer Ivano Aiello explores this idea through three surprising case studies. At the bottom of the Mediterranean, an extraordinary ecosystem blurs the line between ocean and seafloor. In Monterey Canyon, repeated maps reveal a landscape that is constantly being reshaped. And after the Moss Landing battery fire, the way scientists defined something as simple as the “surface” determined whether contamination was detected or missed. Together, these stories reveal how the boundaries we create can change what we see, what we understand, and how we respond to our messy, interconnected natural world. 🌍 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-7:35 --> arrival & chats 7:35-8:20 --> lecture 8:20-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? d4ac5abd-0a8f-4197-bcae-e81235a58320: 💘 What if everything evolutionary psychology told you about dating was wrong? For decades, a buzzy branch of science has spread a deeply flawed story about romantic relationships, cloaking itself in the language of incontrovertible Darwinian fact. Evolutionary psychology claims our minds were shaped by primal drives that pit the genders against each other, from the myth that men are wired to be promiscuous to the notion that wealth, status, and beauty are the ultimate aphrodisiacs. In this talk, UC Davis psychology professor Paul Eastwick, author of Bonded by Evolution and co-host of the Love Factually podcast, draws on original experiments from his own lab to reveal that these stories bear little resemblance to how attraction really works. Success in relationships does not hinge on finding the universally good partner, he argues, but on compatibility. Popularity may shape first impressions, but its influence fades fast. And once we look at what men and women actually want, the supposed gender differences tend to evaporate. Eastwick reveals attraction as a process of finding, and often creating, a compatible connection. 💫 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-8:00 --> arrival & chats 8:00-8:40 --> lecture 8:40-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? dea495c1-21de-4aa2-bc62-b842ae1c253b: 🤖 How did a set of math rules from the 1940s end up defining what it means to be rational? In the 1940s, mathematicians and engineers set out to build machines that could make critical decisions under uncertainty. Within a decade, they had invented tools that not only launched modern computer science but quietly rewrote what it means for a human being to make a "rational" choice. Benjamin Recht, a professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences at UC Berkeley, will draw on his new book The Irrational Decision to trace how these academic rules for machines came to define rationality in economics, public policy, and everyday culture. Ben will walk through where automated decision systems have thrived, from accelerating computers to regulating pharmaceuticals to powering e commerce, and where they break down. The pattern he has found is consistent: these systems excel in well defined spaces with clear rules and measurable goals, and turn brittle or absurd outside them. The talk will close with a genuinely open question. How do we keep using these powerful tools without surrendering human judgment and agency in the process? 🧮 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-7:35 --> arrival & chats 7:35-8:20 --> lecture 8:20-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? About the Book: In a heart-wrenching debut, author Sonny Buttar delivers a multigenerational family saga at once haunting and hopeful. Teacher Salma Chaudhry lives a quiet life, avoiding all attachments. But after a call from her estranged father, the protective shell she lives within starts to crack and the trauma she's buried for eighteen years emerges. Salma and her older sister Asma were inseparable growing up in small-town Rosebud. While Asma was bold and fearless, Salma tried to keep the peace in their fractured family. But amid their mother's decline and their parents' rigid expectations, Asma makes a choice that tears the family apart. The fallout changes everything--and forces Salma to choose between her sister and her parents. Salma has spent years trying to forget. But as she recollects her past and considers reconciliation with her father, a young student opens a surprising connection to Asma's past. In finally facing her history, Salma finds the bravery to love and hope again. The Daughters of Rosebud is a powerful exploration of sisterhood, family loyalty, and the courage it takes to heal. About the Author: Sonny Buttar was born in Pakistan and raised in England and the American Midwest. Her first novel, The Daughters of Rosebud, will be released in October 2026. About the Conversation Partner: Vanessa Hua is the nationally bestselling author of Coyoteland, A River of Stars and Forbidden City , and the story collection Deceit and Other Possibilities , a New York Times Editors’ Pick. A National Endowment for the Arts Literature Fellow, she has also received a Rona Jaffe Foundation Writers’ Award, the Asian/Pacific American Award for Literature, a California Arts Council Fellowship, and a Steinbeck Fellowship in Creative Writing, as well as honors from the de Groot Foundation, the Society of Professional Journalists, and the Asian American Journalists Association. She was a finalist for the California Book Award, the Northern California Book Award, and the New American Voices Award. Previously, she was an award-winning columnist for the San Francisco Chronicle . She teaches at the Warren Wilson MFA Program, Sewanee Writers Conference, and elsewhere. This fall, she is an Ann-Getty Endowed Visiting Artist-Scholar at the University of San Francisco. Her debut narrative nonfiction, Uprooted, is forthcoming.

fa5c1bd2-3034-4f0c-990a-e72397c379e8: SF Short Film Festival presents: KEEPSAKE When Lily’s husband transports them back into their happiest memory together, she must choose whether to face the harsh reality of their present or start over in an idyllic past. The romantic gesture devolves into a surreal nightmare and Lily must find a way to save herself and her future. ENTER, MACHINE The short film is structured in three traditional acts, yet shot almost entirely from the fixed perspective of a motionless red sedan that never truly moves relative to the camera. The audience feels as though stepping into a time machine, witnessing three devastating tragedies unfolding inside this single vehicle across different eras: Ryan’s joyful purchase of his first car quickly collapses into family ruin amid financial rage and abandonment; years (or moments) later, Ian’s secret affair with Mary spirals into vehicular manslaughter after a rage-fueled chase kills a food-stealing addict; finally, in a midnight forest, a bound and masked Ryan brutally slays an unknown opponent in the back seat, only for the car to lurch forward once in vain before snapping back to its original position—revealing the terrified original salesperson Hannah (kidnapped by Ryan) escaping from the trunk. The film’s single futile movement delivers a sharp satire on humanity’s illusion of progress trapped in an unchanging cycle of destruction. I WILL COME TO YOU Orphaned as a baby, Julian grows up in a Catholic boys’ home. As he uncovers his family’s buried past, he becomes fixated on a new couple living in a secluded farmhouse. Under the guise of a singing lesson, Julian gains access to Esa, a celebrated opera singer, whose poise and control are quickly eroded by his unsettling confidence. What starts as discomfort slips into a brief, charged intimacy before Esa realizes she has made a grave mistake. Julian refuses her orders to leave. LUCIA, THE WOMAN WITHOUT A FACE Javier is haunted by a recurring nightmare - he's trapped in a strange house with something waiting for him in the basement. Despite his mother's reassurance that they're only dreams (solo son sueños), he can't shake the growing sense that an ominous presence is getting closer. MY NAME IS JOHN An otherworldly doppelgänger tries something new. OH, DEER When a couple's explosive argument is interrupted by a tragic accident, the night takes a turn they never saw coming. THE RETURN A man returns to the office for a mandatory meeting and discovers that workplace culture has mutated into something strange, ritualistic, and inhuman. The Return is a surreal workplace horror film about conformity, alienation, and the fear of being absorbed by the hive. WIGHT Marion, a young Chinese-American woman, returns to her childhood home in a cramped San Francisco Chinatown apartment, after her grandmother is hospitalized under mysterious circumstances. Back home, she navigates a strained relationship with her Auntie Lam and her cousin, Amelia, and processes her guilt for not being around during the incident. Marion steadily grows more paranoid and becomes determined to prove that her grandmother was attacked in a hate crime, only to find that the family is actually haunted by a Jiangshi, a vampire-like creature that takes the form of a reanimated corpse to drain the life force of its victims. The short film— what a perfect genre. Like the perfect snack. Or the very best poem: intensity and imagination distilled down to the most crucial and poignant of words. Short films are the quintessential starting point, and for some filmmakers, the definitive end goal. The San Francisco International Festival of Short Films was launched in 2006. Since then SF Shorts has showcased incredible engaging independent films that are quick to make a statement, tell a story or express an idea. Recently this festival merged with the 29 year old San Francisco IndieFest, combining SF Shorts' curatorial vision with SF IndieFest's festival presentation expertise. This combined event now presents one week of the best short films from around the world at an historic San Francisco art house theater. Tickets Festival Pass

f676a36c-7a0c-47da-a0b9-55e29467783e: Green Film Festival presents: FENCELINE: SHADOWS OVER THE RIVER PARISH For generations, families in Louisiana's River Parishes built communities along the Mississippi River. Many trace their roots to formerly enslaved people who settled the region after the Civil War, establishing churches, schools, farms, and neighborhoods that remain today. Now surrounded by one of the largest petrochemical corridors in the world, residents confront pollution, illness, industrial expansion, and growing pressure on the places they call home. Through the voices of those living on the frontlines of this industrial corridor, Fenceline offers an intimate portrait of communities determined to remain where their families have lived for generations. HYPERSCALED Increased energy and water demands from the rapid development of large data centers driven by technological advancements like “AI”, are increasing threats to communities across the Southeast. HYPERSCALED unearths the real world cost of AI as residents fight to get answers about the costly impacts of this water and energy sucking industry. Much like a vampire, the proposed “Project Marvel” is projected to consume unprecedented amounts of water and energy from the backyards of concerned communities. IN EARTH WE TRUST The rise and fall of the evangelical Reverend who nearly saved the planet. And how becoming a taxi driver influenced him to continue his mission of finding common ground on the issue of climate change. Fifteen years ago Reverend Richard Cizik had the attention of 30 million Evangelical christians and was generating momentum for a faith-based moral obligation to care for the planet. This idea of ‘Creation Care’ was controversial, but Rev. Cizik was a media darling, popular with the youth – the face of the more reasonable modern-day Evangelical. Until one fateful interview changed his life. This is the story of how a man, set on changing the world, went from Vice President of one of the biggest religious organizations in America, a speechwriter for Ronald Reagan, and one of TIME Magazine’s top 100 influential people, to a part-time Lyft (electric vehicle) driver almost overnight; the story of how his work continues to influence modern election campaigns; and ultimately, a story about finding common ground in a polarized world. GRASSROOTS: THE RE:WILD YOUR CAMPUS STORY Re:wild Your Campus (RYC) protects over 700,000 students each year from toxic pesticides. Started by a beach volleyball player at UC Berkeley, this environmental non profit has worked across the country protecting front line workers, students, and staff from toxic pesticide exposure on their college campuses. RYC is up against the largest chemical companies in the world and this is RYC's story. RYC's founder, Mackenzie Feldman, was nominated to the Forbes 30 U 30 Class of 2026 for her work. Forget the guilt trip, the Green Film Festival of San Francisco, the mischievous, tree-hugging cousin of the 29 year old SF IndieFest, returns Oct 15-22 to prove that saving the planet doesn't have to feel like homework. We've ditched the doom-and-gloom documentaries that make you want to crawl under a (sustainably sourced) blanket and never come out. The line-up this year pairs sharp environmental storytelling with wit, weirdness, and unapologetic irreverence. And yes, our Eco-Horror midnight movie is back! Whether you’re an eco-curious cinephile or a die-hard activist, come join in the fun because if we're going to talk about the end of the world as we know it, we might as well laugh, gasp, and maybe even dance a little on the way there. Through this experience the festival hopes audiences can begin to engage with sustainable solutions to the problems facing the planet. Tickets Festival Pass

39fbf402-efca-48c0-ba29-ceb6f61be6d1: Jad Youssef is chef patron of the award-winning Lebnani in Reigate, Surrey which Jay Rayner highly praised in The Observer: ‘one taste of its gloriously zingy Lebanese flavours and you know you’re in the right place.’ Jad was born in Beirut during the Lebanese Civil War, the youngest of six siblings. He learnt to cook in his mother Khadija’s kitchen and in his father’s pastry shop before training at the Ecole Hoteliere in Beirut. After early work in local hotels and restaurants, he moved to Oslo in 2000 as Head Chef at Jeppe Restaurant, later relocating to London to lead the kitchen at Fakhreldine in Piccadilly and serve as Executive Chef at the Levant Group. In 2009, Youssef founded Yalla Yalla in Soho, one of London’s first Lebanese street food restaurants, expanding to Fitzrovia and Shoreditch in the following years. The restaurant received wide critical attention and achieved a cult following. His signature dish, Sawda Djej (chicken livers with pomegranate molasses), developed an equally devoted following and was named one of Time Out London's "100 Best Dishes." After time in Hong Kong, Youssef and his wife Aga returned to the UK to open Lebnani in Reigate, Surrey, in 2020. The restaurant was named Best Restaurant in Surrey by Muddy Stilettos in 2024, awarded an AA Rosette, and was the recipient of the Be Inclusive Hospitality Middle Eastern Food Award in 2025. Jad has also appeared at Meatopia, Taste of London, and Taste of Hong Kong, served as a judge on Celebrity MasterChef UK, appeared on BBC's MasterChef, and worked with Miele among many others. His work has been featured in The Times, The Observer, Financial Times, The Guardian, and numerous other publications. Lebnani - In Lebnani , celebrated chef Jad Youssef invites readers to experience the warmth, generosity and soul of Lebanese cooking through recipes passed down through generations of his family. In his debut book, Jad returns to the dishes and memories that shaped his life in Beirut and beyond, celebrating Lebanese food as it is truly lived and eaten. Featuring 84 authentic recipes from his family’s kitchen in Lebanon and his award-winning restaurant Lebnani in Surrey, the book reveals secret spice blends, time-honoured techniques and beloved family dishes that bring people together around the table. Chapters echo the rhythm of daily life - Lebanese Mornings, Mezza at Home, Tabkha (everyday meals), Mashawi (grills), Sandwiche (street wraps), Helweyet (sweets) and Namlieh (the pantry) - reflecting the meals and moments that shape Lebanese identity. Family stories are woven throughout, tracing how food sustained Lebanese families through conflict, change and celebration. From gathering wild za’atar to mornings spent collecting trays of freshly baked mana’eesh, Jad’s memories root Lebanese cuisine in gratitude, connection and resilience. With evocative imagery and heartfelt storytelling, Lebnani offers a rich portrait of a culture where food, memory and family life are deeply intertwined.

96a1315b-2f93-4c93-b14e-3b59ae27bb22: Co-presented with Yerba Buena Center for the Arts Sherry Turkle has spent decades studying how digital technologies isolate us from one another. Now, in her latest book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk To Machines, the psychologist who pioneered our understanding of human-computer relationships explores the seductive and beguiling nature of chatbots presented as “perfect” companions. How does their popularity point to existing wells of deep loneliness in our current culture, and how does increasing reliance on a one-sided digital ear affect users’ ability to maintain offscreen relationships with other humans? In conversation with New Yorker cartoonist Amy Kurzweil, whose graphic novel Artificial: A Love Story suggests an alternate path in which A.I. isn’t used as a human connection substitute, but rather a tool to support and deepen the real-world relationships we already have. The conversation is part of Free Wednesdays at YBCA, which offers extended gallery hours, hands-on afternoon art-making, and special evening programs—all for free. Doors at 6:00pm.

02cfec45-0bd6-43ad-b9ef-3847e9455a9f: This is an ongoing monthly group designed to support the integration of mystical, psychedelic, or otherwise transformative experiences. Each session combines guided listening to curated music with expressive arts such as drawing and writing to help you process what a single conversation can't resolve. Come once, or return each month. No musical or art background is required. During the evening, we will: Enter a brief guided relaxation Listen to a short, curated music passage Express what surfaces through drawing and writing Share and witness in the group (optional) Leave with a deeper understanding or perspective Rooted in the Bonny Method, this circle draws on Guided Imagery and Music (GIM), developed by Helen Bonny from her work with LSD-assisted therapy at the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center in the 1960s and 70s. Bonny found that music paired with deep relaxation could open the same expanded states she observed in psychedelic sessions, and that the imagery work done afterward carried much of the lasting change. GIM's approach to music and imagery now informs how integration is supported across modern psychedelic-assisted therapy. Please arrive no later than 7pm. Doors lock at 7:10pm. Sophia Wang is a violinist, board-certified music therapist (MT-BC), integration practitioner, and life coach whose work centers on music, imagery, and non-ordinary states of consciousness. With over a decade of clinical experience across oncology, palliative care, and mental health settings, she draws on Guided Imagery and Music, expressive arts, and depth-oriented inquiry to support emotional healing, insight, and meaningful change. Sophia works with people across a wide range of inner terrain: those in cancer care or facing the end of life; people moving through grief, depression, or anxiety; and high-performing professionals and seekers drawn to deep self-inquiry and the integration of transformative experiences. Her approach blends clinical training with creative exploration, emphasizing safety, pacing, and integration.

773bf904-115d-47d3-936c-5ef1219b9d2f: Local author Fleisher presents his gripping historical novel based on the life of little-known naturalist Eugene Marais. Join us at Mrs. Dalloway's Bookstore on Wednesday, October 21 at 7:00 PM when Berkeley author Seth Fleisher comes to the store to launch his new novel The Farther Shore. Seth will be joined by Mindela Ruby for the conversation and will sign copies of his book after the presentation. The Farther Shore is a sweeping novel about fathers and sons, memory and race, and the dangerous fictions that shape us—inspired by the true story of Eugene Marais, one of history's most extraordinary and forgotten minds. Southern Africa, 1890s. Eugene Marais is a brilliant naturalist and iconoclastic journalist whose evolving theories about memory, addiction, and the hive mind are decades ahead of their time. But when tragedy strikes, he abandons his newborn son and disappears into a remote South African forest—leaving behind his child and his conscience, and embarking on research that will haunt both their lives. Thirty years later, his son Charles—now a professor of ancient Buddhist history at Harvard—discovers that his father's work has been weaponized. University faculty are mining Eugene's research to bolster theories of racial hierarchy, and their ambitions are growing darker by the day. Accompanied by a mysterious Jewish graduate student whose fate is becoming entangled with his own, Charles will make an epic journey across continents to heal his fractured past and stop a sinister plot quietly taking root at the world's most prestigious institution. Set across two interlocking timelines—from the British concentration camps of the Boer War to the rising shadow of the Third Reich and WWII— The Farther Shore is a heart-breaking, exhilarating novel about memory, love, and identity, and about the vast distances we’ll travel to find our way home. SETH FLEISHER is an American author whose work has appeared in the Bellevue Literary Review, Pearl, the Journal of Anthropological Research, and elsewhere. Based in Berkeley, California, he has worked with the World Bank Group and other NGOs in South Africa, India, and more than 40 other countries, and co-founded Walk the Walk USA, a U.S.-based democracy initiative to counter the rising tide of authoritarianism. A former Fulbright scholar in Sri Lanka, Seth did Ph.D. work at Harvard in Buddhist social history, a fellowship at Harvard's Center for the Study of World Religions, and a B.A. in literature at Swarthmore, where he and his wife first met in a Chaucer seminar. The Farther Shore is his first novel. MINDELA RUBY is an author, editor and educator. Her novel, Mosh It Up , is about Bay Area garage punk rock. Her prose and poetry appear in T he Dribble Drabble Review, Terrain.org, Santa Monica Review, WomenArts Quarterly, Coachella Review, Rivet: and other outlets plus the anthology Unmasked with a foreword by Gloria Steinem. Her works have been Pushcart and Best Of the Net nominated, including her poetry series Africa Safari Journal (in haiku) (with footnotes). She holds a Ph.D. from UC Berkeley. Her new memoir is currently on submission.

7edd6537-4486-430c-9da6-3c4d052625da: A conversation between fiction writers Donna Miscolta and Marianne Villanueva about where stories come from, what scares them and what makes them laugh when they’re creating characters and situations. Marianne Villanueva, author of four books of dystopian, surreal, and fantasy fiction, will pose questions to Donna Miscolta about her new realist novel Ofelia and Norma . Miscolta, author of four books of fiction, will ask Villanueva about her latest story collection Residents of the Deep . Donna Miscolta’s latest of four books of fiction is Ofelia and Norma . Her stories, essays, and book reviews have appeared in dozens of journals and anthologies. A recording of her work is part of the Library of Congress PALABRA Archive, a showcase for Latin American and Latino writers. She recently moved to Spain and blogs monthly at donnamiscolta.com . Marianne Villanueva is the author of the story collections Ginseng and Other Tales from Manila , Mayor of the Roses , The Lost Language , and Residents of the Deep . A recipient of fellowships from Stanford University and the California Arts Council, she is writing her first novel, set in 16th-century Spain and the Philippines. In Ofelia and Norma , large-bodied twin sisters struggle for a sense of self. When Ofelia sheds pounds from long, solo walks, Norma senses their twinness slipping away. She slips away to an out-of-town college, leaving Ofelia for the first time, and each sister confronts alone life as a large person in an anti-large-person world. Ofelia, having previously lost weight without trying, now makes a deliberate effort to do so, resulting in a disaster that shakes her to her senses. Meanwhile, Norma escapes into her solitude by swimming laps in the college pool where she suffers an experience that sends her into emotional retreat. They move into careers, still estranged until a tender moment leads to the sharing of their secrets and revenge for what one of them has suffered. In Residents of the Deep , Marianne Villanueva explores human resilience in moments of extremity through a series of gripping stories. In “Ice,” two men confront their future in a barren, post-apocalyptic world where survival itself becomes the only meaning: “The point is, there is no point. You just keep going.” In Dumaguete, a young boy is forced to protect his mother, a role that threatens to unravel him. The title story follows a ship captain who discovers a submerged city and is thrust into a moral reckoning that challenges his understanding of responsibility. Clear-eyed and unflinching, these stories reveal the raw tenacity and unyielding spirit of humanity, even in the face of profound vulnerability and hardship.

Crises of capitalism are pushing human civilization toward its breaking points, presenting what sociologist William Armaline calls overlapping threats to human survival: climate change and nuclear war, both potentially made worse by the destabilizing effects of frontier AI. Yet the conversation in Washington and Silicon Valley remains fixated on treating China as our greatest existential rival. In this talk, Armaline, Professor of Sociology and founder of the Human Rights Institute at San José State University, argues that the world cannot survive this great power rivalry. Solving climate change, preventing nuclear war, and regulating dangerous new technologies will require real cooperation and coordination between the United States and China. For the U.S., Armaline says, this means fundamentally rethinking its relationship with China and rejecting the traditional geopolitics of imperial competition. de77c3a6-65f7-4ed1-bc98-f5224c7fe868: 🌊 Could a supercomputer warn you about a tsunami before the wave even forms? Tsunami early warning systems today rely on models that can take precious minutes to run — minutes that coastal communities don't have. New research is changing that by building a "digital twin" of the earth's crust, one that can simulate the physics of an earthquake and its resulting tsunami in near-real time using some of the most powerful supercomputers on the planet. In this talk, Tzanio Kolev will walk through how his team used Bayesian inversion techniques on the El Capitan supercomputer to model the Cascadia subduction zone — the fault line that threatens the Pacific Northwest with a potentially catastrophic earthquake and tsunami. This work, recognized with the 2025 ACM Gordon Bell Prize, represents a major leap in how we use extreme-scale computing to protect lives. Join us for a look inside the intersection of high-performance computing, applied mathematics, and disaster preparedness — and what it takes to simulate the planet fast enough to matter. 🖥️ 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-7:35 --> arrival & chats 7:35-8:20 --> lecture 8:20-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? dffc38a2-fe08-4e32-a865-8be7d71aebb2: An evening of storytelling with Dead Reckoning · There is an Oakland where the apparition of a woman appears in the mist at Joaquin Miller Park after dark, where the doorbell at the two-story Clarke Mansion at 16th and Castro begins clanging incessantly just after midnight, and where the Camron-Stanford House, one of the last Victorian homes that once lined Lake Merritt, has urged more than one living visitor to "get out." These are just a few of the stories that blur the line between the living and the dead that have lingered in Oakland for generations, passed between those who have witnessed things they still can't explain. Join us for an evening of storytelling with Beth Winegarner and Courtney Minick, hosts of Dead Reckoning : the podcast where death isn't the end of the story. The hosts of the San Francisco-based podcast will share local ghost stories, explore the legends surrounding some of Oakland's most notable residents, and uncover the histories that linger long after death. As the veil grows thin, come prepared to share your own story if you've experienced a haunting in the East Bay. You never know who, or what, might be listening. Courtney Minick is a storyteller with a career spanning technology, law, politics, and creative media based in San Francisco. She is the creator of Here Lies a Story a multi-platform storytelling project that explores history, folklore, and the way the buried past continues to shape our present including the Lost Cemeteries of San Francisco series . Beth Winegarner is a journalist and writer who’s contributed to the New York Times, the New Yorker, The Guardian, and many others. She is the author of several books, most recently San Francisco’s Forgotten Cemeteries: A Buried History and Swim Poems , and she is the co-host of the Dead Reckoning podcast.

In conversation with Daniela Blei.

111199a9-0c45-4b97-be4e-a8ac4ba4db33: In this new work, Adam Grant illuminates the surprising science behind building strong connections. Adam will be joined in conversation with Mark Rober, the creator of the STEM subscription box company CrunchLabs. A vibe—a special connection between people that creates a spark—is an engine of happiness and success. Yet building meaningful ties is one of the most pressing problems of our time. As social media forces face-to-face interaction behind digital screens, communication gets outsourced to AI, and the world becomes more polarized than ever, our loneliness crisis shows no signs of slowing. To reveal how we can forge faster, stronger, and longer bonds, Grant offers groundbreaking studies, expert insights, and myth-busting stories. Filled with the eye-opening takeaways that have brought millions of readers to his books, Vibe teaches us that similarity is not necessary for solidarity, chemistry doesn’t always happen quickly, and closeness doesn’t always take time. Along the way, Grant introduces us to a crew of astronauts who learned to trust people they don’t like, a comedy troupe that swears by taking time apart as a key to staying together, a band that grew closer by learning to fight more, and a journalist who designed a gathering that led to seventy-eight marriages. He also opens up about his personal struggles to find his place as a shy introvert and the lessons that propelled his transformation into an enthusiastic convener. Through these examples and more, Grant uncovers the keys to creating deeper relationships and tighter communities. Vibe will change how you approach your interactions. No matter how good you are at connecting, you can always get better—and help others get better too. As an organizational psychologist, Adam Grant is a leading expert on how we can find motivation and meaning, and live more generous and creative lives. He is the author of Think Again, Give and Take, Originals, Option B, and Power Move s and host of the podcast WorkLife. Mark Rober spent nine years as an engineer at NASA before becoming world famous on YouTube for his science and engineering projects. He is creator of the STEM subscription box company CrunchLabs. 6536f3cb-2838-47fc-b328-5d16f2783ec4: Multi-platinum Idol alum known for his big voice · America first fell in love with Clay Aiken's extraordinary voice and undeniable charisma on the second season of American Idol . His journey on the show became a cultural phenomenon, drawing nearly 40 million viewers to the finale—one of the highest-rated live television broadcasts of the 21st century—and launching one of the most successful recording careers to emerge from the series. Aiken's first single, “This Is The Night,” made history as the first track by a brand-new artist to enter the Billboard Hot 100 at No. 1, selling nearly 400,000 copies in its opening week. The follow-up, “Invisible,” became a defining early-2000s pop hit, climbing to No. 37 on the Hot 100 and earning RIAA Gold certification. His debut album, Measure of a Man , then entered the Billboard 200 at No. 1 and went multi-platinum, cementing him as one of pop music's biggest new artists. Among his early highlights was the chart-topping holiday album Merry Christmas with Love , which still holds the record for the largest debut week ever for a holiday album in the SoundScan era. During the first seven years of his recording career, Aiken sold more than six million albums worldwide while becoming a fixture on television and one of the most successful touring artists to emerge from the early 2000s pop era. His rich tenor voice, emotional delivery, and ability to effortlessly move between contemporary pop, adult contemporary, inspirational music, and timeless standards have earned him a loyal, multi-generational audience. Aiken’s career has extended well beyond the recording studio, including a Broadway run in Monty Python’s Spamalot and a reunion with Ruben Studdard in 2018 for Ruben & Clay’s First Annual Christmas Carol Family Fun Pageant Spectacular Reunion Show , which The New York Times hailed as “a Christmas miracle.” The pair reunited once again in 2023 for a tour celebrating the 20th anniversary of their landmark American Idol season before competing together on Fox’s The Masked Singer in 2024 as The Beets. Beyond his music, Aiken has long been an advocate for children with disabilities. Drawing on his pre-fame experience as a special education teacher, he co-founded the National Inclusion Project in 2003, which has since helped thousands of kids with disabilities take part in camps, after-school programs, and community activities in more than 40 states. He also spent a decade as a UNICEF ambassador, traveling to Afghanistan, Somalia, Indonesia, Mexico, Uganda, and Kenya to advocate for children's protection and education. In 2026, Aiken began an exciting new musical chapter with the release of his first new music in eighteen years. His single "Rewind," written by Colton Avery and Grammy Award-winning producer and songwriter Dave Audé and produced by Audé, marked both a return to recording and a fresh creative direction. The release coincided with Aiken's homecoming to the American Idol stage, where he debuted the song during the season finale. As he reintroduces himself to longtime fans and new listeners alike, Aiken is once again focused on what has always defined his career: exceptional songs, unforgettable performances, and one of the most recognizable voices in popular music. "Rewind" is the first offering from a new full-length studio album, due at the end of 2026, his first in nearly two decades.

a774e622-fd7a-4709-bd8c-2ff1dfb05fcd: Multi-platinum Idol alum known for his big voice · America first fell in love with Clay Aiken's extraordinary voice and undeniable charisma on the second season of American Idol . His journey on the show became a cultural phenomenon, drawing nearly 40 million viewers to the finale—one of the highest-rated live television broadcasts of the 21st century—and launching one of the most successful recording careers to emerge from the series. Aiken's first single, “This Is The Night,” made history as the first track by a brand-new artist to enter the Billboard Hot 100 at No. 1, selling nearly 400,000 copies in its opening week. The follow-up, “Invisible,” became a defining early-2000s pop hit, climbing to No. 37 on the Hot 100 and earning RIAA Gold certification. His debut album, Measure of a Man , then entered the Billboard 200 at No. 1 and went multi-platinum, cementing him as one of pop music's biggest new artists. Among his early highlights was the chart-topping holiday album Merry Christmas with Love , which still holds the record for the largest debut week ever for a holiday album in the SoundScan era. During the first seven years of his recording career, Aiken sold more than six million albums worldwide while becoming a fixture on television and one of the most successful touring artists to emerge from the early 2000s pop era. His rich tenor voice, emotional delivery, and ability to effortlessly move between contemporary pop, adult contemporary, inspirational music, and timeless standards have earned him a loyal, multi-generational audience. Aiken’s career has extended well beyond the recording studio, including a Broadway run in Monty Python’s Spamalot and a reunion with Ruben Studdard in 2018 for Ruben & Clay’s First Annual Christmas Carol Family Fun Pageant Spectacular Reunion Show , which The New York Times hailed as “a Christmas miracle.” The pair reunited once again in 2023 for a tour celebrating the 20th anniversary of their landmark American Idol season before competing together on Fox’s The Masked Singer in 2024 as The Beets. Beyond his music, Aiken has long been an advocate for children with disabilities. Drawing on his pre-fame experience as a special education teacher, he co-founded the National Inclusion Project in 2003, which has since helped thousands of kids with disabilities take part in camps, after-school programs, and community activities in more than 40 states. He also spent a decade as a UNICEF ambassador, traveling to Afghanistan, Somalia, Indonesia, Mexico, Uganda, and Kenya to advocate for children's protection and education. In 2026, Aiken began an exciting new musical chapter with the release of his first new music in eighteen years. His single "Rewind," written by Colton Avery and Grammy Award-winning producer and songwriter Dave Audé and produced by Audé, marked both a return to recording and a fresh creative direction. The release coincided with Aiken's homecoming to the American Idol stage, where he debuted the song during the season finale. As he reintroduces himself to longtime fans and new listeners alike, Aiken is once again focused on what has always defined his career: exceptional songs, unforgettable performances, and one of the most recognizable voices in popular music. "Rewind" is the first offering from a new full-length studio album, due at the end of 2026, his first in nearly two decades.

af63542e-bd6a-4f25-9a10-ea4cd2bca432: Embodiment Practices is an invitation to practice giving ourselves permission to arrive fully to where we are, and gently explore movement and stillness to care for our bodies and ourselves. This event happens each week at the Alembic. As an element of self attunement, we will practice making intuitive choices through a lens of self love, meaning that we are each making choices that are nourishing and responsive to ourselves as individuals in that moment. Part of this practice includes being very intentional and explicit about what kinds of choices we might consider, and being curious about how it feels to try them. There will be many options provided throughout, with guidance around how to navigate choice making, including if this is new to you or you are navigating a limitation or injury. There will be a corner of the room set aside in case you’d like to opt out of the facilitated structure and take a moment for yourself to rest. Opening Circle: We'll ground and check-in with whatever feels present for each of us. We get to welcome ourselves to come as we are. Warm Up: We'll do a guided, full-bodied warm up, tuning the instruments of our bodies and attention, giving ourselves time to shake it out, stretch, wiggle, and move through whatever feels stuck. Movements will be simple enough to follow along, giving us a chance to get out of our heads and drop into our bodies, regulating our nervous system. Drawing on contemporary dance and yoga, there will be flow, rhythm, and music. Movement Explorations: We'll explore movements that deepen our connection with our bodies and our intuition, focusing on concepts and areas of the body that can help us settle and release. Meditation: Finally, we'll settle into meditation and rest. Finding stillness might be sitting/standing/lying down and might include cozy props, having eyes open or closed, and suggestions to make yourself comfortable, including allowing some body movement within that quiet space. Please bring clothes you feel comfortable to move in. It’s recommended to bring long sleeves, long pants and socks with you, in case we are moving on the floor. Bring a journal if you’d like. About Suzanne (Zan): With three decades of contemporary/modern dance experience and 15 years of teaching, Suzanne Beahrs guides students in exploring movement as a pathway to deeper connection—with ourselves, our surroundings, and each other. Her classes blend technical training, creative expression, and guidance on being intentional with how we are each practicing. Her movement style was described by The New York Times as “grounded, silken.” In addition to contemporary dance, she is currently heavily influenced by house dance, contact improvisation, and mindfulness practices. She is currently on faculty at Shawl-Anderson Dance Center and teaches around the Bay Area, including ODC, the Berkeley Alembic, and Finnish Hall. Zan has previously taught extensively at Gibney, Elon University, ADF studios, and many more. She has shown her choreography in NY, NC, CA, AZ, MA, and MO, and performed in works by Ishika Seth, Mo Miner, and others. Beyond the studio, Suzanne is a facilitator and has worked as a DEI consultant. She also enjoys exploring writing, visual art, nature, music, and belonging. Education: MFA in Dance, NYU Tisch School of the Arts; BA in Geology, UC Berkeley Learn more about Suzanne, upcoming classes/workshops (contemporary, embodiment, improvisation, contact improvisation and private lessons): IG @suzannebeahrs suzannebeahrs.com

5e9bfbf7-79fb-4aa8-88b7-5c6716b495a2: Johansson Projects presents Night Watch, a striking exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Gregory Rick that boldly reimagines history painting through the fractured lens of contemporary life. Apocryphal yet deeply referential and incisive, Rick’s compositions collapse past events with biblical and mythological imagery, art-historical allusions, and capitalist spectacle into hypersaturated scenes that are at once facetious and unsettling. A burning cross, a feline maw, a tree of serpents, and tigers charging toward machine-gun fire populate a world where violence–and communal acts of resistance–appear both ancient and immediate. Figures clad in Fila jackets, yellow Hokas, and other recognizable markers of contemporary consumer culture anchor these frenetic compositions in the present. As a veteran, citizen, and subject, Rick draws upon collective memory to confront the cognitive dissonance of navigating everyday life amid recurring cycles of violence, surveillance, and oppression. In works such as Night Watch (We Got Us), Rembrandt’s civic militia meets Picasso’s Guernica, transforming the historical tableau into a contemporary cry for help and vision of mutual aid. A few of the works are painted and collaged on silk mesh, their transparencies exposing the layers of their construction and underscoring history itself as an unstable, assembled narrative. In Night Watch, Rick contends with what it means to stay woke and on watch in the 2020s. Night Watch runs from September 30 to October 31, 2026 with an opening reception Friday, October 2 from 5-8pm.

5bf183d3-902b-4eb3-a16a-882445eefcde: An interactive exploration of how we connect, protect ourselves, and relate to others. Why do we pull away when we want connection? Hold on tighter when we're afraid of losing someone? Or find ourselves repeating the same patterns in relationships, even when we know they're not serving us? Attachment styles can help us understand how we relate to others, but what if we approached them with curiosity instead of treating them as labels we need to fix? Just like our emotions, our attachment patterns may be trying to tell us something. What are they protecting us from? What do they need us to pay attention to? And what happens when we listen instead of judge? In this interactive gathering, we'll explore attachment theory while challenging some of the ways we use it to define ourselves and others. Through guided reflection, creative exercises, and small-group conversations, we'll get curious about the needs, fears, and experiences beneath our relationship patterns. This isn't about figuring out which attachment style you are or trying to become someone else. It's about understanding ourselves a little better, building awareness of how we show up in relationships, and exploring what more intentional, connected relationships might look like. No expertise or personal sharing required. Just bring yourself, your curiosity, and a willingness to explore together. Because our patterns may tell a story, but they don't have to define what comes next. Hosted by the You Aren't Alone Project, creating space to talk about the mental health struggles most of us keep quiet. Through art, creative expression and storytelling, people find the words for what they're carrying and discover they're not the only one.

1f7b1f0b-9bd6-4770-b495-0fc0ba766bc9: From the author of prescient best seller and classic Reclaiming Conversation , Sherry Turkle, comes an urgent warning about how our ever-increasing reliance on human-like AI chatbots is eroding our capacity for empathy, caring, and the very qualities that make us human. Sherry will be joined in conversation by national bestselling author Tiffany Shlain. If social media came for our attention, artificial intelligence is now coming for our capacity for attachment. Chatbots that speak to us in a human voice offer themselves as best friends, lovers, and psychotherapists. As of 2025, over 70% of teens and nearly one-third of US adults rely on AI for companionship and emotional support, with many preferring these chatbot relationships over human ones. When we talk to chatbots in these roles, as intimate machines, we accept as sufficient what machines can offer: the mere performance of intimacy, empathy, and love. We begin to think that pretend empathy is empathy enough. We redefine human capacities for care, solitude, and intimacy in terms of what machines can do. Sherry Turkle, the psychologist who pioneered our understanding of human-computer relationships, calls the new culture of chatbots artificial intimacy,our new AI. Through compelling storytelling, framed by Turkle’s decades of experience as a chronicler and analyst of digital culture, Artificial Intimacy evokes the seductive and beguiling nature of chatbots. They can organize our calendars, plan our travel, or analyze our stock picks, all with an efficiency that outstrips what a person might do. And then, they promise to be more — to be our “perfect” companion. They will always be there for us, listen to us, and support us — and ask for nothing in return. But these intimate machines, warns Turkle, are producing a generation more alienated, depressed, and lonely than ever before. More than that, we become less equipped to reverse course — machine relationships do not offer practice for getting along with people. Artificial Intimacy is unique in how it traces our new habit of talking to machines through the lifecycle — from children’s earliest attachments to how we face death. But technology, by offering to do everything, teaches us that we neither need nor have the capacity to take risks, have hard conversations, struggle through uncertainty or insecurity, or rely on our own faculties and judgment. Turkle has spent decades studying how digital technologies isolate us from one another. Now, in her long-awaited follow-up to Reclaiming Conversation, she offers both a cautionary tale and a roadmap for reclaiming our humanity in the age of AI. Sherry Turkle is the Abby Rockefeller Mauzé Professor of the Social Studies of Science and Technology at MIT and the founding director of the MIT Initiative on Technology and Self. A leading expert in humans’ relationship with digital objects, she continues to revolutionize our understanding of the role of technology on psychology and culture. She is the New York Times bestselling author of Alone Together,Reclaiming Conversation, and The Empathy Diaries. Turkle is a recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship, a Rockefeller Humanities Fellowship, the Harvard Centennial Medal, and is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. She received a joint doctorate in sociology and personality psychology from Harvard University and is a licensed clinical psychologist. Honored by "Newsweek" as one of the "Women Shaping the 21st Century," Tiffany Shlain is an interdisciplinary artist, Emmy-nominated filmmaker, national bestselling author, and the founder of the Webby Awards. Working across mediums, Shlain's work explores ideas in feminism, philosophy, technology, neuroscience, and nature. Her work has been shown at institutions including Museum of Modern Art, Sundance Film Festival, and US embassies globally. Her ongoing moveable monument Dendrofemonology: A Feminist History Tree Ring has been installed on the National Mall in D.C. and Madison Square Park in NY and serves to shine a light on women’s rights. Her recent collaborative exhibition with Ken Goldberg Ancient Wisdom for a Future Ecology: Trees, Time & Technology , was presented as part of the Getty’s PST ART: Art & Science Collide initiative in Los Angeles and continues to travel most recently in San Francisco at di Rosa Center for Contemporary Art and was named by Artnet as one of the "Must-See Museum Exhibitions." Her awards and distinctions include selection by the Albert Einstein Foundation for their Genius100 list, the Neil Postman Award for Career Achievement in Intellectual Activity, and inclusion in NPR’s list of best commencement speeches for her speech at UCBerkeley. Shlain’s national bestselling book, 24/6: Giving up Screens One Day a Week to Get More Time, Creativity, and Connection , received the Marshall McLuhan Outstanding Book Award. She has been writing a monthly newsletter, "Breakfast @ Tiffany's" for 30 years. Shlain is represented by Nancy Hoffman Gallery in New York and lives and works in the San Francisco Bay Area. 215f28a2-31c2-4e42-9743-7ffef5d5e990: "What an incredible life of triumph and tragedy, faith, and love." — Anderson Cooper, #1 New York Times- bestselling author of Vanderbilt We are pleased to welcome Kerry Kennedy as she shares a vivid, intimate biography of her mother, American icon Ethel Kennedy, told through her firsthand memories and exclusive access to Ethel’s personal papers. Kerry will be joined in conversation by KQED News politics correspondent Marisa Lagos. When her husband Robert F. Kennedy was killed in 1968, Ethel Skakel Kennedy—then pregnant with their eleventh child—drew national attention for her grace, dignity, and resolute commitment to furthering his work in human rights, even in her grief. But as her daughter Kerry witnessed, Ethel was so much more than a dutiful wife and keeper of Robert's legacy of service. She was courageous, curious, compassionate, boisterous, and witty, always guided by faith and an instinct for speaking truth to power. Kerry delves into her own memories, her family's recollections, and her mother's private papers, describing: Ethel's family's journey from a working-class Chicago background to life in tony Greenwich, Connecticut Ethel's fairytale romance with Kerry's father RFK—a courtship that inspired a Taylor Swift song half a century later How the bold, athletic Ethel quickly became "more Kennedy than the Kennedys" The years on the famed family properties in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, and the Hickory Hill estate in Virginia, where Kerry and her ten siblings grew up amidst presidents and politicians, Olympians and Hollywood stars, and a rambunctious menagerie of pet animals Moments of pain and loss—RFK’s death just five years after that of his brother; and the tragic deaths of two of Kerry’s siblings Ethel’s unflagging commitment to global human rights causes that carried on through the decades Ethel Kennedy inspires us to reject cynicism and to live bigger and bolder. The book includes 24 pages of color photographs. "Ethel Kennedy was more than the anchoring matriarch of a history-making family. She was a force who helped to shape the turbulent times she lived in with a set of values that can serve as a beacon in our own. In this beautifully written book, Kerry Kennedy amplifies the strength of her mother’s example and gives us hope that we, too, can rise above." - Henry Louis Gates, Jr., Alphonse Fletcher University Professor, Harvard University "Kerry Kennedy has written a beautiful and moving account of her remarkable mother. What an incredible life of triumph and tragedy, faith, and love." - Anderson Cooper, CNN anchor and #1 New York Times bestselling author of Vanderbilt and Astor "Hers was one of the most tumultuous of American lives, led in public in years of tragedy, yet Ethel Kennedy never lost hope. Sustained by her faith and by her family, Mrs. Kennedy refused to surrender to the darkness; instead, she forever sought the light. Kerry Kennedy's moving biography of her mother tells us this story with warmth and insight, reminding us anew of our common duty to make gentle the life of this world." - Jon Meacham, #1 New York Times bestselling author of The Soul of America and And There Was Light "The Kennedy clan has had more than its share of tragedy... but this is a joyful remembrance, an intimate portrayal of Ethel, who until her death remained the north star of the family, and a force for social justice and human rights." - Nina Totenberg, NPR correspondent and New York Times bestselling author of Dinners with Ruth Kerry Kennedy is a human rights lawyer, activist, New York Times -bestselling author, and daughter of Ethel Skakel Kennedy and Robert F. Kennedy. Kerry is the president of Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights, the organization Ethel founded in 1968 to continue Robert's unfinished work, and served as chair for the Amnesty International USA Leadership Council for over a decade. During her forty years working in human rights, she has led hundreds of delegations and negotiated with leaders around the globe. She is the author of three previous books: Robert F. Kennedy: Ripples of Hope ; Speak Truth to Power; and Being Catholic Now . In 2022, she and Shafer moderated the only gubernatorial debate in California. She has worked at the San Francisco Chronicle, San Francisco Examiner and Los Angeles Times. A UC Santa Barbara graduate, she lives in San Francisco with her two sons and husband.
