7386dcd9-0d77-4373-91d6-33aa8c4771bb: 🌿 About Event Conversations With My AI: How to Work With a Digital Thought Partner Most of us use AI like a vending machine. Type in a request, get back something generic, and walk away a little unimpressed. But the people getting real value from it are doing something different. They aren’t writing better prompts. They’re having better conversations. This gathering explores what changes when you stop commanding a tool and start thinking out loud with a partner. We’ll hold a few paradoxes together: you have to think differently about AI, and you also have to talk to it the way you’d talk to a thoughtful person. It isn’t a person. Treating it a bit like one is still how you get the most from it. You’ll learn a simple conversation starter, try it on something that actually matters in your life, and leave with one question that changes every conversation after it: “What is it I am not asking you that I should?” Why now? Because AI is moving into everything we do, faster than we can reflect on it. It can make us sharper, or it can quietly take over our judgment. The difference is how we show up to the conversation. Context is king, and you are the only one who can give it yours. 🕰 Flow / Schedule [5:30 – 6:00] Arrival [6:00 – 6:20] Think Different, Think the Same: the paradoxes of working with AI [6:20 – 6:35] The Conversation Starter: seven parts, one question [6:35 – 7:00] Your Turn: a real conversation with your AI about something you care about [7:00 – 7:20] Small Group Share: what surprised you, what shifted [7:20 – 8:00] Closing + Mingling 👥 Facilitator Name: Chris Heuer Bio: Chris has been in conversation with technology since he coined “context is king” at his first startup in 1995, and he was an IBM futurist working with Watson long before AI was a dinner-table topic. He’s writing a book, Conversations With My AI, about using AI to think more clearly, not less, and he talks with his own AI, Q, every day. Website: HTTPS://linkedin.com/in/chrisheuer 💫 Who This Is For This space is for anyone curious about AI, from people who’ve barely tried it to daily users who feel they’re getting generic answers back. No technical background needed. It’s especially for people who want AI to help them think, reflect and create without giving up what makes their perspective their own. 🎒 What to Bring A laptop or phone with any AI you can use (the free versions of ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini all work but paid accounts are better). One real thing you’re working on, wondering about or stuck on. A notebook if you like to write things down. 🏛 About The Commons The Commons is a community-based "Fourth Place" that catalyzes each member's path to authenticity, full self-expression, and aliveness - rooted in the belief that community is essential to that journey. Located in the heart of San Francisco, we are redefining what it means to gather, work, and connect. By day, we're a playful co-working space; by night, a vibrant community meeting house. 🚪 Arrival Info The Commons is located at 550 Laguna St, San Francisco (corner of Hayes & Laguna). Enter via the stairway under The Commons sign at the basement level.

b3df0ddf-854e-4fad-9723-2dd474efe327: An inspiring and eminently useful guide to the art of letter writing, including prompts and exercises to help deepen our most important connections and heal old wounds, by a beloved “letter midwife.” Unfinished Business: Writing the 5 Essential Letters of Your Life by Frish Brandt is the guide we’ve all been waiting for on letter writing, the next personal step after reading books centered on the art of letters. Frish will be joined in conversation by the Chronicle’s arts and culture columnist, Tony Bravo. Given this zeitgeist-like moment around letters, UNFINISHED BUSINESS fills a gap in the available literature. Frish is a letter writing midwife who teaches essential letter writing at Stanford University’s School of Medicine, and with UNFINISHED BUSINESS, she presents the work of her life: how to write five essential letters (Thank you, I’m sorry, I miss you, I love you, and Goodbye) that provide her clients, students, and readers with a path forward to never let the most essential messages of our life remain unsaid. We all have unfinished business: thank-you notes we meant to write, goodbyes we never spoke, apologies we never managed to give. Here to help us put those words on paper, letter midwife Frish Brandt provides singular guidance on how to write the five fundamental missives that make up the meaning of our lives: Thank you, I’m sorry, I miss you, I love you, and Goodbye. With real-world examples from her experience of teaching at Stanford Medical School, Harvard Divinity School, and in workshops and individual sessions around the country, she weaves practical writing prompts with gentle reflections on grief, connection, forgiveness, and closure, offering the tools—and the courage—to help us write what we have long held inside. At once a permission slip, a guidebook, and a lyrical ode to the power of the written word, Unfinished Business is a book to read, to write alongside, and to return to again and again. “Unfinished Business is a pragmatic, empathetic, urgent call to stop avoiding the hardest conversations and start enjoying the world beyond hurt and regret. A true service to readers.”—Kelly Corrigan, New York Times bestselling author of Tell Me More and The Middle Place “This is an antidote to despair and a practice of peace, a book of intimacy and radical reflection. Frish Brandt is a magical presence in the world.”—Terry Tempest Williams, author of The Glorians and When Women Were Birds “Frish Brandt has tapped into a secret vein of gold lurking in every human heart. Even the best-designed and well-lived life has some unfinished business. Kindly, compassionately, and with unexpected ease, Brandt reveals how to find and finish your essential letter. Completing your letter is life-changing—and it awaits you in these pages. Don’t miss it.”—Dave Evans, New York Times bestselling author of Designing Your Life, Cofounder of Stanford Life Design Lab “Unfinished Business offers a way to come safely closer to the unfathomable, bringing light to emptiness and love to fear. Brandt’s work is an extraordinary tool to help heal, connect, and transform your relationships. Her work is altogether a gorgeous phenomenon, and I’ve seen it work wonders time and again.”—Dr. B.J Miller, Director of the Center for Living and Dying, author of A Beginners Guide to the End “Frish Brandt evokes relief, wonder, and immense gratitude in all who encounter her letter writing practice. Unfinished Business is a book for every one of us.”—Nancy Horan, New York Times bestselling author of Loving Frank and The House of Lincoln Frish Brandt teaches essential letter writing at Stanford University’s School of Medicine and to individuals and institutions around the country, including museums, universities, hospitals, and caregiving associations. She worked in the arts for more than four decades before becoming a full-time Letter Midwife. She lives and writes in San Francisco. Tony Bravo is the Chronicle’s arts and culture columnist. He joined the Chronicle in 2015 as a reporter for the Style section: His beats include visual art, LGBTQ issues and the culture of clothes. Bravo is also an adjunct instructor at the City College of San Francisco Fashion Department, where he teaches journalism. With photographer Stephen Lam Bravo is the recipient of the 2026 Excellence in Online Journalism Award from the NLGJA Association of LGBTQ+ Journalists. d0dea6d9-7de5-4936-9645-60a749306bd4: LOCATION GLBT Historical Society Museum 4127 18th Street San Francisco, CA 94114 ADMISSION $10; Free for GLBT Historical Society Members RSVP and reserve your tickets here The GLBT Historical Society presents a screening of short films and archival footage that highlight the beauty, grief, joy, and community found in the spaces queer and trans people call home. In conjunction with the current exhibition, Where We Made Room , the program will showcase films and footage centered upon the thesis of queer space and carving out room for ourselves. The screening will be followed by a discussion between Where We Made Room artist and curator Aleo Landeta and filmmaker Jenni Olson ( 575 Castro Street) on these themes and their work. About the Films Image courtesy of Frameline Distribution 575 Castro St. (2008) - a film by Jenni Olson 7 min. A powerful elegy from acclaimed queer filmmaker Jenni Olson, 575 Castro St. reveals the play of light and shadow upon the walls of the Castro Camera Store set for Gus Van Sant’s Academy Award-winning film Milk as we hear excerpts from the audio-cassette that Harvey Milk recorded to be played, “in the event of my death by assassination.” The film features Milk’s now legendary line, “Ya gotta give ‘em hope,” and his eloquent, timely, and timeless denouncement of right-wing anti-LGBTQ hate (calling out Anita Bryant and California Senator John Briggs). The tape was made in November 1977 (after Milk’s election to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, which made him one of the first openly gay elected officials in the United States). Milk and San Francisco Mayor George Moscone were assassinated by SF Supervisor Dan White one year later, in November 1978. Commissioned by FilmInFocus.com to be showcased online in conjunction with the theatrical release of Milk , 575 Castro St. world premiered at the 2009 Sundance Film Festival and has played at festivals and museums across the globe. About the filmmaker: Jenni Olson is an acclaimed queer filmmaker, film historian, and writer. Her contemplative 16mm essay films have screened internationally to awards and acclaim. Among Jenni’s many achievements she has been recognized with the prestigious Special TEDDY Award at the Berlin Film Festival for her decades of work championing LGBTQ film and filmmakers. She is now in post-production on her third feature-length essay film, Tell Me Everything Will Be Okay (2027) and an essayistic memoir of the same name. Image courtesy of Ira Sachs Last Address (2009) - a film by Ira Sachs 9 min. Keith Haring, Robert Mapplethorpe, Norman René, Peter Hujar, Ethyl Eichelberger, Felix Gonzalez-Torres, Cookie Mueller, Klaus Nomi....the list of New York artists who died of AIDS over the last 30 years is countless, and the loss immeasurable. In Last Address , filmmaker Ira Sachs (The Delta, Married Life , and the 2005 Sundance Grand Jury Prize winning Forty Shades of Blue ), who first moved to the city himself in 1984, uses images of the exteriors of the houses, apartment buildings, and lofts where these and others were living at the time of their deaths to mark the disappearance of a generation. The elegiac film is both a remembrance of that loss, as well as an evocation of the continued presence of their work in our lives and culture. About the filmmaker: Ira Sachs is a NYC-based filmmaker whose feature films include The Man I Love, Peter Hujar’s Day, Passages, Frankie, Little Men, Love is Strange, Keep the Lights On, and Forty Shades of Blue. A Rockefeller, Guggenheim, MacDowell, and Yaddo Fellow, Sachs’s work is held in the permanent collections of New York’s Museum of Modern Art and the Whitney. He is also the Founding Director of Queer|Art, an arts organization built to support mentorship for LGBTQ+ artists and born out of the recognition of a generation of artists and audiences lost to the AIDS crisis. Image courtesy of Frameline Distribution Ifé (1993) - a film by Lenn Keller 5 min. Written, produced and directed by H. Lenn Keller, Ifé chronicles a day in the life of a black French lesbian in San Francisco. This humorous short pays stylistic homage to Jean Luc Godard's 50's film, Breathless. Ifé won Best Short Film at the '94 Madrid International Women's Film Festival, and is distributed by Frameline Films and is also available on a video compilation called Dyke Drama, distributed by Wolfe Video . Ifé premiered at the San Francisco Lesbian & Gay Int'l Film Festival in 1993, and has screened in festivals internationally, including KQED's Living Room Festival, the London Lesbian & Gay Film Festival, Berlin Film Festival, SXSW, and Women in the Director's Chair. About the filmmaker: Lenn Keller was a photographer, filmmaker, and activist who played a significant role in documenting and promoting lesbian culture in the United States. In 2014, she founded the Bay Area Lesbian Archives, recognizing the critical need for Bay Area lesbian history to be preserved. Lenn’s vision was a physical and online archives dedicated to the preservation of the richly diverse lesbian history of the Bay Area -- an archives where anyone could access materials about a community that contributed so much to the Bay Area and California. A core group of women who shared Lenn Keller’s vision came together to help make the archives a reality. Excerpts from the Daniel A. Smith and Queer Blue Light Videotapes Collection In 2021, the GLBT Historical Society digitized a unique archival collection, the Daniel A. Smith and Queer Blue Light Videotapes , which consists of nearly 100 half-inch videotapes recorded by the Queer Blue Light (QBL) Collective. QBL was a grassroots guerilla project that documented the politics and culture of the local LGBTQ community in the 1970s. While the majority of the tapes document QBL activities, they also contain footage by QBL members of friends relaxing together and living everyday life. For this program, we will screen excerpts from some of our favorite tapes, including footage from a 1980 “Leap Day” dinner party, a home drag runway show, and more. 'I begin to take an interest in life,' she writes at a moment few would dare (this is not the only audacious moment here, far from it). 7fb44a2b-ddd7-4930-a072-3238477df3ad: View from the Precipice: A Retrospective Monograph · For over forty years, David Maisel has made work that spans photography, painting, and video, situating himself above the surface—of the Earth, of the canvas—in such a way that his unmistakable sensibility transcends any given medium. His aerial photographs and video installations address the aesthetics and environmental impact of landscapes radically transformed by mineral extraction, natural resource reclamation, desertification, and military weapons testing. Seen through Maisel’s lens, these sites become abstractions that pulse with other-worldly colors and geometries — endangered landscapes imbued with a disquieting allure. Across each series, Maisel uses beauty “as a tool, a device for helping us focus our attention.” His large-scaled, immersive abstract paintings respond to catastrophic climate change events such as wildfire and flood. In each of these mediums, Maisel’s images are spatially ambiguous and destabilizing, and describe a world wholly remade by human activity. View from the Precipice , a new monograph published by Radius Books, is the most comprehensive survey of Maisel’s career to date and is the first to place his paintings and lens-based works in direct dialogue. The volume begins with a chronological primer offering both technical insight and anecdotal background information, provided by Maisel, for projects spanning four decades of his practice. Essays by art historian Alexander Nemerov and writer Geoff Manaugh and a conversation between Maisel and novelist Samantha Harvey weave through the visual chapters that comprise the second half of the book. Together, the images and texts offer an expansive account of one of the most distinctive artistic practices of the past several decades. This evening’s event will bring Maisel, Nemerov, and Clio’s founder Timothy Don together in conversation around the themes of Maisel’s practice and the development of his new survey monograph. DAVID MAISEL is a visual artist. He is the recipient of Fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Getty Research Institute, and the National Endowment for the Arts, and has been an Artist in Residence at the Headlands Center for the Arts, among other awards and honors. His work is in the permanent collections of more than fifty museums internationally and has been the subject of eight monographs, the latest being a survey on his career, View from the Precipice , published by Radius Books in fall 2026. Maisel’s photographs were featured this year at the National Gallery of Art in Beneath the Surface: Mining and American Photography . His series Spiraling , on severe drought conditions at the Great Salt Lake, is being developed as a solo traveling museum exhibition by the Barry Lopez Foundation for Art and Environment. ALEXANDER NEMEROV is the author of Fierce Poise: Helen Frankenthaler and 1950s New York (Penguin), praised by Vogue as one of its best books of 2021 and a finalist for the National Book Critics Circle Award in Biography that year. Nemerov’s most recent book, The Forest: A Fable of America in the 1830s , has been called by the novelist Annie Proulx “one of the richest books ever to come my way…Deeply beautiful, achingly painful, and astonishingly tender.” Nemerov is featured in Nathaniel Kahn’s HBO documentary about the art world, The Price of Everything (2018). At Stanford University, Nemerov is the Carl and Marilynn Thoma Provostial Professor in the Arts and Humanities and served as chair of the Department of Art and Art History from 2015 to 2021.

Online ticket sales close 2 hours before each performance, and additional tickets may be available for purchase at the door. 75 minutes | No Intermission | Ages 14+ Please do not bring infants to the show Winner 2015 Theater Bay Area Award Outstanding Production of a Solo Play This show is an unrelenting look at a ten-day period in Copeland’s life—the mandatory ten-day waiting period before he could lay his hands on the newly purchased gun with which he planned to take his own life. Even in the midst of this tragedy, however, his wonderful sense of the comedy of life does not desert him (how much should he spend on the gun?), indeed serves him insidiously well as a buffer against the grim reality of his intention. Copeland hopes this very personal, and ultimately redemptive, story will reach people who struggle with depression—often called the last stigmatized disease—as well as their families and loved ones. Interspersed with interviews with other sufferers, the play, like so many Marsh stories, also offers outsiders an insider’s view, thereby expanding our understanding and, hopefully, our humanity. As critic Sam Hurwitt put it in The Idiolect: “ It’s a play I’d strongly recommend to anyone who is now or has ever been depressed or who knows someone in that situation. But honestly, it’s such a strong piece that I’d recommend it just as heartily to anyone who’s ever been human .” Artist Biography Brian Copeland has been in show business since he first stepped on the comedy stage at the tender age of 18. Soon he was headlining clubs and concerts across the country and opening for such artists as Smokey Robinson, The Temptations, Ringo Starr, and the Queen of soul Aretha Franklin, in venues from The Universal Amphitheater to Constitution Hall in Washington DC. He spent five years as co-host of San Francisco FOX affiliate KTVU breakfast program Mornings on 2 and two years hosting San Francisco ABC affiliate KGO’s Emmy Award winning afternoon talker 7Live. In 1995, ABC affiliate KGO Radio premiered “The Brian Copeland Show”. It’s unique mix of talk and entertainment soon made it the most listened to program in its time slot. Copeland branched out into theater in 2004 with his first solo play, NOT A GENUINE BLACK MAN. Hiromi will be in Japan February 1-21 but will resume classes when she gets back Hiromi Vardy is a certified Zen Shiatsu, Yang style Tai Chi, and Zhineng Qigong healer and practitioner. She first encountered Tai Chi in 1973 while studying theater design and performance art in London. Initially drawn to the beauty of the movements, she soon discovered that the practice had a profound effect on her consciousness, awakening a deep interest in the healing arts. While collaborating on stage with dancers in London, Hiromi began treating injuries in overworked bodies. In 1976, after a serious accident that resulted in loss of circulation in her leg and concern about possible amputation, she turned to daily Tai Chi practice, self-massage, and treatment from a Japanese acupuncturist. This experience became a turning point in her healing journey and led her back to Japan, where she studied Shiatsu at the Namikoshi School and trained at the Zen Shiatsu Center under Shizuto Masunaga. After moving to the United States with her family in 1987, Hiromi continued deepening her practice and teaching. During a period of significant stress later in her life, she encountered Master Ming Tong Gu and began studying Zhineng (wisdom healing) Qigong under his guidance, eventually becoming licensed to teach. The healing shift she experienced through this practice was profound and continues to inform her teaching today. Since 2013, Hiromi has been dedicated to teaching Zhineng Qigong, expanding her offerings to include online classes in 2020. Her work invites students to explore the foundations of Qigong and Tai Chi as embodied, healing practices that cultivate awareness, vitality, and resilience.

7b1c05c5-5bb0-4867-98e9-f60823e6cc12: Retired LAPD detective Harry Bosch delves into the darkest chapter of his past in this electric thriller from #1 New York Times bestselling author Michael Connelly. When Harry Bosch was eleven years old, his mother was murdered and he became a ward of the state, housed in MacLaren Children’s Center, a notorious facility where abuse was rampant. Decades after its closure, a massive class action lawsuit has resulted in a multibillion-dollar settlement for former residents. But when Bosch’s half-brother, defense attorney Mickey Haller, brings him word that Harry is entitled to $400,000, Bosch says he doesn’t want the money. He wants justice. News of the settlement awakens his memories of a place he had hoped never to revisit, and a boy named Chops, a fellow inmate who wound up dead. Chops’s body was found in a hidden space under a staircase that the staff used to discipline their charges. The kids knew it only as “the hollow.” But Chops’s death was covered up and never solved. Now Bosch knows he must reopen the investigation and learn the truth, even if the killer is long dead. As Bosch digs into the files, he picks up the trail of a predator who not only survived, but went on to a life of vicious crime. Forced to face a history that both scarred him and launched him on his mission as a cop, Bosch must bring down a sadistic criminal and finally put to rest the demons of his past. d4fff399-7e06-40c5-bbae-e400df519b0f: Join us on Friday, October 30 at 6:30pm when we welcome Kirk Lombard for the release of his book, The Shadow Stream, at Sports Basement Presidio! Refreshments and live music followed by an author talk and book signing Free to attend, Please RSVP Praise for The Shadow Stream "Kirk Lombard’s The Shadow Stream is a book of great originality, a book like no other, propelled by brilliant storytelling and original thinking (and fish!) that will engage readers of all ages—a perfect family book."⸺Mark Kurlansky, author of Cod and Salt and World Without Fish "The Shadow Stream is a book that will change your mind: brilliantly told, it is an odyssey and an oddity, a tale that defies expectations and redefines the notion of hero." ⸺Annie Barrows, bestselling co-author of The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society and author of the Ivy & Bean series About The Shadow Stream A throwback to family reads of yore, this epic follows a troubled boy and a host of hilariously vexed animals who must save a river before it’s dammed, so they can save themselves. Gabriel (“G” for short) is wasting away in the Abiddon County Juvenile Center when he’s introduced to the Shongunk River by his dying uncle. The river valley—trash-heaped but chock-full of mysteries and fish—wins G over. But, as G has learned, good things can’t last. The Shongunk is scheduled to be dammed by a local developer. In a matter of days, it will cease flowing, and all of the talkative creatures who live there in the river valley will be as homeless as G. Just as G decides it’s no time to accept his fate, so too do the animals. To inspire an uprising, a young trout is nominated to make a fateful journey up the river; a raccoon swears a violent oath against humans; and a newly sober buck leads his skittish flock out of harm’s way. Together with G, they show that good can triumph and that there is power in all of us, even the smallest minnow. About Kirk Lombard Kirk Lombard is an author, angler, sustainable fishmonger, and tuba player who once worked inside the juvenile rehabilitation system. His first book, the award-winning Sea Forager's Guide to the Northern California Coast, was described as "poetry" for fish by NPR. He lives in the Bay Area with his family, raising his children on herring and sea shanties.

7b26acbe-557e-4c68-bdc4-28d2bfdf91c5: In Death Sangha we will play with the fantasies of both eternalism and nihilism, and experiment with the awakening that lies beyond both. Spirituality • Mysticism At its core, all spirituality is about Death. The Buddha, Buddhism, and meditation practice have always been deeply concerned with Death, dying, and mortality. Every living thing has to face the reality of Death, and yet in modern meditation circles there is almost no confrontation with this ultimate question and primordial mystery. Instead there is denial, obfuscation, minimalizing, and—essentially—painting a smiley face on the whole subject. If that seems ridiculous to you, as well as something that misses the whole point, then Death Sangha is for you. In Death Sangha we meet to honor the fact of Death, to face our own and others’ mortality in a clear, unsullied, fierce, humble, and gracious manner. In Death Sangha we will play with the fantasies of both eternalism and nihilism, and experiment with the awakening that lies beyond both. We will confront experiences such as Cosmic Horror, Cosmic Shame, and Total Meaninglessness. We will also engage with the mythological, occult, psychological, historical, and phenomenological aspects of this most important topic. And of course we will do plenty of meditation. Death Sangha is not a spectacle for the curious, nor is it a soporific for the frightened. In Death Sangha, you will confront your deepest fears, your most difficult warts and shadows, and learn to meditate with the reality of your own imminent demise. It has often been said that until we truly accept Death, we cannot actually live. In Death Sangha, we will not meekly accept Death, but rather learn to passionately and exuberantly dance with this final and most intimate partner. Taft is a non-traditional meditation teacher, bestselling author, and podcaster. He has often taught meditation at Google, worked on curriculum development for SIYLI, and is currently core faculty at Wisdom Labs, in San Francisco. Michael is also a featured teacher on the Simple Habit app, and an official advisor to the Therapeutic Neuroscience Lab. 1700ddfd-bf06-4282-91f3-332cc0f753d8: Master of the trumpet and flugelhorn · Over three decades, 20+ albums, and more than 20 #1 Billboard hits into one of contemporary jazz's most inspiring careers, Rick Braun remains a master of the trumpet and flugelhorn. The Allentown, Pennsylvania-born Braun began playing music in elementary school, ultimately winding up at the prestigious Eastman School of Music. There, he hooked up with like-minded musicians to form the jazz-fusion combo Auracle. Braun's first big break came when he composed "Here With Me," a Top 20 hit for REO Speedwagon. He soon became a highly regarded pop sideman, touring and recording with the likes of Rod Stewart, War, Sade, Tina Turner, Natalie Cole, Glenn Frey, Tom Petty, and Crowded House. The trumpeter became a Smooth Jazz fixture with his 1993 debut, Intimate Secrets, and broke through with 1995's Beat Street. His records have consistently ranked in the Top 10 of Billboard's Contemporary Jazz Chart, with Kisses in the Rain reigning at #1 for 11 weeks. The recipient of numerous awards, he shared a Best Collaboration honor with Boney James for their hit Shake It Up, and his duo project RnR with Richard Elliot also hit #1. He's recorded three albums with the all-star trio BWB alongside Grammy winners Kirk Whalum and Norman Brown. 196fec8c-311a-4b32-a3c7-e8a0b4d5e971: Master of the trumpet and flugelhorn · Over three decades, 20+ albums, and more than 20 #1 Billboard hits into one of contemporary jazz's most inspiring careers, Rick Braun remains a master of the trumpet and flugelhorn. The Allentown, Pennsylvania-born Braun began playing music in elementary school, ultimately winding up at the prestigious Eastman School of Music. There, he hooked up with like-minded musicians to form the jazz-fusion combo Auracle. Braun's first big break came when he composed "Here With Me," a Top 20 hit for REO Speedwagon. He soon became a highly regarded pop sideman, touring and recording with the likes of Rod Stewart, War, Sade, Tina Turner, Natalie Cole, Glenn Frey, Tom Petty, and Crowded House. The trumpeter became a Smooth Jazz fixture with his 1993 debut, Intimate Secrets, and broke through with 1995's Beat Street. His records have consistently ranked in the Top 10 of Billboard's Contemporary Jazz Chart, with Kisses in the Rain reigning at #1 for 11 weeks. The recipient of numerous awards, he shared a Best Collaboration honor with Boney James for their hit Shake It Up, and his duo project RnR with Richard Elliot also hit #1. He's recorded three albums with the all-star trio BWB alongside Grammy winners Kirk Whalum and Norman Brown. A much-in-demand producer, he has delivered #1 radio hits with artists including David Benoit, Marc Antoine, Peter White, and the late Jeff Golub. His most recent release, Rick Braun Plays Chuck Mangione, is his first-ever tribute album, honoring one of his musical heroes. Braun says with a grin, "I am one of the luckiest guys in the world. 83822244-d8fe-40a2-af4b-1490baf5a426: What if we stopped treating death as the thing we're not supposed to talk about? Death Day: Facing Mortality, Mourning, and the Strife of Endings is an Alembic gathering for turning toward the inevitable with curiosity, irreverence, reverence, and even defiance. Through talks, storytelling, and conversation, we'll explore death not as an abstraction, but as a force that shapes how we live, love, grieve, create, and make meaning. The day includes three presentations and is hosted by Maria Mangini. *Facing the Wave: Ecological Grief as an Act of Reverence with Kirra Swenerton As an ecologist and healer, Swenton has been asked to bear witness to the extraordinary loss of biodiversity that defines our moment, while continuing to plant seeds and lay down prayers for an uncertain future. Through stories from the wild world, they'll explore what dreams, gurus, ancestors, butterflies, and plants can teach us about living with loss. Here, ecological grief can become more than an expression of despair, and grow into an act of reverence: a way of honoring what is dying while remaining in relationship with what is still alive. * Mourning Dress: Making Grief Visible with Maria Mangini Grief may be universal, but mourning is cultural. This illustrated lecture traces the visible language of bereavement from the Middle Ages to the present, exploring mourning dress, etiquette, sumptuary laws, textiles, colors, and the elaborate rules that once governed how (and for how long) the bereaved were expected to signal their loss. We'll look at how mourning customs differ across social classes, how they reflect status and aspiration, and why making grief visible can matter to those living through it. *Gliomancy: Acknowledging and Resisting the Proximity of Thanatos with Tom Banger What would you do if you were diagnosed with a "terminal," "incurable" condition? In 2023, Tom Banger was diagnosed with brain cancer and began developing what he calls gliomancy: a syncretic mashup of mysticism, shamanism, Stoicism, Shinto, Zen, pop psychology, and the Kübler-Ross grief model. Drawing on performance art, ritual, humor, and what he calls "medical tourism," Banger has spent three years confronting mortality with dignity, courage, and poise. Part lecture, part spell, part ceremony, this participatory session asks how we might meet unwelcome news — and our own impermanence — without surrendering our sense of agency. Teacher Bios: Kirra Swenerton (she/they) is an edge-walker, healing artist and scientist. Kirra runs Root Wisdom, a healing arts practice integrating her expertise in both ecological science and animist spirituality. Her dharma includes picking up trash and planting seeds. Kirra’s specialties include land and water tending, Ancestral Lineage Healing, Compassionate Deposession and curse unravelling, plant medicine and psychedelics, dreamwork and ceremony. Kirra upholds the traditions of her British, Irish, Armenian and Italian ancestors and is an initiated Völva in the Old Norse ways. She is a Certified Iyengar Yoga teacher, in the lineage of Yogacharya Sri B.K.S. Iyengar, and offers regular classes both online and in person. Kirra holds a Masters of Science degree in Restoration Ecology and a Doctorate of Divinity and serves as the custodian of two salmon-bearing creeks in the Eel River watershed. You can connect with Kirra at http://www.rootwisdom.com or the Atihana Nature Preserve. Mariavittoria Mangini, PhD, FNP has written extensively on the impact of psychedelic experiences in shaping the lives of her contemporaries, and has worked closely with many of the most distinguished investigators in this field. She is one of the founders of the Women’s Visionary Council, a nonprofit organization that supports investigations into non-ordinary forms of consciousness and organizes gatherings of researchers, healers, artists, and activists whose work explores these states. She is a visiting scholar at the Berkeley Center for the Science of Psychedelics, and Professor Emerita in the School of Science, Allied Health, and Nursing at Holy Names University. For the last 50 years, she has been a part of the Hog Farm, a well-known communal family based in Berkeley and in Laytonville, California. Tom Banger is an artist, writer, occultural technologist, iterative thinker and prankster. As Tom Headbanger, he promoted hundreds of punk and industrial shows in the 1980s. He founded the influential North American Station of the Temple ov Psychick Youth in 1986. His collection of punk and occultural artifacts are now part of the Denver Public Library Western History Collection. His written work has been featured in Thee Psychic Bible, The Occult Harry Smith, The Fenris Wolf, Rituals and Declarations, The Trapartisan Review, Abraxas, Augenblick, Gnostic Technology, and WestWord. He has spoken on various magicko-historical topics at Occulture, Trans-States, Re-Writing the Future, and the Southwestern Popular American Culture Association. He co-hosts the Banger and Andrew podcast. As Tom Hallewell, he expostulated on digital technology and cyberdefense to the National Association of Broadcasters, the Information Systems Security Association and the Caribbean Broadcast Union. His Facebook and Instagram implants answer to @tombanger.

ea9e0f80-0b97-492a-9bfc-0be5b0416f30: Please join us for Ellen Bepp’s Artist’s Talk, Saturday, October 31st, staring at 2 pm with a traditional Japanese drum and flute procession. Ellen will discuss the 10 pieces on view in the gallery reflecting on the legacy of the mandatory relocation and confinement of Japanese Americans during WW II and its aftermath, with a keen awareness of current events. More than 120,000 people of Japanese descent were remanded to these camps in a wave of fear that swept America in response to attacks on Pearl Harbor, including Heart Mountain in Wyoming, where Bepp’s family was incarcerated.​ Incorporating fragments of familial writing, traditional textiles, imbedded text and Japanese imagery, Bepp’s work reflects on the xenophobia, racial slurs and casual taunts aimed at Asian Americans as well as the pain and despair of the camps. Beyond the fear and loss, emerges the powerful story of resilience and perseverance that sustained detainees through their experience and in resuming their place as autonomous citizens. A thoughtful examination of the work, standing with the elemental history of the objects and absorbing the words, honors that journey.

d2ea08f7-7c58-422d-8c8e-8c99fbbf8376: Living within a grief phobic culture, many of us abandon, suppress, or deny our own sorrows and loss. Yet grief surrounds us all in this life. The grief tending circle is a space to slow down and honor grief with others, creating a container that can help us metabolize, transmute, and move with our grief. Here we will honor and tend our grief through somatic exploration and movement, dream tending, and creative art making. We work with altar building, writing, and ritual, all in support of holding personal and collective grief. This is not a therapeutic group process aimed at talking through our grief, but rather a grief tending space focusing on earthy, concrete practices that support us in moving through our grief and befriending grief as an ally. Grief is a living entity that needs care, expression, and ritual engagement. This circle is for all types of grievers. We welcome those navigating the death of loved ones, shifts in identity, life transitions, chronic illness, aging, the end of relationships, or unfulfilled dreams. We also hold space for the continuous, heavy grief of our collective reality — from global and climate crises to systemic violence to the exhausting pressures of living within late-stage capitalism. Please bring a journal and writing materials, as well as comfortable clothing that offers freedom of movement. Art supplies and restorative yoga props will be provided. We may be asking participants to bring specific objects to each session. Teacher Bios: Shannon has been a somatic educator and therapist, movement and wellness facilitator and fellow grief tender for twenty plus years. She intersects somatic therapy, depth psychology, mindfulness, expressive arts, nature and land based practices, dream tending, and ritual, to support ones returning, remembrance and coming home to self. She creatively weaves various healing arts as we navigate through the terrain of the unconscious and unknown, moving towards integration and wholeness, and deeper belonging to self and the greater world. website: www.tendingourwildroots.com Instagram: www.bodyrootandsoul.com/instagram Petra is a somatic and relational counselor working with individuals, couples, and adult family members at Axis Mundi Center for Mental Health. She orients to the body as a source of information on what needs tending, and as the vehicle that carries us where our minds and hearts alone cannot go. In her work she explores how we connect to self and others through movement, ritual, and expression, as a way of coming into healthier relationship with ourselves and each other. Grief can be a persistent companion. Meeting it asks for time, space, and contact in so many different and at times unexpected ways.
308ce2d5-9022-4ab7-b43e-cd681836035d: 5Rhythms® dance is a profound medicine, offering a dynamic movement map into the vast, unexplored wilderness between our head and feet. Each rhythm - Flowing, Staccato, Chaos, Lyrical, and Stillness, is a gateway, a wisdom teacher guiding us toward greater presence, healing, and transformation. This event occurs every two weeks at the Alembic. In a Sweat Your Prayers®, we support your individual practice with the rhythms and your movement journey by dancing wave after wave with light guidance. People often leave feeling cleansed, grounded, more alive, and more connected to themselves and their deeper knowing. 5Rhythms® is for every body. Many have discovered that not having prior dance training is actually liberating! Bring your body temple and a willingness to be surprised by what's waiting to move in and through you. The dance will end around 12:15pm, followed by a closing circle until around 12:30-ish. We encourage spacious arrivals and unhurried departures. So plan your time generously: a little time to land, a little time to linger, and a little less rushing back into the busy world. This dance can be your mini-retreat for the week! Teacher Bio: Qibei is a 5Rhythms® teacher, mindfulness teacher, holistic healer, and Associate Marriage and Family Therapist, though no title could fully capture the many worlds she moves between. Her work bridges the clinical and the mystical, the tender and the fierce, the grounded intelligence of the body and the mystery of Spirit moving through human life. For over 20 years, alongside 5Rhythms®, her path has been richly shaped by Continuum Movement, Open Floor, somatic contemplative practice, and relational communication. Over time, these disciplines began weaving together into the way she listens, guides, and teaches. For Qibei, dance is medicine, prayer, and creative laboratory, a place where we can move beyond numbness, habitual defenses, and rigid identities we’ve learned to carry, and reconnect with our raw aliveness and deeper knowing. She believes embodied presence is what brings depth, vitality, connection, and magic into our lives. In her movement spaces, Qibei creates a trauma-sensitive and inclusive field for all bodies, inviting authentic expression and the dynamic interplay between body, heart, psyche, and spirit. Her music and facilitation are often described as exquisite, nourishing, and deeply transporting, guiding movers into inner landscapes they didn’t know they could reach. Qibei also facilitates women's circle and retreats. Learn more about her work at www.Qibei.be.

f19a9506-42ab-4f8c-9b46-4b47c86b9afe: “Valuable and dauntless.” — The New York Times “We badly need [this] book.” —Tina Brown A devastating reckoning with the people and institutions whose failure to stand up to Trump’s brazen grab for authoritarian power has been particularly shocking and consequential It may be scant solace, but history will be particularly harsh to a subset of Trump enablers with a few key things in common: They have money and power. They represent intuitions that are central in determining whether America remains a free, functioning democracy or not. And they absolutely know better. History starts now. In Profiles in Cowardice , Jacob Weisberg has written one of the first defining books of the Trump Era—how this pitch-black political moment happened, why so few resisted, and what it reveals about the character of American leadership. Jeff Bezos, Amazon, and Big Tech. Stephen Schwarzman, Blackstone, and Wall Street. Brad Karp, Paul, Weiss, and Big Law. Mitch McConnell and the United States Senate. Eight individuals in all, together forming an entwined network of power in America, and a new way to understand how authoritarianism can take root in an open society—not by overthrowing institutions, but by bending and bullying them into submission. The book is a masterful study of the ways people create rationalizations to justify basic human instincts such as greed, vanity and fear—above all fear. Fear is the great enemy of democracy, and the book illuminates how it operates, how it disguises itself, and how it spreads. The book is timeless: its profiles are case studies, but they are also mirrors. They ask readers to examine their own instincts, their own silences, their own thresholds for action. This is not a morality tale with easy villains. It is an attempt to describe the moral mechanics of democratic failure. By studying that failure up close, we may better understand what courage truly requires—and why it is so rarely summoned when it matters most. “A cutting compendium of collusion.” — Publishers Weekly “A highly readable study of the politics and price of capitulation.” —Kirkus Reviews “In this perilous moment in American history, much political courage is required; understanding where it went is essential to bringing it back. In Profiles in Cowardice, the extraordinary Jacob Weisberg examines how, when, and why so many Americans and American institutions capitulated to monstrous abuses of the office of the American presidency. The appeasement of Donald Trump is a sordid story. It is also, in Weisberg’s hands, a gripping one.” —Jill Lepore Jacob Weisberg is the author of books including Ronald Reagan (2016) , The Bush Tragedy (2008), and In an Uncertain World (2003), co-written with former Treasury Secretary Robert E. Rubin. A native of Chicago, he is the former longtime editor of Slate and the co-founder of the podcast company Pushkin Industries. He serves as Chair of The Committee to Protect Journalists and is a regular contributor to the New York Review of Books. 043199b6-0524-45d7-8bcc-0e38aa539d72: Many of us work with psychedelics without a guide or with limited support to integrate these experiences. Even the most joyful experiences are best metabolized when witnessed. Together, we become a mosaic – a colorful and varied community, greater together than the sum of our parts. Mosaic is a psychedelic integration circle for self-identified women. Here, you’ll find a supportive space to integrate the lessons, challenges, and wisdom from psychedelic journeys so that you can apply those learnings to everyday life. Together, we’ll seek to understand our psychedelic experiences and make profound insights accessible and actionable. This is a drop-in, monthly supported peer group rather than a psychotherapy group. We create space for sharing stories and experiences, receiving support, and forging genuine connections. Meditation, mindful movement, somatic practices, Internal Family Systems parts work, and creative tools are all part of the fun. Dr. Lyssa Menard is a psychologist, psychedelic therapist, and professor (Northwestern University Medical School) with specialties in Integrative Medicine, trauma treatment, and health psychology. Dr. Menard’s book, "Results May Vary: Hope & Healing through Psychedelic-assisted Psychotherapy" is scheduled for release in 2026. As a beneficiary of excellent (and also, sadly, lackluster) psychedelic treatment, she is a skeptic of the field, a critic when necessary, and a true believer in the healing possibilities offered by these medicines. She serves as an advocate for community and patient education and fights for legal access to psychedelics for health and healing. As a recent transplant to California's Bay Area, Dr. Menard spends a ridiculous amount of time at The Berkeley Alembic, cavorting in nature, worshipping the sun, and developing community. e698b231-997c-4557-b187-49a21221cd97: An empowering story of self-actualization by a former Christian pop star whose life was transformed by reading. “In telling her story, Julianna Glasse blazes a trail for every woman who has ever felt oppressed by religion and the patriarchy and muted by other people’s rules and judgment. This is a page-turning, sexy, and eye-popping memoir of liberation. I couldn’t put it down.”—Chelsea Handler, author of the #1 New York Times -bestseller Life Will Be the Death of Me Julianna will be joined in conversation by Tara Schuster. In 2017, Julianna Glasse performed at President Trump's first National Prayer Breakfast. At the time, she was a Christian pop star married to a star MLB player. They were a glamorous, high-profile Evangelical power couple. She led prayer sessions for players' wives. She wrote handbooks for Christian women. And she hid books like contraband. When her husband discovered books she'd hidden in her lingerie drawer—Plato, Dickinson, Rumi, de Beauvoir—he threw them on the floor and shouted, "This is what happens when women read!" His condemnation became her wake-up call. Now, in THIS IS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN WOMEN READ (Spiegel & Grau; October 13, 2026), Julianna tells the unforgettable, unvarnished, deeply moving story of her escape from the cave—her personal path to freedom and the power of books to change lives. When Julianna began reading Plato’s Republic, something in her shifted. She started asking questions, hiding books around the house, and reading late at night. What followed: a very public, contested divorce. Horrific public shaming. Self-hatred, depression, suicidal impulses. But also: befriending the gay couple next door (one a pastor who opened her to a new understanding of Christianity), sexual liberation, an Oxford business degree, and the creation of a nonprofit, also called “This Is What Happens When Women Read,” which provides scholarships, curriculum, and community to women breaking free from fundamentalist religions around the globe. In an America where book bans are being imposed, when the cultural moment is obsessed with shows like The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives and endless tradwife discourse, and when American women are questioning who gets to decide their futures, the timing of this book is ideal. Julianna believes & "the political future of this country lies in the votes of the women I'm writing for"—women trapped in patriarchal religious systems. Julianna refused to accept her cage—and has built a ladder for others to climb out. This isn’t just a memoir, it’s a manifesto. I invite you to read this remarkable book and join her mission: to help women become "autonomous, curious, fully realized human beings." “Powerful debut memoir . . . Patient and curious rather than rageful or high-minded, Glasse’s account is a love letter to art, literature, and finding beauty in the world on one’s own terms. It makes for empowering reading.” —Publishers Weekly “This book is a searing bibliography of self-expression, one book at a time. It’s breathlessly propulsive, with courage mounting on every page. In an era of rising illiteracy, I found myself as a reader alternately lamenting what non-readers miss and cheering for what Julianna found. This book is what happens when women read: they transform into who they were always meant to be. Julianna uses her radiant light to liberate, and I’m so grateful that she persevered in her journey of revolutionary reading.” —Tia Levings, author of The New York Times bestseller A Well-Trained Wife and I Belong to Me “Women's reading is often dismissed as a hobby or a trivial distraction. But as Glasse's fierce own story and fierce analysis shows, a woman reading can be the most radical act.” —Soraya Chemaly, author of Rage Becomes Her Julianna Glasse is the founder and CEO of This Is What Happens When Women Read, a global movement advancing women's intellectual autonomy through education, scholarship, and community. An alumna of the University of Oxford and a member of the Saïd Business School Dean's Circle, Glasse leads a growing global scholarship initiative in partnership with Oxford that provides women access to one of the world's leading graduate business programs. She has spoken at global forums including the United Nations, the Skoll World Forum, and the Clinton Global Initiative on women's leadership and the role of intellectual agency in social transformation. She currently resides in New York City.For more information, go to https: // www.thisiswhathappenswhenwomenread.org . About Sarelyn Wager Sarelyn is a 98-year-old Marin County-based artist who has been painting since childhood. Educated at Chouinard Art Institute and UCLA, her work has been exhibited in various locations and private salons over the years. Sarelyn's art embodies her interior life and her curiosity about people, capturing their goodness through her vibrant use of color and form. Sarelyn has been painting for over 80 years. Her passion and creativity capture the essence of the human experience through her masterful use of color and texture. "I live and dream in color," says Sarelyn. "My paintings speak for themselves. I'm a feisty, opinionated nonagenarian with a quirky world view, and my art is my most potent natural expression." Sarelyn's journey as an artist has been shaped by the challenges faced by women in the art world throughout her lifetime. Despite these barriers, she chose to follow her heart and dedicate herself to her craft, painting tirelessly for decades. Her work stands strong alongside accomplished artists, showcasing a remarkable abstract composition within figurative paintings. Sarelyn’s artistic expression is influenced by artists such as Pierre Bonnard, Picasso, and Rico LeBrun. Sarelyn's style is characterized by vibrant, expressionistic paintings that capture the attitude and inner stirrings of her subjects. "Every painting is a world of its own," Sarelyn explains. "Art comes from within me, not conforming to any objective criteria. Using oil paint allows me to continue to evolve a painting over time."

61b4e182-deb4-42ce-b524-d91764f86beb: What if Earth came with a user manual? Regen360 argues that humanity’s crisis is not a lack of care, but a broken operating system—and introduces the Earth Code, a practical framework for aligning human systems to work in harmony with the planet. When incentives, governance, and institutional structures prioritize short-term gain, even well-intentioned efforts can accelerate harm. Sustainability stalls because systems are designed to reward immediate profit over long-term regeneration. Regen360 reframes regeneration as an operating discipline rather than an aspiration, showing how economics, leadership, technology, and daily decisions can be realigned with the self-regulatory patterns of Earth. As AI accelerates decision-making and shortens time horizons, the consequences of systemic misalignment intensify. Regen360 explores how human and institutional behavior responds under pressure—and how emerging technologies can either reinforce short-term priorities or support long-term stewardship. Bridging inner purpose with outer systems, David Gottfried, founder of the global green building movement, demonstrates how values, identity, and responsibility shape outcomes at every scale. The framework for a regenerative future is here—but the question remains: will it be embraced? "David Gottfried doesn't moralize; he analyzes. He gives us code — fifteen Earth Code equations, nestled in a framework called HOPE. At this bleak moment in our planet's history, hope is just what we need." — Denis Hayes, founder of Earth Day; President Emeritus, Bullitt Foundation " Regen360 is his most honest book yet — part memoir, part systems manifesto, part father's reckoning with what his daughter's generation is inheriting. He's not selling optimism. He's offering an operating system. That distinction matters, and so does this book." — Chip Conley, New York Times bestselling author and founder of MEA " Regen360 is what happens when someone who helped build the green building movement steps back and interrogates his own life's work with total honesty. It's essential reading for the journey forward." — Joel Makower, Chairman and Co-founder, Trellis Group David Gottfried is widely recognized as a father of the global green building movement. He founded both the U.S. Green Building Council and the World Green Building Council, which now spans 85 countries. His pioneering work catalyzed a global movement resulting in billions of square feet of certified projects across more than 186 countries, over a trillion dollars of economic activity, and hundreds of thousands of accredited professionals. Gottfried serves as Founder and CEO of Regen360 Inc., providing strategic advisory in decarbonization, sustainability, and regeneration for leading global green building companies. His personal mission is accelerating HOPE. Previously, Gottfried was Chief Commercial Officer of Blue Planet Systems, a carbon sequestration start-up. He spent two decades as CEO of Regenerative Ventures and its RegenNetwork, and held senior leadership roles in real estate development, including Senior Vice President at Thomas Properties Group. His new book, Regen360: An Operating System for a Regenerative Earth (Morgan James Publishing, October 2026), asks a question: what if everything we've built isn't enough — and the problem isn't technological or economic, but the operating logic underneath everything? The book proposes an Earth Code of 15 governing codes for a regenerative civilization and a framework called HOPE — Health on Planet Earth. His earlier book, Explosion Green, was an Indie Book Awards winner with a cover testimonial from President Bill Clinton. He is the author of four books and hosts the Regen360 podcast with 80 episodes. Gottfried holds a degree in Engineering and Resource Management from Stanford University, where he has lectured for three decades. His honors include the WorldGBC Global Green Building Entrepreneurship Award, USGBC Leadership Award, induction into the Green Industry Hall of Fame, and the 2025 NetZero/Metropolis Magazine Trailblazer Award. The USGBC Northern California Super Hero Award is now given annually in his name. He serves on the Advisory Boards of USGBC California, the Smart Surfaces Coalition, My Superhuman Race (India) and Verdant Building Products. Gottfried is a devoted father, painter, martial artist, fly fisherman, and cyclist — a five-time finisher of the Death Ride. He lives in the East Bay of Northern California with his Labradoodle, Juneau. A New Play by the San Francisco Neo-Futurists · The San Francisco Neo-Futurists present our latest long-form play, We Bought A Gun!, written and performed by jeb and Willie Caldwell, current and former Artistic Directors of The San Francisco Neo-Futurists, respectively. Set in the Bay Area in 2026, We Bought A Gun! weaves historical, cultural, and personal threads through its central narrative: a couple deciding to buy a gun together for the first time. Intimate and occasionally intense (but never macabre), We Bought A Gun! brings the audience beyond the fourth wall and into the dialogue, inviting a communal exploration of compassion, compromise, pain, and purpose. A depature from The Infinite Wrench format of 30 plays in 60 minutes, this Beyond-the-Wrench production is a full play that adheres to the theatrical tenants of Neo-Futurism: we are who we are, we are where we are, we are doing what we're doing, the time is now. Many parents feel unsure about what steps to take next, especially when facing cultural stigma or other life stressors like housing or employment issues. Our families come to us for guidance and emotional support as they navigate this challenging time and figure out their next steps. Transition to Adulthood: Becoming Young Adults When young adults with disabilities or special health care needs age out of school services, families often don’t know what comes next. Parents seek help understanding available options and supporting their child’s transition to adulthood. Young adults need to make decisions for what comes next. We can assist you in exploring opportunities for continued education, independence, and job readiness. Navigating the Systems: A Need for Guidance Many families are receiving basic services like IEPs or therapies but feel frustrated with the results. They turn to us for help navigating complex systems, advocating for better services, and accessing additional resources. We provide the knowledge and strategies families need to improve their child’s care and achieve better outcomes. FRN's offices are located in San Leandro. 8571dd6f-c16b-4683-a716-9c0ba8489a7b: Khir Johari is the author of the multi-award-winning book The Food of Singapore Malays: Gastronomic Travels Through the Archipelago . His seminal work explores the cultural anthropology of Malay food and showcases its role in shaping Singapore’s Malay culture. The title is the result of 11 years of painstaking research, drawing on material that dates back as far as the 7th-century Srivijaya Empire. The book is richly detailed, combining historical anecdotes and information with captivating photography. Since its release, the book has won numerous awards, including the internationally coveted Best of the Best in Food Culture at the 2025 Gourmand World Food Awards. Following this success, Khir founded Dialogues by Khir Johari, a platform dedicated to exploring the Nusantara’s (maritime Southeast Asia) food, culture, and history through events and online discussions. Its inaugural event, Serumpun: Tasting Tradition, Telling Tales held in 2024 now returns for its third edition. The day-long symposium features talks, panel discussions, and restaurant collaborations. Khir’s journey toward becoming a respected figure in promoting the Nusantara’s culinary culture began in his childhood. Born and raised in Kampong Gelam, he grew up in the historic Gedung Kuning (Yellow Mansion) — once an annex of the Sultan of Singapore’s royal palace. It was in this sprawling home, housing a four-generation household, where his earliest food memories were shaped. Both celebratory and everyday dishes were prepared in the house’s four kitchens, under the watchful eye of his great-grandmother. His mother, an accomplished cookery teacher, also taught him how to cook. Khir’s interest in his cultural identity deepened in 1994 when he left Singapore for university in California. Reflecting on his roots from afar, he longed to read in Malay, taste the food of home, and reconnect with his heritage. In California’s libraries and bookstores, he discovered a wealth of books on Southeast Asia, offering valuable insights into the Malay Archipelago’s culinary culture. After seven years teaching mathematics in California, he returned to Singapore in 2007 and joined the Singapore Heritage Society, eventually serving as its Vice President from 2015 to 2017. There, he applied years of research to cultural preservation efforts which affirmed the idea for The Food of Singapore Malays. For the next decade, Khir delved into researching and documenting the history of Singapore’s Malay community. Along the way, he amassed a unique Southeast Asian collection of artworks, rare books, artefacts, food anthropology items, and music recordings. “I was pretty much on my own,” he says. “With information so scattered, you have to be not just a historian, but a botanist, zoologist, and anthropologist to connect the dots.” Today, Khir’s work continues beyond his book as he shares his field notes through Dialogues by Khir Johari, a cultural initiative where events and social media posts work together to foster discussions on the Nusantara’s food, culture, and history. Now in its third year, Serumpun: Tasting Tradition, Telling Tales continues as a day-long symposium bringing chefs, thinkers and makers from across the region. Through talks and panel discussions, it deepens ongoing conversations about food, memory, and identity across the Nusantara. “My hope is that we continue the important work of preserving and celebrating our rich culinary heritage,” says Khir. “Our shared cultural roots are an essential starting point for understanding how food connects us across generations and borders.” Awards for The Food of Singapore Malays: Gastronomic Travels Through the Archipelago 1. Gourmand World Cookbook Awards 2025 – Best of All across Gourmand’s history 2.⁠ Gourmand World Cookbook Awards 2025 (30th anniversary) - Best of the Best in Food Culture 3. National University of Singapore (NUS) Singapore History Prize 2024 - Winner 4. Alan Chan Spirit of Singapore Book Prize 2024 – Merit Award 5. Gourmand World Cookbook Awards 2023: ● Best Book of the Last 25 Years ● Best of the Best in the World ● Best Asian Cuisine ● Best Culinary History ● Best Book of the Year (Singapore) 6.⁠ ⁠⁠⁠Asian Print Awards 2023 (Markono) - Best in Offset & Best Book Printing. 7. Singapore Book Awards 2022: ● Book of the Year ● Best Illustrated Non-Fiction Book 8. Wardah Books of the Year 2021 The Food of Singapore Malays - This is not a cookbook. It is the unwritten story of a people. Between the vast Indian and Pacific oceans lies a realm of extraordinary natural abundance: the Malay Archipelago, known widely as the Nusantara. These islands of Southeast Asia have nourished the lives of indigenous Malays throughout the centuries and nurtured the diverse peoples that have set foot on their shores. Today, the Malays make up less than a fifth of the population in Singapore, a city with ancient ties to the Malay world. This book explores their food, not just as a means of sustenance but as a cultural activity. Inheriting the Nusantara’s rich flavours, Singapore Malays have a grand culinary heritage reflecting their worldviews, social values and historical interactions with other cultures. Through close examination of their daily objects, customs, art and literature, these pages reveal how the food Malays enjoy is deeply embedded in different aspects of their identity. Following the broad sweep of Malay cuisine’s evolution – from the 7th-century kingdom of Srivijaya to the 21st-century emporium of cosmopolitan Singapore – this book traces the continuity and dynamism of a shared cultural consciousness. Sumptuously served with stunning photographs, delicious recipes and diligent research, this is essential reading for anyone – gourmets and amateurs alike – hungry for a deeper understanding of the relationship between people and their food.
