037860f3-a870-4588-b40c-77798ebe0753: From the bestselling author of literary sensation The Art of Fielding comes an urgent, deeply felt story of friendship, art, love, and grief, following two young women on the brink of irrevocable change. Parties and weddings, messy hookups and marred friendships, art and love and grief— The Brightness follows the electric, chaotic, everything-can-happen lives of Pella and her best friend, Irma, as they fumble their way out of sleepy, Midwestern Westish College and into a larger world that will upend their connection and everything they thought they understood about their own place within it. At 27, Pella’s life looks settled: she’s a recent college grad, engaged to Mike, her longtime boyfriend, and helping her friend Owen pull off his own destination wedding on Block Island. But over that wild wedding weekend, Pella’s past and present collide spectacularly, blowing up her plans and sending her spiraling toward an unplanned future in New York City. Meanwhile, back at Westish College, 21-year-old Irma’s involvement with a politically charged prank—one that has roiled both the campus and the world beyond—threatens to derail her brilliant future. As Irma and Pella cycle through possibilities and identities, both navigate the heights and depths of passion and ambition, and the incalculable wages of love and loss. In stunning scenes and spectacular characters—each drawn with an almost superhuman vividness and humanity—Chad Harbach captures that specific, shimmering anxiety of your twenties when life still feels wide open, even as hard and irreversible choices start closing in. Energetic, funny, and deeply human, this much-anticipated follow-up to The Art of Fielding confirms Chad Harbach as one of the most accomplished and deep-seeing writers of our time. One of The New York Times, Chicago Review of Books, Literary Hub, and Publishers Weekly ’s Most Anticipated Books for Fall 2026 “A good book is propulsive, you can’t put it down, etc. A really good book fosters scarcity and you want to put it down as frequently as you can to live in the narrative longer. But a great book makes you feel a sort of frustration with the author that they wrote it before you. This is a good, really good, and great book. It captures a, what it was like to be a girl in college in 2016, which I was but imagine Chad wasn’t, which makes it all the more impressive, b. the complicated nature of female friendship, and c. the wonderful excruciating confusion of growing up, I could not put it down, except when I had to in order to savor it.” — Madeline Cash , author of Lost Lambs “As in his acclaimed debut, Harbach immerses readers in the world of Westish, but he broadens his scope, plunging his characters into new environments and broaching topics such as love and talent and literature, as well as campus sexual assault, feminism, the fraught politics of victimhood, and the volatile media landscape that complicates all of these. Apt evocations of Shakespeare’s The Tempest abound. While this novel can certainly be enjoyed independent of its predecessor, those who’ve read the first book will more fully appreciate the continued growth and dilemmas of Pella, Mike, and Own (the Skrimmer makes appearances, too), to say nothing of the clever metafictional twist Harbach pulls off via Owen’s novel which is titled–well, take a guess. Brilliant, poignant, and absorbing.” — Kirkus (starred) “With prose that is characteristically assured, detailed, and wise, [ The Brightness ] is sure to be the Big Cozy Read of the autumn.” — Lit Hub , Most Anticipated Books of the Year Chad Harbach is the author of the bestselling novel The Art of Fielding, which has been translated into more than twenty languages, and a founder of n+1. He was raised in Racine, Wisconsin, and educated at Harvard and the University of Virginia. He lives in Northern California with his son Ansel, and their dog, Curtis. About the book: For fans of Ann Patchett, a layered, multigenerational family novel about three sisters carrying on the legacy of their family’s pearl farm in small-town Tennessee. Three estranged sisters—Helen, Anna, and Penn Lockshire—are bound by the shimmering but fragile legacy of their family’s freshwater pearl farm in rural Tennessee. When the business that once made them famous faces collapse, the sisters are pulled back into each other’s lives and forced to reckon with old betrayals, unspoken resentments, and the complicated truth of their inheritance. Soon, what began as a fight for survival becomes a reckoning with the myths that shaped them and the secrets buried in the family’s past. From the discovery of a rare pearl in 1981 to the struggles of a failing farm in 2008, the Lockshire sisters must navigate love, loss, ambition, and forgiveness to decide whether their heritage is a blessing to preserve—or a burden to escape. Rich with emotional depth and anchored by the pearl’s enduring symbolism—a thing of beauty born from irritation—this sweeping story of family, identity, and resilience will captivate readers of Celeste Ng and Claire Lombardo. Stacey Gordon grew up in the Appalachian foothills of southern Ohio and began her career as a trade journalist covering the cultured pearl and jewelry industries, visiting farms across Asia and companies around the world. For the past twenty-five years she’s worked in marketing and user experience design for the Silicon Valley tech industry. This is her debut novel. She lives with her family in Alameda, California.
5158f3a1-da02-47ca-8406-f6d78ddc6da0: RSVP and reserve your tickets here Please join the GLBT Historical Society and Crowded Fire Theater as we jointly present the first of two staged readings of How to Live in a House on Fire , a new play by Kari Barclay and directed by M. Graham Smith. Presented for the first time in the San Francisco Bay Area where the story takes place, this staged reading of a new play by performance scholar Kari Barclay looks to queer history as a lens to understand our current moment of climate grief. Attendees to the program will be treated with a live staged reading of the new play with a cast of actors, followed by a talkback discussion with the creative team after the show and an opportunity to share audience feedback and participate in the development process! About the play HOW TO LIVE IN A HOUSE ON FIRE asks how we care for each other in moments of crisis. It builds on a quote from Tennessee Williams: "We live in a perpetually burning building, and what we must save from it, all the time, is love." The Chateau Homosexuel is a gay commune on the brink of collapse. It's 1970 in Berkeley, California, and as characters bicker over the future of gay liberation, Benny and Jeremy are falling in love. When they try to decide what to do with an eviction notice, suddenly something starts burning in the oven. Smoke fills the stage, and Benny and Jeremy re-enter in K95 masks. We're transported to 2020 in the same house in the midst of the California wildfires. Benny and Jeremy are married, and they're figuring out what to bring with them in preparation for an evacuation. As they sort their belongings and try to pack fifty years of queer history into a cardboard box, they're confronted with what histories to remember and what to forget. SPEAKERS Kari Barclay (they/them) is a playwright, director, and theater maker interested in deepening audiences’ sense of time and sparking curiosity about sexuality and gender. Based in Cleveland, Ohio, they serve as Associate Professor of Theater at Oberlin College. Kari is a 2026 Dramatist Guild Foundation National Fellow and Ohio Arts Council Individual Excellence in Playwriting awardee. Kari's playwriting and directing has shown at Ars Nova, Cleveland Public Theatre, convergence-continuum, and Duke University, among other theaters. Kari’s original comedy Can I Hold You? was one of the first full-length plays about asexuality performed in the U.S. and enjoyed a sold-out run in San Francisco and workshop in New York. It has been taught at colleges and universities across the country and published in Marathi language translation. Kari’s play Stonewallin’ was the winner of the 2021 Southern Queer Playwriting Festival and opened at Richmond Triangle Players in February 2022. In their other life, Kari is a theater scholar and historian. Their nonfiction book, Directing Desire , examines the rise of intimacy choreography in theater and is out now from Palgrave Macmillan. Kari earned their PhD in Theater and Performance Studies in 2021 from Stanford University, where they studied with playwright Young Jean Lee. kari-barclay.com . c92e8227-266a-4a4e-b717-2a8b376f3fc0: Secret weapons and a government cover-up · An evening discussion between Pulitzer Prize winning author Lowell Bergman and the authors of "The Havana Syndrome," Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados, about their book digging into a secret weapon that has baffled and confused the US public, amid years of government denial. From Havana to Tbilisi, from Vienna to Key West, the authors reveal how they spoke to the victims of Havana Syndrome attacks -- diplomats, covert intelligence officials, FBI agents and military officials -- to get the true story of what happened to them and how their government employers to this day are fighting them to hide the truth. The U.S. government fumbled its response so severely that one high-ranking former US intelligence official calls this "the biggest cover-up in my adult life." Bergman will ask the authors about their ten-year investigation at CBS News, "60 Minutes" that led to this book, and the struggles to break down the wall of classified material to get inside the investigations at CIA and the Pentagon. The authors put aside their own professional skepticism to keep digging when, over and over, they began to discover new leads the government had ignored, video evidence, eyewitness testimony about the perpetrators and internal documents placing adversaries close to known incidents. As scientists warned them that the technology was indeed possible, the authors found clues to a new type of highly specialized weapon that is both frightening and very, very real. Lowell Berman is a journalist, television producer and professor of Journalism. Bergman was a producer, reporter and director of investigative reporting at ABC News and later a producer for CBS News "60 Minutes." His investigation into the tobacco industry at "60 Minutes" was depicted in Michael Mann's movie The Insider, which was nominated for seven Academy Awards and featured Al Pacino as Bergman. From 1999 to 2008, Bergman was an investigative correspondent for The New York Times, where he was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Public Service in 2004 for "A Dangerous Business," about worker safety and environmental law violations in the cast-iron pipe industry. Bergman was a producer and correspondent for PBS "Frontline." He founded the investigative reporting program at the Graduate School of Journalism at UC Berkeley, where he taught for 28 years. Michael Rey is an Emmy-award winning investigative producer at 60 Minutes. He has produced a series of stories about the mystery behind the Havana Syndrome, Cuban spies' networks in the United States, and Lance Armstrong's use of performance enhancing drugs, among many other long-form investigative projects. He was a senior producer for the CBS Evening News and a founding member of the CBS News Investigative Unit. He and Oriana were awarded the Alfred I. duPont/Columbia Journalism Award for their reporting on the U.S. border crisis and family separation policies. Oriana Zill de Granados has been an investigative producer for 60 Minutes since 2011. She has produced a series of stories about the mystery behind the Havana Syndrome, the mysterious deaths of the enemies of Vladimir Putin, allegations of fraud by insurance companies in Florida, scams targeting senior citizens, child separation policies of the first Trump Administration, sexual harassment in the restaurant industry, and Lance Armstrong's use of performance-enhancing drugs, among others. Her work has been awarded a duPont Award, multiple Writers' Guild and Emmy Awards, a Peabody and an IRE medal for investigative reporting.

For nearly a decade, two dueling guitarists and songwriters, Austin Smith and Mark Tegio, built the backbone of their namesake outfit, honing their hard-worn Americana songwriting. Their music shaped by years of troubadouring up and down I-5, from San Diego to Seattle. Over time, their sound evolved from its more folk roots, inspired by the likes of Doc & Merle Watson and their guitar interplay, as well as mining the lines left by Townes Van Zandt and Blaze Foley, trying to learn the lessons those broken heroes left behind. As Smith and Tegio split their time between Portland and Santa Cruz, a new crew of musicians entered the Central California mix, expanding their sound in ways the duo perhaps didn’t know they needed—until they knew they did. Enter The Lowtimers. This new 5-piece band—Tegio (guitar and vocals), Smith (guitar, vocals and harmonica), Tim Kelso (drums), Andrew Dreher (bass and harmonies), and Payton Vermeesch (pedal steel)—remain rooted in soulful Americana, but they now lay it over a new sonic landscape, injecting fresh empathy and drive into songs that paint wise western portraits of lives and loves on the road to redemption, where the goal is less about prosperity and more about peace of mind. We may remember the past, but we should never forget what the future may hold. To be open and honest with art, it’s evolve or creatively die. And often, evolution delivers an entirely new animal. Bandcamp | IG Red McAdam Although he was born in the industrial heart of New Jersey, Red McAdam’s mother Maggie made damn sure to rear him on country and folk music. She served up a steady diet of celebrated songwriters and singers on their kitchen radio day after day, from classics like Patsy Cline and Ernest Tubb to burgeoning legends like Lucinda Williams and Brad Paisley. Red’s father Bartholomew, a lifelong bass player, took it from there, teaching him banjo, mandolin, bass, and guitar. A self-proclaimed ‘Western fraud,’ Red makes no effort to fit the country mold, but rather draws from the unique and largely unsung landscape of his world. Stranger-than-fiction episodes from his time on the road, preposterous characters with bizarre motives, and plain old bullshit mingle with vulnerable expressions of a tumultuous life and a threadbare heart. A first responder, passionate outdoorsman, recovering alcoholic, and heartbroken songwriter—Red earned whatever authenticity the country audience craves through his life, not place of birth. McAdam’s playful outsider country music presents an inventive vision of what the genre can be. His rich, risky blend of traditional honky-tonk and Western swing draws on indie rock, R&B, and beyond, reflecting a lifelong love of all music and disdain for genres and rules of any kind. A consummate road dog, he brings his frenetic, dynamic, and occasionally delirious performances to dives, dancehalls, clubs, and theaters across the country. Listeners will recognize the Lone Star eccentricities of Terry Allen and Guy Clark, forlorn folk sensibilities of Elizabeth Cotton and Karen Dalton, and the driving genre-bending of The Band and Bob Dylan. Over the past several years, he spent time working in National Parks and schools, bars and the backwoods, and most recently between emergency departments and ambulances across the country. After a spell hidden away in his high desert Arizona home, Red hit the road full tilt. In two barnstorming years, he and his band played 37 states over 13 tours, logging 90,000 miles and averaging over 200 shows a year. Red now lives outside of Austin in his 1976 Dodge Jamboree as the newest resident of the storied hill country and absolute greenest in a hallowed lineage of Texas songwriters. Hiromi will be in Japan February 1-21 but will resume classes when she gets back Hiromi Vardy is a certified Zen Shiatsu, Yang style Tai Chi, and Zhineng Qigong healer and practitioner. She first encountered Tai Chi in 1973 while studying theater design and performance art in London. Initially drawn to the beauty of the movements, she soon discovered that the practice had a profound effect on her consciousness, awakening a deep interest in the healing arts. While collaborating on stage with dancers in London, Hiromi began treating injuries in overworked bodies. In 1976, after a serious accident that resulted in loss of circulation in her leg and concern about possible amputation, she turned to daily Tai Chi practice, self-massage, and treatment from a Japanese acupuncturist. This experience became a turning point in her healing journey and led her back to Japan, where she studied Shiatsu at the Namikoshi School and trained at the Zen Shiatsu Center under Shizuto Masunaga. After moving to the United States with her family in 1987, Hiromi continued deepening her practice and teaching. During a period of significant stress later in her life, she encountered Master Ming Tong Gu and began studying Zhineng (wisdom healing) Qigong under his guidance, eventually becoming licensed to teach. The healing shift she experienced through this practice was profound and continues to inform her teaching today. Since 2013, Hiromi has been dedicated to teaching Zhineng Qigong, expanding her offerings to include online classes in 2020. Her work invites students to explore the foundations of Qigong and Tai Chi as embodied, healing practices that cultivate awareness, vitality, and resilience.

5f0f493b-af96-4723-8fc6-e21c225868d3: Restaurateur, entrepreneur, and New York Times- bestselling author Danny Meyer reveals the secrets of his widely admired leadership philosophy and the tools he uses to build an energized, cohesive, and motivated culture. “Danny Meyer’s stories and lessons are as memorable as the flavors in his restaurants. I’ve been waiting two decades for this book, and it was worth it.”—Adam Grant, #1 New York Times bestselling author of Hidden Potential and Think Again and host of the podcast Re:Thinking NY Times article must-read! In 2006, Danny Meyer owned eleven restaurants, was nurturing a single parkside burger kiosk called Shake Shack, and had just written a bestselling book, Setting the Table, about his company’s unique culture of Enlightened Hospitality. On the first page of that book, Danny proudly declared that in twenty-five years he had never closed a restaurant. But just a few years later, he shuttered his beloved Tabla, a decision that filled him with shame—but sparked a reckoning within him about what it means to be a leader. Danny realized that his fear of failure wasn’t just misguided: it was also an impediment to his innate entrepreneurial spirit. In What Could Possibly Go Right?, he takes the reader along on his journey to learn how he’s delivered a winning culture of excellence at scale. Businesses and organizations have long understood how to scale systems of production. But it's a much trickier challenge to scale uplifting human relationships, particularly in a fluid, growing organization—one that has now spawned 700 businesses spread across twenty-four countries. As Danny writes, “Along the way, I’ve tripped and scraped my knee more times than I can count, and yet the general trajectory has been upward and to the right.” What Could Possibly Go Right? offers fascinating, lively stories from the last twenty years of Danny’s career, along with plenty of his trademark mantras (D.F.S—Don’t F’ing Settle; Change Your Grip; and Think Like a Winemaker) and leadership concepts (the Hospitality Quotient; the Rule of Two; and the Four Gears of Leadership). Together, they offer an insightful, practical, and transformative roadmap for success, yes, but more important: for making things that matter and endure. Danny believes that culture is an aspiration, not a destination. When you get your culture on the right path in any field, your missteps end up mattering far less than the innumerable lives you’ll have changed for the better. **** Danny Meyer is the New York Times bestselling author of Setting the Table, a book on his leadership philosophy of Enlightened Hospitality; the founder of Shake Shack, which he began as a hot-dog cart in Madison Square Park; and the founder of Union Square Hospitality Group (USHG), which has created some of New York’s most beloved and acclaimed restaurants, including Union Square Cafe, Gramercy Tavern, The Modern, Maialino, Eleven Madison Park, Tabla and more. He has been named a TIME 100 Most Influential Person and won the 2017 Julia Child Award; USHG has won twenty-eight James Beard Awards. Danny and his wife, Audrey, live in New York City and have four children. Danny Meyer - photo credit WaitWhat, Inc. dbd07dcf-e4d9-4067-a54c-3926adcce195: Description What becomes possible when we truly listen? This is a 2-hour introductory workshop in Imagery and Music — an experiential group practice inspired by the Bonny Method of Guided Imagery and Music (GIM), a recognized music-psychotherapy modality. You'll lie down, relax, and listen to two curated classical music programs that open space for inner imagery, emotion, and insight to surface. Then, you’ll give that experience form through simple mandala drawing. No musical or art background is needed; the only requirement is a willingness to listen. Most of the time, we listen to music. Here, we listen from inside it and music becomes less something you hear than somewhere you go. During the evening, we will: Enter a guided relaxation - Experience two curated classical music journeys - Create simple mandalas for integration — not as art, but as a way of catching what words would flatten (no experience needed) - Share reflections (optional) - Explore how Imagery and Music differs from just talking about our experiences Rather than using words, this practice lets it arrive as image, color, weight, motion — the language the psyche actually speaks. No substance is involved, only music, deep relaxation, and attention. Yet the states it opens are real: the same expanded awareness Helen Bonny first observed in psychedelic sessions, reached through sound alone. The Psychedelic Lineage: GIM was developed by Helen Bonny directly out of her work using music to support LSD-assisted therapy at the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center, where she joined the research team in 1969 alongside Stanislav Grof, Walter Pahnke, and Joan Kellogg. Bonny discovered that music, not the substance, was often the true catalyst for change. Facilitating sessions without the drug, she found that carefully selected classical music, combined with deep relaxation and verbal guidance, could open similar altered states and therapeutic imagery on its own. The mandala practice this evening traces to that same era, from Bonny's collaboration with Joan Kellogg, comparing inner imagery with the mandalas participants drew after their sessions. Today, GIM's principles are widely recognized as foundational to modern psychedelic-assisted therapy, informing how music is used to structure the arc of various psychedelic assisted therapies sessions, support emotional release, and facilitate integration. For those in the KAP and psychedelic-assisted space Whether you come as a client or a practitioner, this practice offers a structured, music-supported path for continued inner exploration and integration, between sessions, or as a standalone depth practice. This experience may resonate if you are: - Curious about music and consciousness - Seeking an experiential alternative to talk therapy - Looking for new ways to integrate mystical or non-ordinary experiences - Wanting to explore your inner world in a structured, safe way No musical background is required — only a willingness to listen. Please arrive no later than 7:10 pm. Doors will be locked to keep a safe container. *This event series honors Helen Bonny's 1973 book Music and Your Mind: Listening with a New Consciousness, the popular work that introduced her method of music-centered inner exploration. Teacher Bio: Sophia Wang is a violinist, board-certified music therapist (MT-BC), integration practitioner, and life coach whose work centers on music, imagery, and non-ordinary states of consciousness. With over a decade of clinical experience across oncology, palliative care, and mental health settings, she draws on Guided Imagery and Music, expressive arts, and depth-oriented inquiry to support emotional healing, insight, and meaningful change. Sophia works with people across a wide range of inner terrain: those in cancer care or facing the end of life; people moving through grief, depression, or anxiety; and high-performing professionals and seekers drawn to deeper self-inquiry and the integration of transformative experiences. Her approach blends clinical training with creative exploration, emphasizing safety, pacing, and integration. She holds an MA in Music Therapy from New York University and a BA in Violin Performance from Tongji University, and a Certificate in Psychedelic-Assisted Therapies and Research at the California Institute of Integral Studies (CIIS), and is an advanced trainee in the Bonny Method of Guided Imagery and Music.

Janet Thornburg (writer/performer) is a soloist whose solo show Cognitive Divine won the Best Full-Length Comedy award in the In Front of Your Eyes Festival 2026 at the Marsh. She has written and performed eight solo shows in San Francisco at venues including The Marsh, StageWerx Theatre, Theatre Rhinoceros, Theatre of Yugen, Venue Nine, Next Stage Theatre,Young Performers’ Theatre, and the Solo Mio Festival. Her multi-character play Dinner Roles was presented at the San Francisco Repertory Theatre, and her play Antony and Cleopatra Meet Godzilla enjoyed two runs at the Intersection Theatre. She holds an MFA in playwriting from San Francisco State University and an MFA in fiction from Warren Wilson College. Her fiction has been widely published in literary journals, and Rhubarb Pie , a collection of her short stories, was published by Thunderegg Press. For further information about her performances and publications, visit www.janetthornburg.com. 313149ea-e218-42ca-afd1-5f02a727f77a: (Please do not bring infants to the show) Born into a radical theater company, Joyful Raven was tasked from the tender age of 5 with the daunting mission to save the world from impending doom… using theater. Forced into animal-print unitards and political positions long before she was a consenting adult, she never had a fighting chance at anything resembling a normal life. You think your parents were embarrassing? Did you have to sing about salmon sex on stage, in a unitard, at 12 years old… WITH your parents? I didn’t think so. In an attempt to heal her hippie trauma, she runs away from home to seek solace in the arms of a spiritual teacher… and accidentally finds herself in the yoga-to-fascism pipeline. Can she save herself? Can she save the world… using theater?! Blending standup, drag, storytelling, & clown, Raven takes audiences on a dystopian and hilarious romp through the looking glass. ACTOR : Joyful Raven is an award-winning actor, director, and “story midwife” known for her powerful and thought-provoking solo shows, where she tackles thorny social issues with humor, heart, and nuance. Born into an iconic political theater family, she has been devising original work for over 20 years. Her first solo comedy, Tales of a Sexual Tomboy , was dubbed “…one of the funniest shows now on display on Bay Area stages” by the SF Chronicle, won Best of the Fringe at the 2016 San Francisco International Fringe Festival, and enjoyed an Off-Broadway run in 2017. Her latest solo show, Breed or Bust , was nominated for Best Comedy at the 2022 Hollywood Fringe Festival, critically acclaimed at the 2023 Edinburgh Fringe, where it won an Offie (OffWestEnd Award), and went on to have an extended run at The Marsh, where it received a Critics’ Pick in the SF Chronicle. She co-founded the award-winning theater company Rococo Risqué and co-authored four plays for the Prize of Hope-winning company Human Nature. As an actor, she has appeared in numerous stage and film projects, including Odyssey Works, the film The Pursuit of Happyness alongside Will Smith, and Spring Awakening, directed by Stafford Arima. Joyful holds an MFA in Dramatic Art from the University of California, Davis, and teaches solo performance and storytelling at Berkeley Rep School of Theatre, The Marsh, and her own studio in Berkeley. Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/joyfulraven/ Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/joyful.raven DIRECTOR : Jael Weisman , a founding member of the Dell’Arte Players Co. and a multi-Obie-winning director, is a trailblazer in actor-based theater, directing acclaimed productions like “Whiteman Meets Bigfoot,” “Performance Anxiety,” and “Mad Love.” With Dell’Arte, his works have toured extensively in South America and Europe, earning him numerous Dramalogue Awards for Directing. Noteworthy projects include “The Dragon Lady’s Revenge,” which traveled to New York and was awarded an Obie, the American premiere of “Red Noses” at the San Diego Repertory Co., “Uncle Gunjiro’s Girlfriend” at the Adelaide Festival, and “Mermaid Meat” for the Berkeley Symphony Orchestra. He has collaborated with luminaries like Carlo Mazzone-Clementi and Joe Chaikin and worked with renowned Bay Area performance artists including Jeff Raz and Brenda Wong Aoki. In his early career, he worked with The San Francisco Mime Troupe, directing among other things “The Dragon Lady’s Revenge,” which was awarded an Obie. Weisman holds a BA from Reed College and an MFA from Carnegie Tech Lighting Design : Kiara Valderrama Show Photos : Cynthia Smalley It is with great love and a deep bow of gratitude that I roast by inimitable parents, Jane Lapiner and David Simpson and their theater company Human Nature. 4d4d519a-5293-4ec9-8ba4-72e5dc7ed8c3: Trailblazer of this generation's newfound Soul/ R&B era · Who is the man who consistently sells out all of the sophisticated & chic venues throughout North America, like City Winery, and legendary venues all around Europe like The Jazz Café in London for several consecutive nights? Dwele (pronounced dwell-lá) hails from the legendary music mecca of Detroit and lives a life in song. From stirring melodies composed on piano keys, he writes poignant music, performs with natural grace, and captivates with his clear, silky tone. He is a songwriter, producer, multi-instrumentalist, and vocalist carrying on a Motown-inspired tradition, instilled in another era. Yet Dwele has cultivated his own spirited road with five critically acclaimed albums "Subject", "Some Kinda", "Sketches Of A Man", "W.ants W.orld W.omen" and "Greater Than One" behind him. His Motor City story in sounds and upbringing resonates with genuine soul, and he's in full stride of scriting his own musical legacy. Dwele was brought up in a highly musical family that was tragically pared down to his mother and younger brother, once his father was gunned down outside their home. Dwele was only 10. ''The loss of my Father really inspired my creative side," Dwele recalls. "By getting into music, it provided me with a way to cope with his death." Dwele's music impresses with maturity beyond his years. He captures the rawness of inner city blues with hip-hop nuances that speak to his generation and beyond. His ear was shaped by Donny Hathaway, Marvin Gaye, and Miles Davis, which his family played regularly in their home. What is most compelling about Dwele's work is its timeless nature and the fact that he remains loyal to his foundation. As a multiple Grammy Award Nominee and a shared win with legendary rap icon Kanye West, he has blazed a trail for this generation's newfound Soul/ R&B era. Although being the humble young man that he is, Dwele says, " ... No matter how many Grammy nominations that I receive, I've always repped Detroit to the best of my abilities. That feeling is like exhaling, to be home while riding in the car upon my return. I see the sights, and I'm back," he muses. "When I sit down at the keyboard, as soon as I get home, the material just flows out." Dwele has toured around the globe with sold-out crowds in his wake and still seeks to mystify his audience, which makes them eagerly anticipate what his next move will be. Deemed by media queen Wendy Williams as one of "Big R&B's Best Kept Secrets", there's no doubt he has surpassed the benchmark of just getting a "Hit Record" but more so a "Hit Career." With all of that said ... It's no wonder why he was the first one chosen by McDonald's as their National Brand Ambassador for the "face and voice " of their launch of McCafe in North America. With a multitude of television appearances on Jay Leno, Jimmy Kimmel, MTV Base in Europe, and the BBC Studios Live, Dwele shows no signs of slowing. Especially since " ... He's The People's Choice," says Ronald Ron E. Estill, head of REvision/Rt Music Group, who has guided his career since inception, "it's been proven by the rave reviews for ALL of his albums." So, it's hard to even imagine when he says that "His Best is Yet to Come ... "

413af4bb-6c91-49f6-ab00-8a95b56a654e: This layered multigenerational novel follows three sisters upholding their family’s Tennessee pearl farm legacy. Rich with emotional depth and anchored by the pearl’s symbolism of beauty born from irritation, this story of resilience will captivate fans of Ann Patchett, Celeste Ng, and Claire Lombardo. Three estranged sisters—Helen, Anna, and Penn Lockshire—are bound by the shimmering but fragile legacy of their family’s freshwater pearl farm in rural Tennessee. When the business that once made them famous faces collapse, the sisters are pulled back into each other’s lives and forced to reckon with old betrayals, unspoken resentments, and the complicated truth of their inheritance. Soon, what began as a fight for survival becomes a reckoning with the myths that shaped them and the secrets buried in the family’s past. From the discovery of a rare pearl in 1981 to the struggles of a failing farm in 2008, the Lockshire sisters must navigate love, loss, ambition, and forgiveness to decide whether their heritage is a blessing to preserve—or a burden to escape. Rich with emotional depth and anchored by the pearl’s enduring symbolism—a thing of beauty born from irritation—this sweeping story of family, identity, and resilience will captivate readers of Celeste Ng and Claire Lombardo. “Gordon expertly handles her ambitious narrative and sprawling cast . . . A textured tale of renewed kinship and self-discovery.” —Kirkus Reviews “Heart-warming story of sisterhood, purpose, and family legacy.” —BookLife Reviews “ The Pearl Farmers was such a satisfying read . . . It’s an uplifting tale that resonates in these times.” —Ann Bancroft, author of Almost Family “I fell in love with Penny, Helen, and Anna, and was pulling for these three sisters to find a way back to each other. The Pearl Farmers is Yellowstone meets Little Women —but with way better jewelry!” —Emma Tourtelot, author of No One You Know Stacey Gordon grew up in the Appalachian foothills of southern Ohio and began her career as a trade journalist covering the cultured pearl and jewelry industries, visiting farms across Asia and companies around the world. For the past twenty-five years she’s worked in marketing and user experience design for the Silicon Valley tech industry. This is her debut novel. She lives with her family in Alameda, California. 0b4d665c-f0ca-424f-9b75-06be258e6a2b: A throwback to family-reads-of-yore, this epic follows a troubled boy and a host of hilariously vexed animals who must save a river before it’s dammed, so they can save themselves. Perfect for ages 10+ and all adults! School Library Journal: Review of the Day “Kirk Lombard’s The Shadow Stream is a book of great originality, a book like no other, propelled by brilliant storytelling and original thinking (and fish!) that will engage readers of all ages — a perfect family book.” — Mark Kurlansky, author of Cod and Salt and World Without Fish Gabriel (“G” for short) is wasting away in the Abiddon County Juvenile Center when he’s introduced to the Shongunk River by his dying uncle. The river valley — trash-heaped but chock-full of mysteries and fish — wins G over. But, as G has learned, good things can’t last. The Shongunk is scheduled to be dammed by a local developer. In a matter of days, it will cease flowing, and all of the talkative creatures who live in the river valley will be as homeless as G. Just as G decides it’s no time to accept his fate, so too do the animals. To inspire an uprising, a young trout is nominated to make a fateful journey up the river; a raccoon swears a violent oath against humans; and a newly sober buck leads his skittish flock out of harm’s way. Together with G, they show there is power in all of us, even the smallest minnow. Kirk Lombard is an author, angler, sustainable fishmonger and tuba player who worked inside the juvenile rehabilitation system. His first book, the award-winning Sea Forager’s Guide to the Northern California Coast , was described as “poetry” for fish, by NPR. He lives in the Bay Area with his family, raising his children on herring and sea shanties. 5895be96-05df-43cc-92de-d5c19c3c22bb: What if sound is something you felt in the body as much as heard in your ears? Long before it was music, sound served as medicine, prayer, and portal — a technology for shifting consciousness that predates language itself. Join Grammy-nominated artist and teacher Radhika Vekaria for an immersive afternoon built around direct, felt experience: exploring mantra and the intelligence of sound through your own body, breath, and voice. Through direct practice and philosophical insight, this session works with sound as an organizing intelligence, one that refines focus, strengthens presence, and cultivates inner coherence. This is active work: chanting, mudras, and breath practice done together as a group. You will explore: - The relationship between sound and resilience - The deeper meaning behind mantra - Chant as a practice of clarity and courage - Mudra and Nāda yoga as embodied extensions of the practice Rooted in yogic philosophy and grounded in contemporary life, this immersion offers an approach to cultivating steadiness, awareness, and peace. No prior experience is required. The afternoon closes with a 75-minute live performance with Radhika singing in a communal setting, drawing on the same deep lineage that guides the whole workshop. Teacher Bio: Radhika Vekaria is a Grammy®-nominated artist and composer working at the crossing point of Sanskrit and Vedic sacred sound and contemporary music. Her voice draws on devotional and contemporary vocal styles as well as Hindustani classical tradition — she studied for several years under Meher Paralikar, a disciple of Padma Bhushan Pandit Ajoy Chakrabarty of the Patiala-Kasur gharana — alongside classical piano trained since childhood. That grounding shows up in every performance: precise, disciplined, and unmistakably rooted in lineage, even as the music itself moves into new territory. Her project SAPTA: The Seven Ways, an exploration of Vedic mantra, became a healing practice for everyone who encountered it, and made her the first mantra artist to perform at SXSW in 2022. Her 2025 album Warriors of Light earned a Grammy nomination and extended that same inquiry into how ancient sound moves through a contemporary ear. Named after Radha, the Vedic symbol of devotion, she treats sacred sound as a living practice — one she has carried from concert stages to sacred gatherings across the globe. Radhika has performed at Harvard, Omega Institute, the Grammy Museum, and prestigious venues like Estelle Manor and Naviva, reflecting the wide lens through which she is able to convey this wisdom and reach people. Growing up in a British East African Indian family, Radhika was immersed in Vedic rituals since childhood. Learning music from early infancy and with continuous exploration of the multiple arenas of Vedic traditions and philosophy, she has a refreshing approach to how this wisdom can be imbibed and applied in the world today. In 2022, her live audio rooms online reached over 100,000 people with meditation and mantra sessions. She offers a room an experience of return — voice and mantra used deliberately to move people from thinking into feeling, from the head to the heart. That instinct shapes both her performances and her workshops: through similar sessions, she works directly with people's own relationship to sound and voice, drawing on the same tradition and training behind her stage work. For a space built around inquiry and embodied practice, she brings a performance to be moved by, and a practice to be moved through. Explore more at www.radhikavekaria.com

4425820a-7b08-4636-aedb-4133a4f1159e: Andrea Brewster, Draft 1, 2026, giclee print, woven vellum, 10″ x 10″, photo courtesy of the artist Andrea Brewster’s new body of work, Draft, begins with the fundamental structure of weaving: warp and weft, whose interlacing creates both fabric and an underlying grid. She approaches the grid not as a rigid system, but as a living structure capable of variation, interruption, rhythm, and ambiguity. The work draws from weaving drafts, diagrams that function as instructions for generating complex patterns, resembling a form of pre-digital code. The term “draft” also refers to an initial idea or work in progress, connecting structure with imagination and instruction with image.This connection between weaving and digital systems is central to Brewster’s thinking. Although digitally constructed, these pieces retain the appearance of hand-drawn marks, creating a tension between material and virtual, order and improvisation. Through line, color, repetition, and interruption, Brewster explores the relationship between visible patterns and the structures beneath them. Bio: Andrea Brewster is a multidisciplinary artist who investigates the intersection of nature, fiber art, and technology through intricate forms and layered textures. Brewster earned a B.A. in Sculpture from Pomona College and an M.F.A. in New Genres from the San Francisco Art Institute. A 1993 NEA grant recipient, she has exhibited widely in the San Francisco Bay Area, with solo shows at Mercury 20, The Lab, and Southern Exposure, as well as group exhibitions at Metal Haus Gallery, Chandra Cerrito Contemporary, The Oakland Museum, and the Peninsula Museum. Her work has been featured in fiber art exhibitions in Ireland and the U.S. She has participated in the Djerassi Resident Artist Program, and in 2025, her AI work appeared at Load Gallery, Barcelona, and in the book Neo Botanica. She has been a member of Mercury 20 Gallery since 2020. bbc0f6b3-54cc-4ef5-b10e-2262ff88de9d: Jill McLennan, Walter, 900 years old, watercolor, collage, ink, 26″x20″. photo by artist Jill McLennan’s work gives voice to the harmless, reflecting on the federal government’s decision to rescind the definition of harm (2026) as it applies to the protection of animals and their habitats, listed under the Endangered Species Act (1975). In her art, she depicts animals adapting, inventing new ways to thrive amidst human impact. Using sumi ink, a brush, and mulberry paper, she paints mammals, birds, amphibians, plants, trees, and rivers. Then, tearing the paper, she applies these images to wood panels. Adding watercolor and handmade paper, she creates a transformation from reality to wonder. McLennan states, “The animals are here alongside us, they have always been here, and it is our duty to ensure that they remain, that their habitat is here on earth for generations to come. May my art be a message to harm less, a cry to the present and a hope for the future.” Bio: Jill McLennan creates paintings, collages and prints inspired by her surroundings and the stories that she collects. She has been a member of Mercury 20 Gallery since 2007. She is an active member of her neighborhood, Jingletown Arts, Business + Community (JABC), organizing Open Studios as well as beautification projects. She recently printed a series of linoleum blocks with poems, telling stories of migration and climate change, through a residency at the Kala Art Institute in Berkeley, CA. McLennan has completed two public art projects: Jingletown Birds at 401 Derby and Emeryville Perspectives at 65th and Christie Streets. Both are cut steel fences depicting the local shoreline with birds, designed by McLennan and executed by local metal fabricators. Her work was accepted to the deYoung Open in 2020 and 2023. As an artist and teacher, she is deeply invested in protecting her environment, inspiring the youth, and spreading hope and joy into the world. 2306c9c2-971b-445d-8d27-f4ffa39efbac: RSVP and reserve your tickets here Please join the GLBT Historical Society and Crowded Fire Theater as we jointly present the first of two staged readings of How to Live in a House on Fire , a new play by Kari Barclay and directed by M. Graham Smith. Presented for the first time in the San Francisco Bay Area where the story takes place, this staged reading of a new play by performance scholar Kari Barclay looks to queer history as a lens to understand our current moment of climate grief. Attendees to the program will be treated with a live staged reading of the new play with a cast of actors, followed by a talkback discussion with the creative team after the show and an opportunity to share audience feedback and participate in the development process! About the play HOW TO LIVE IN A HOUSE ON FIRE asks how we care for each other in moments of crisis. It builds on a quote from Tennessee Williams: "We live in a perpetually burning building, and what we must save from it, all the time, is love." The Chateau Homosexuel is a gay commune on the brink of collapse. It's 1970 in Berkeley, California, and as characters bicker over the future of gay liberation, Benny and Jeremy are falling in love. When they try to decide what to do with an eviction notice, suddenly something starts burning in the oven. Smoke fills the stage, and Benny and Jeremy re-enter in K95 masks. We're transported to 2020 in the same house in the midst of the California wildfires. Benny and Jeremy are married, and they're figuring out what to bring with them in preparation for an evacuation. As they sort their belongings and try to pack fifty years of queer history into a cardboard box, they're confronted with what histories to remember and what to forget. SPEAKERS Kari Barclay (they/them) is a playwright, director, and theater maker interested in deepening audiences’ sense of time and sparking curiosity about sexuality and gender. Based in Cleveland, Ohio, they serve as Associate Professor of Theater at Oberlin College. Kari is a 2026 Dramatist Guild Foundation National Fellow and Ohio Arts Council Individual Excellence in Playwriting awardee. Kari's playwriting and directing has shown at Ars Nova, Cleveland Public Theatre, convergence-continuum, and Duke University, among other theaters. Kari’s original comedy Can I Hold You? was one of the first full-length plays about asexuality performed in the U.S. and enjoyed a sold-out run in San Francisco and workshop in New York. It has been taught at colleges and universities across the country and published in Marathi language translation. Kari’s play Stonewallin’ was the winner of the 2021 Southern Queer Playwriting Festival and opened at Richmond Triangle Players in February 2022. In their other life, Kari is a theater scholar and historian. Their nonfiction book, Directing Desire , examines the rise of intimacy choreography in theater and is out now from Palgrave Macmillan. Kari earned their PhD in Theater and Performance Studies in 2021 from Stanford University, where they studied with playwright Young Jean Lee. kari-barclay.com . Lynne Kaufman ( Playwright ) is the author of 20 full-length plays that have been produced in San Francisco, Los Angeles, Washington D.C., and Louisville at such theatres as Magic Theatre, Actors Theatre of Louisville, TheatreWorks Silicon Valley, and many more –with Shameless Hussy being her most recent work which premiered at The Marsh San Francisco spring 2025. Four of Kaufman’s plays, Extreme Acts, Acid Test, Two Minds , Who Killed Sylvia Plath , and Poetic Justice, have premiered on stage at The Marsh, while two others, Exposing Margaret Mead and The Smartest Woman in America, have appeared on The Marsh’s digital platform MarshStream. Who Killed Sylvia Plath went on to win Best Play in The Marsh’s 2020 MarshStream International Solo Festival. Kaufman’s plays have won many awards including the Glickman Award for Best New Play ( The Couch ), the Kennedy Center’s Fund for New American Plays Award ( Speaking in Tongues ), and the Neil Simon Festival New Play Award ( William Blake in Hollywood ). Kaufman has published four novels, and her short stories have appeared in Cosmopolitan , Redbook , and McCall’s . She was also the recipient of the Otis Guernsey Outstanding New Voice in American Theatre Award from the William Inge Theatre Festival. Warren David Keith ( Director ) is delighted to be reunited with Playwright Lynne Kaufman. His work with her began in 2012 with the Marsh Berkeley premier of Acid Test: The Many Incarnations of Ram Dass , a solo piece in which he played the title role. The play was extended twice in Berkeley then transferred for one performance to a massive tent on Maui, Hawaii where it was seen and enjoyed by Ram Dass and about 300 devoted followers. Subsequently, Acid Test opened at the Marsh San Francisco in 2013 where it also had several runs. Keith has acted in theaters throughout the Bay Area, most recently in 1984 at the Aurora Theatre Company and as the Porter in the California Shakespeare Theater’s production of Macbeth . His film credits include Nomadland , The Last Black Man in San Francisco , Haiku Tunnel , Love and Taxes , Raising Arizona , Fargo , A Serious Man , and The Big Lebowski . As a director he mounted more than 15 productions for American Conservatory Theater’s Young Conservatory Program. He reunited with Ms. Kaufman to direct Who Killed Sylvia Plath and The Smartest Woman in America about the final days of Susan Sontag, both at the Marsh San Francisco. Arwen Anderson ( Performer ) returns to The Marsh, where she previously collaborated with Lynne Kaufman on a staged reading of her musical Map of Your Mind and performed in Kaufman’s Extreme Acts . Selected regional credits include Testmatch, Men On Boats, Heisenberg , Let There Be Love , A Christmas Carol , and Tales of the City (workshop) at American Conservatory Theater; King Lear , Romeo and Juliet , and The Verona Project at California Shakespeare Theater; August: Osage County , Anne Boleyn , Circle Mirror Transformation , Bellwether , and A Streetcar Named Desire at Marin Theatre ; An Accident , Mrs. Whitney , Expedition 6 , The Rules of Charity , and Mauritius at Magic Theatre; A White Girl’s Guide to International Terrorism, The Fit, and 77% at San Francisco Playhouse; Miss Julie at Stanford Repertory Theater; Lobby Hero and The Shape of Things at Aurora Theatre Company; You Know When the Men Are Gone and 4 Adverbs with Word for Word; and roles with American Stage Festival, San Jose Repertory Theatre, Marin Shakespeare Company, Brava Theater, Encore Theatre Company, and Central Works Theater Company. Her film work includes Hog Island , Ashley 22 , and Dark Retreat . Johnny Moreno ( Performer ) returns to The Marsh, where he previously performed in Lynne Kaufman’s Extreme Acts . He has also appeared at theaters throughout the Bay Area including American Conservatory Theater, Berkeley Repertory Theatre, San Francisco Playhouse, San Jose Stage Company, Marin Shakespeare Company, Center Repertory Company, Marin Theatre , Crowded Fire Theater, and Pacific Repertory Theatre. He has played award winning roles, such as Macheath in San Francisco Playhouse’s production of The Threepenny Opera (Theatre Bay Area Award for Best Actor in a Musical) , and Henry Higgins in San Francisco Playhouse’s production of My Fair Lady (San Francisco Bay Area Theatre Critics Circle Award for Best Actor in a Musical). He has appeared in numerous film and television productions, such as “Betas,” Callback (winner of the Chicago Indie Fest for Best Film), Upside Out (with Olympia Dukakis), Paradise Club, and I’m Still Here (with Joaquin Phoenix). California Shakespeare Theater, Center Repertory Theatre, B Street Theatre, Capital Stage, San Francisco Shakespeare Festival, San Jose Stage. FILM/TELEVISION: Trauma, All About Evil, The Optimist . b9fe64fe-5481-455b-947c-fc106aacd356: Join Anjuli and Alok for an incredible opportunity to study the practice of ZenThai Massage and develop your sensitivity and awareness through touch. Dive into the world of ZenThai Massage with experienced practitioners Alok and Anjuli, who have over 20+ years of experience as therapists and teachers. Their welcoming and supportive approach helps students feel safe and empowered as they hone their healing touch skills. Join them for a rewarding day of exchanging deeply nourishing bodywork and gaining the tools and guidance needed to further refine your own practice. Anjuli & Alok have traveled the globe, studying under esteemed master teachers and crafting their unique style of bodywork. During this daylong immersion, they'll share their ZenThai practice, blending Thai Massage and Shiatsu techniques passed down by their mentor Gwyn Williams from Australia. Rooted in Thai Medicine and Buddhist Zen philosophy, their approach emphasizes respect, balance, and compassion. They'll also cover Chinese Meridians and specific acupressure points, enriching the practice even further. ZenThai Shiatsu is an exceptional therapeutic technique that incorporates joint mobilization, mindful passive stretching, acupressure, and a focus on breath. With proper body mechanics, the practice truly becomes an effortless dance between giver and receiver. As yogis themselves, your teachers will be emphasizing the most fluid and easeful ways to offer compressions and stretching in this course, encouraging the giver to stay present with the receiver’s experience. This training welcomes everyone, whether you're a yoga teacher, massage therapist, or simply interested in well-being and bodywork. You'll wear comfortable clothing and work on a mat. They’ll guide you through simple practices to enhance sensitivity and intuition, focusing on the client's experience while caring for your own body as well. You’ll practice both giving and receiving throughout the immersion, regardless of prior yoga or massage experience. Feel free to come alone or with a friend—no partner required. In addition to all that you will learn during the immersion, you’ll also receive a complete manual, videos, and have access to our community. Come with a friend or solo - no partner needed. There will be a one hour break for lunch. In this course you will learn: + How to give a full body sequence and bring someone up to seated + How to cultivate energy and develop sensitivity + How to use your full body and weight for effective and deep massage + Bio-mechanics to give a massage with the least effort + Thai Yoga moves to adjust, balance and correct yoga postures + Basic principles of Chinese Meridians and Acupressure points + Tools to work with special conditions and injuries + An introduction to mindfulness and breathing

8acc4dd7-eadb-4cc3-9de8-6f70c06acf9d: Mothers and Daughters: Writing Formative Relationships in Memoir What does it mean to reckon with the past and find yourself on the other side? In this panel, three She Writes Press memoirists, Robin Rosenbluth, Georgine Hodgkinson, and Rosanne Annoni, explore the profound and complicated ways their mothers shaped them, and the unexpected journeys that led each of them home to herself. From a young white woman navigating the semi-nomadic communities of 1970s Kenya while carrying the wounds of the U.S. foster care system, to a spiritual seeker tracing the long arc between a childhood vision of Christ and a solitary winter at Gampo Abbey, to a college professor who upended her carefully controlled life for the wilds of Puerto Rico's cryptocurrency scene, these are stories of displacement, desire, and hard-won transformation. Moderated by She Writes Press publisher Brooke Warner, this panel is an invitation to explore those moments that break us open and the unlikely places where healing takes root. Each of these memoirs reminds us that growing up isn't something that happens only in childhood, and that our mothers, for better or worse, are the first maps any of us is given to navigate ourselves and our lives. Robin Rosenbluth is a former foster teen who advocates for finding permanent homes for older foster youth. She has worked in the nonprofit sector in New York as a fundraiser, an adjunct professor at Columbia University and New York University. She has studied memoir and the craft of writing with many renowned authors and writes a Substack, My Jagged Journey as a Debut Writer . Robin and her wife have raised two children who now have families of their own. She lives in Brooklyn, New York. Rosanne Annoni was a successful psychotherapist for thirty-five years in the Bay Area before becoming an ordained teacher of the Diamond Approach in 2000. She has taught students and mentored teachers in the United States, the UK, and the EU. In 2024, she was awarded an Emerging Writer Fellowship from Aspen Words. She is married, has one son, and lives with her husband and dog on Cape Cod. Georgine Hodgkinson is a professor of communication studies at Cosumnes River College in Sacramento, where she also served as program coordinator for Re-Emerging Scholars, a program for formerly incarcerated students. Her published scholarship includes book chapters, journal articles, and essays exploring politics, gender, and spirituality. In 2025, she was a People’s Choice Winner for the Amy MacRae International Memoir Award. A certified yoga instructor who loves to run and play pickleball, Georgine splits her time between Dorado, Puerto Rico, and Folsom, California, with her husband, Mark. Brooke Warner is publisher of She Writes Press, a memoir coach, and author of Write On, Sisters!, Green-light Your Book, What's Your Book?, and three books on memoir. She’s a TEDx speaker, weekly podcaster (of “Write-minded” with co-host Grant Faulkner of NaNoWriMo), and publishes a weekly newsletter, Writerly Things, on Substack at brookewarner.substack.com . 3b2763ae-6a70-475c-8ee5-a0d177483736: Dissecting the Data Center Backlash · Data centers have quickly gone from virtually invisible to the target of the public’s ire, such that Oakland recently passed a 45-day moratorium on new data center projects. Join Hyperscale author Paris Marx for a conversation with Alex Hanna about the tech industry’s buildout of hyperscale data centers, what’s driving the opposition to them, and whether we really need to accept the future being foisted on us by Silicon Valley’s billionaires. In Hyperscale , journalist Paris Marx uncovers the excesses of hyperscale data processing. He exposes the deceptive, exploitative ways tech companies are siphoning energy and resources from vulnerable communities in their pursuit of digital power, abandoning the pretense of social responsibility. Amid energy shortages and tech-induced battles over drinking water, Marx makes a powerful case for technology that promotes the social good over the bottom lines of tech billionaires. He joins the incredible efforts of people and social movements pushing back against the profit-driven interests of Big Tech, illuminating a path toward the sustainable future we all deserve. Paris Marx is a Canadian tech critic and host of the acclaimed Tech Won’t Save Us podcast. He speaks around the world about the politics of technology and writes the Disconnect newsletter. Paris is the author of Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires . Dr. Alex Hanna is a writer and sociologist of technology, labor, and politics. She is the Director of Research at the Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR). With Emily M. Bender, Dr. Hanna is the co-author of The AI Con (Harper, 2025), a book about AI and the hype around it. They also run the Mystery AI Hype Theater 3000 series, playfully and wickedly tearing apart AI hype on their livestream and podcast. Her next book, under contract with MIT Press, is about ImageNet, a dataset of 14 million images which helped build modern AI practices.

db847257-cf52-42e0-a7b6-d0b015bca9ae: Prize-winning historian Kevin Waite uncovers an extraordinary story of survival in this first book-length biography of Biddy Mason. The narrative follows Mason's journey from the cotton South to metropolitan California, detailing how she crossed the continent, broke free from slavery, and built Black Los Angeles. Through the lens of the Civil War, Reconstruction, and the dawn of Jim Crow, Waite reveals Mason's profound impact on California's history. Los Angeles’s leading Black property owner entered the city as a piece of property herself. Born enslaved in 1818, Biddy Mason was forcibly transported 3,000 miles to California before winning her freedom in a landmark 1856 court case. By the time of her death, she had become one of the wealthiest African Americans in the West – an entrepreneur, philanthropist, and founding mother of Black Los Angeles. The Boundless Biddy Mason: An Odyssey from Slavery to Freedom Across the American West, Kevin Waite’s masterful biography of Mason – the first full-length study of her extraordinary life – places Mason at the center of a larger American story: the expansion of slavery into the West, the legal battles that tested freedom’s meaning, and the rise of a vibrant Black Los Angeles community she helped build. Waite documents Mason’s early years in Mississippi and follows her forced journey across the continent, as one of roughly 1,500 enslaved African Americans who were trafficked from the slave states to the frontier. Her enslaver, Robert Smith, a convert to Mormonism, marched Mason and her children from Mississippi to Utah and ultimately to California. Despite the state’s constitutional ban on slavery, Smith became the largest slaveholder in California, with fourteen people under his control. But it wasn’t until Smith attempted to relocate his human chattel to Texas that the law intervened. A pitched legal battle in Los Angeles resulted in freedom for Mason, her three daughters, and ten other women and children. From that moment forward, Mason reshaped her destiny – and the destiny of her city. She built a respected practice as a nurse and midwife, invested shrewdly in downtown real estate, cultivated influential alliances, and helped found Southern California’s first Black church. Her canny ability to disarm her denigrators with kindness and competence earned Mason a reputation as a leader. Award-winning historian Kevin Waite ably connects Mason’s life to the nation’s great upheavals: the westward expansion of slavery, the Civil War and Reconstruction, and the dawn of Jim Crow. In doing so, he restores Mason to her rightful place in American history, detailing her role as a survivor of forced migration, a litigant in a landmark freedom suit, and an architect of Black Los Angeles. Mason’s legacy in Los Angeles endures to this day, not only as founding member of the First African Methodist Episcopal Church but also in the public works she inspired. “In this astute work of historical recovery, Kevin Waite has provided us with a definitive, modern biography of the remarkable Biddy Mason…a tremendous achievement and a cautionary tale for our own fraught times.” ―Manisha Sinha, author of The Rise and Fall of the Second American Republic: Reconstruction, 1860–1920 “Combining meticulous scholarship with taut, propulsive prose, Kevin Waite tells the story of how the quietly extraordinary Biddy Mason helped break slavery's hold on Southern California. Absorbing and revelatory, this is history at its best.” —Nathaniel Philbrick, National Book Award–winning author of In the Heart of the Sea and The Rush “Kevin Waite has written the book we’ve needed for a long time. Biddy Mason was a most extraordinary woman. With great care and exhaustive research, Kevin Waite has written her biography as part of the stories of enslavement and emancipation as well as faith and community at the western edge of the United States.” —Kelly Lytle Hernández, author of Bad Mexicans Kevin Waite is Anne Stark Watson and Chester Watson Distinguished Professor of History at the University of Texas at Dallas. His first book, West of Slavery , won the 2022 Wiley-Silver Prize and was shortlisted for three other awards, including the Lincoln Prize. His writing appears in The Atlantic , the Los Angeles Times , The Washington Post , Slate , National Geographic , and The New Republic . Kevin moonlights in the TV and film industry, most recently as the writer and producer of a six-episode docuseries on the American Revolution for National Geographic and Disney+. Emerging from the powerful Los Angeles music tradition, he’s known for his deeply expressive sound, high‑energy performances, and his belief in music as a force for healing, elevation, and cultural memory. This performance highlights music from Lawrence’s new recording Turn the Music Up , a vibrant chapter in his catalog that celebrates joy, ancestral memory, and creative freedom. Over his extraordinary career, Lawrence has performed with giants such as McCoy Tyner, Miles Davis, Freddie Hubbard, Woody Shaw, Elvin Jones, Buster Williams, and Pharoah Sanders. His sound channels the spirit of John Coltrane while remaining unmistakably his own—expansive, soulful, and spiritually charged. 5de08497-c902-4676-a9e9-61316a8b359f: Mark Danner in conversation with Arlie Russell Hochschild · How do we recognize history while we are still living through it? A contested election. A war. A financial collapse. An attack on the Capitol. A democracy transformed. We experience history one event at a time. Only later do we begin to see the connections, and wonder when the world we knew began to change. In Crossing the Rubicon , journalist and political thinker Mark Danner traces twenty-six years of American political life, from the disputed election of 2000 and the War on Terror to the rise and return of Donald Trump, asking how democratic institutions have been tested, weakened, and transformed. Joining him is sociologist Arlie Russell Hochschild , author of Strangers in Their Own Land and Stolen Pride , whose work explores the emotions, identities, and experiences beneath America's political divisions. Together, they bring two extraordinary ways of seeing the same history: the political forces that shape a nation and the human lives shaped by those forces. The evening begins with a short introduction from anthropologist and Clio's founding member Cari Borja , placing the conversation within Clio's larger commitment to the history of ideas, and the importance of gathering to understand the history we are living through. The title reaches back to 49 BCE, when Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon River, setting in motion events that would help bring an end to the Roman Republic. More than two thousand years later, the question remains: How do we know when a society has crossed a threshold from which there may be no return? And what can history teach us about what comes next? Join us for an evening about democracy, power, memory, and the future we are still capable of shaping. His work has received many honors, including a National Magazine Award, three Overseas Press Awards, a Gug- genheim Fellowship, an Emmy, and a MacArthur Fellowship. He is currently Class of 1961 Distinguished Chair in Undergraduate Education at the University of California at Berkeley. Arlie Hochschild ’s latest book is Stolen Pride, Loss, Shame and the Rise of the Right . Now out in paperback with a new Afterword , it was among five non-fiction books Barack Obama selected as favorite books of 2024. It followed Strangers in Their Own Land: Anger and Mourning on the American Right , a National Book Award Finalist and New York Times bestseller. 48e17d40-b720-4d33-973e-b298addffc76: Lucid dreaming is not reserved for the special few. Rather, it is a trainable skill, and a doorway into the deeper practice of psychonavigation, the art of moving through your own psyche with clarity, intention, and skill. In this workshop, mother-daughter teaching team Norma Burton and Nisha Burton will guide participants through foundational practices that many cultures throughout history have used to work with dream and the subconscious. Participants will be introduced to lucid dreaming as an accessible, learnable practice, along with complementary inner pathways like dreamwork, shadow work, and drumming journeys. Together, these tools can help build a working map of one's own inner world, supporting healing, sharpening intuition, and strengthening the kind of discernment that can be very useful in a world saturated with noise and division. The workshop is also intended as a foundation for anyone preparing for or integrating psychedelic experiences, offering grounded skills for navigating altered states. During the workshop, participants can expect to: - Learn the fundamentals of lucid dreaming and how to begin cultivating it through simple, evidence-informed techniques - Explore dreamwork and shadow work practices for interpreting dreams and identifying unconscious patterns - Begin building a personal practice, starting with dream journaling, to carry these tools into daily life - Learn both beginning and advanced lucid dreaming techniques Rooted in nearly thirty years of Norma's work in Buddhist practice, Jungian shadow work, and trauma healing, and brought into the present through Nisha's own experience with lucid dreaming, this workshop offers an intergenerational approach to teaching — practical, embodied, and grounded in decades of lived experience. Website: luciddreaminglucidliving.com Instagram: @lucid_dreaming_lucid_living Teacher Bios: Norma J. Burton is a pioneering expert in complex trauma healing with over 40 years of counseling experience. She did M.A. and Ph.D. work at Berkeley's Graduate Theological Union, and M.Div. at Pacific School of Religion with specializations in Hospice Chaplaincy and Psychology. Her distinguished career began with a decade of leadership in domestic violence advocacy, where she served as Director of battered women's shelters around the country, before serving at the National Coalition Against Domestic Violence headquarters. In the early 1990s, Burton developed the Journey to Completion™, an innovative spiritual-psychological, trauma healing process now practiced internationally. Building on this foundation, she founded and directed The Circle of Trust Healing Center in 2014, a state-certified addiction recovery and mental health facility. Under her leadership, the center conducted groundbreaking studies demonstrating the superior effectiveness of holistic approaches in achieving lasting addiction recovery. Burton's unique blend of academic rigor, clinical expertise, and innovative methodology has positioned her at the forefront of transformative healing practices. Nisha Burton is a lucid dreaming practitioner, award-winning filmmaker, and emerging technologies consultant. Raised in a shamanic lineage, she grew up traveling the world as a child to study directly with wisdom keepers. She carries ancestral knowledge of altered states and soul work passed through Choctaw, Santee, and Cree lines, a Yoruba lineage rooted in her father's work, and a Druidic thread on her mother’s Celtic side. From an early age, she was steeped in the disciplined art of navigating one's own psyche with skill - above all through staying impeccable by doing the deep, ongoing work of shadow integration. This lineage-rooted foundation shapes how she guides others through altered states today. Along with linage based knowing she has also extensively studied Tibetan Dream Yoga, Jungian Dream Analysis, and dream researchers such as Stephen LaBerge. As co-founder of Lucid Living Inc., she delivers Lucid Dreaming workshops globally. Nisha has co-authored three books on consciousness exploration: Navigating Liminal Realms (Findhorn), Lucid Dreaming Lucid Living (Red Wheel/Wieser), and The Psychonaut's Oracle (Schiffer). She speaks internationally on consciousness navigation and AI innovation.

b06506cb-d8e9-4e14-bee1-5465dc87b69f: Joshua Jelly-Schapiro in conversation with Nadia Ellis · How does an artist change the way the world sees a place, and ultimately, itself? Harry Belafonte was more than the voice behind “Day-O,” “Jamaica Farewell,” and “Jump in the Line.” The Harlem-born son of Caribbean immigrants brought the music of the islands into American popular culture, becoming a groundbreaking performer whose influence extended far beyond the stage. But behind the music was a life of extraordinary political conviction. From his friendship with Sidney Poitier to his pivotal support of Martin Luther King Jr. and the civil rights movement, Belafonte understood that fame could become a form of power, and that power could be put to work. In Daylight Come: Harry Belafonte and the World He Made , geographer and writer Joshua Jelly-Schapiro explores the remarkable intersections of music, race, migration, celebrity, and political activism, revealing how one artist helped shape both America's imagination of the Caribbean and the course of American history. Joining him is Nadia Ellis , UC Berkeley professor of English and author of Territories of the Soul: Queered Belonging in the Black Diaspora , whose work explores Black diasporic culture, performance, and belonging. The evening begins with an introduction from cultural anthropologist and Clio's founding member Cari Borja , drawing on her doctoral fieldwork in Jamaica to consider how art and performance carry histories, identities, and ideas across borders. Together, they'll explore a question at the heart of Belafonte's life: What happens when an artist becomes not only a voice for a culture, but a force capable of changing the world? An evening about music, memory, Jamaica, the Black diaspora, and the extraordinary possibilities and contradictions, of a life lived in the public eye. Joshua Jelly-Schapiro is a geographer and writer whose books include Daylight Come: Harry Belafonte and the World He Made; Names of New York: Discovering the City’s Past, Present, and Future Through Its Place-Names; and Island People: The Caribbean and the World. He was the co-creator, with Rebecca Solnit, of Nonstop Metropolis: A New York City Atlas, which in 2016 was awarded the Brendan Gill Prize from the Municipal Art Society. His work appears regularly in The New York Review of Books, The New Yorker, and The New York Times, among many other publications, and he is a fellow of the New York Institute for the Humanities. Jelly-Schapiro teaches journalism at New York University and is director of publishing at Pioneer Works in Brooklyn, where he hosts the popular Author Talks series and is coeditor in chief of Pioneer Works Broadcast. Nadia Ellis is a professor in the English Department at UC Berkeley. She's the author of Territories of the Soul: Queered Belonging in the Black Diaspora as well as essays on contemporary Black literature and performance. She is completing a new book about Jamaican religion, ethnography, and aesthetics.

672f901f-a899-4079-b9e5-cf22ee3c1ff5: October Theme: “Broadway and Show Tunes” There’s nothing that brings people together better than singing our favorite songs. It recalls summer nights around the campfire: someone strumming the guitar and all singing a mix of folk music, familiar songs we heard on the radio, and occasional new songs that someone shares. Nobody has to worry about whether you know the songs or can sing like a pro. This is our chance to share the joy of singing simply for the fun of it. Cary Sheldon is a singer, songwriter, and beloved Berkeley voice teacher with 30 years worth of grateful students. She has been playing and teaching in the Bay Area for the last 40 years. Her love for R & B music led her to be part of Zazu Pitts Memorial Orchestra in the 1980’s. Other affiliations include The Henry Kaiser Band, The Henriettas (a recreation of DeZurick sisters, a popular country music duo from the 1940’s), who appeared on Prairie Home Companion, and most recently her band DanceChant, a joyful community-inspired R&B band that encourages audience participation. She continues to be inspired by her love of singing in community. “Singing together with others is one of the greatest joys in my life.” Now in her 60’s, she returns to influences from her early life. Her grade school music teachers included John Langstaff, creator of the Christmas Revels, and the repertoire was based on the American folk tradition, including old English ballads, spirituals, freedom songs, and the popular folk and protest songs of the 1960’s. She hopes to inspire others to explore the depth of this material and rediscover the joy of community singing. Soprano Candace Johnson has led AMN’s Juneteenth Choral Celebration since its inception in 2020. The AMN community knows her through her commitment to the power of the Negro Spirituals tradition, but Candace has a deep connection to theater and to the music of the Broadway stage. A voice instructor at UC Berkeley for 17 years, in 2022 Candace also became the director of the University Gospel Choir. A lyric coloratura soprano, she crosses musical boundaries performing classical, jazz, musical theater, pop and gospel. She has sung on many stages, including Carnegie Hall and The Manhattan Center. Also a playwright and actress, Candace premiered her first one-woman show, Vox in a Box , in UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall in 2018, which led to her becoming a resident solo artist at The Marsh theater (Berkeley/San Francisco). Candace has written and performed 5 full-length one-woman musicals. Her most recent show, Scat-ter Brain: The Music of ADHD , was commissioned by The Marsh in 2024 for its inaugural IFOYE festival of new works by women-identifying playwrights. Following an extended run, Scat-ter Brain was nominated by Broadway World SF for Best Solo Show of 2025. Please read our Health, Safety and COVID-19 Information Our commitment to our patrons
