849db8cb-5276-475d-bac1-187ccd704802: Ten years ago we bought a small plot in the Northern California redwoods. No real vision. Little experience. Just a yearning for space and a desire to build stuff with friends. The land quickly became a magnet for summer-camp type gatherings and a DIY adventure in cabin and tree deck construction. Several years in, a wildfire burned all of it to the ground. The post-fire years and projects that followed were a slower, more deliberate return and a reassessment of what the place actually meant after so much was lost. The Land is the story of that decade. Not a how-to manual, and not a polished showcase—more a record of our learning-by-doing and pushing beyond our capability and comfort. It’s a testament to approachability, and a scrapbook of experiments that champions a Just start mantra. It celebrates the personal and communal growth that comes from getting your hands dirty, and is proof of the surprising magnetism of rallying friends to build some shіt in the woods. Basically, it's a cabin-building book for folks with no plan to build one and a community-building book for those who didn't know they needed one. Jeff and Molly live in The Sunset and have a small plot of land in the Santa Cruz Mountains where they, alongside their community of friends and friends-of-friends, have built cabins, tree decks, outdoor showers, and much more. That ten-year journey, which started with almost no building experience, is documented in The Land, on their website Elevated Spaces, and on Jeff's Substack. They host a weekly sauna night in their backyard and you can check if their sauna is hot at isthesaunahot.com @elevatedspaces

8923b450-8527-4e22-8a93-6b864b575a6e: In this deeply experiential yoga practice, we will explore the dynamic interplay between stability and mobility, strength and relaxation, movement and stillness. Through mindful movement, standing and seated practices, breath, and attention to the subtle ways we organize ourselves in space, we'll investigate what allows us to feel both grounded and free. This event happens each week at the Alembic. Rather than striving for perfect alignment or mastering difficult poses, we'll approach the practice as an exploration. We'll slow down enough to notice, experiment with different possibilities, and discover how the balance between effort and ease can change our experience of movement — and of ourselves.. Teacher Bio: Vickie Russell Bell has been teaching yoga for more than 30 years, bringing together the precision of alignment-based yoga with a deep curiosity about how we inhabit our bodies, regulate our nervous systems, and move through the world. She is an E-RYT 500 and Certified Yoga Therapist (C-IAYT), and has studied with some of the most respected teachers in the Iyengar-influenced yoga tradition. Her teaching is grounded in the belief that yoga is less about mastering poses than developing a more intimate relationship with ourselves. Her classes invite students to slow down, pay attention, and explore the constantly shifting relationships between stability and mobility, strength and softness, effort and ease. She teaches students of all ages and abilities, with a particular interest in yoga as a practice for living fully and well over time.
ab3e9468-7867-46e3-8440-466e4412988b: Every Tuesday morning, the Alembic opens for a half-day of silent meditation practice. This is an unguided silent retreat consisting of three 40-minute meditation periods. There will be no teacher-led instruction during the meditation periods. Participants are invited to bring and engage in their own silent meditation practice. Whether you practice mindfulness, Zen, Vipassana, contemplation, prayer, or another silent form of meditation, all are welcome. The retreat begins promptly at 9:30 AM and concludes at 11:50 AM. Please arrive between 9:15 AM and 9:25 AM to remove your shoes, settle in, and find a seat before the first bell. The morning is divided into three periods of silent meditation: 9:30 AM – 10:10 AM 10:20 AM – 11:00 AM 11:10 AM – 11:50 AM A bell will signal the beginning and end of each meditation period. The meditation hall (Sol) is reserved for silent practice during sitting periods. Between sits, participants may quietly stretch, visit the restroom, or spend time in the tearoom. Conversation is permitted during breaks; however, we encourage participants to keep voices low, as some attendees choose to observe silence throughout the entire morning. You are welcome to leave the meditation hall at any time if needed. If you leave during a meditation period, please wait until the next break before re-entering. We ask that all entrances and exits be as quiet and unobtrusive as possible. This is a “Bring Your Own Silent Meditation” retreat. We provide the structure and the space; you provide your own silent practice. Participants may choose to sit in Sol or engage in quiet movement practice in the tearoom during meditation periods. To minimize disruption, please enter Sol only during the transition periods between sits. If you arrive after a meditation period has begun, you are welcome to practice elsewhere in the Alembic until the next bell. The suggested donation is $10. No one will be turned away for lack of funds. We do ask that all attendees register through the Momence app or via the registration link on the Alembic website. Please note that the retreat ends at 11:50 AM, and we ask all participants to depart by 12:00 PM so that our volunteer teacher and staff may close the space in a timely manner. Thank you for helping us maintain a quiet and supportive environment for practice.

999d35ea-c93e-4d1c-9c83-42b608f3100d: An evening on entrepreneurship, creativity, and human connection · Featuring Mike Alvarez Cohen, Darren Cooke, and Laura Hassner, in conversation with Missy Martin. What does it take to turn an idea into something that changes the world? Behind every successful startup is something larger than a brilliant idea: a web of relationships, organizations, and serendipitous encounters that makes innovation possible. Join us at Clio's for a conversation with Mike Alvarez Cohen , author of Startup Campus and UC Berkeley's Director of Innovation Ecosystem Development; Darren Cooke , Berkeley's Chief Innovation & Entrepreneurship Officer; and Laura Hassner , Strategic Advisor to the Chancellor and Executive Director of Innovation & Entrepreneurship. Moderated by Missy Martin , Berkeley Haas MBA '26 and founder of Cat Eye Collective, the conversation explores how Berkeley became a global center for entrepreneurship—and what it takes to create a culture where ideas flourish. The evening begins with a grounding introduction from cultural anthropologist, UC Berkeley PhD alumna, and Clio's founding member Cari Borja, asking a question at the heart of Clio's: How do ideas move between people, and what kinds of places make that movement possible? Because perhaps the most interesting thing about an entrepreneurial ecosystem isn't simply what gets built—it's what happens between the people doing the building. Together, we'll explore how ideas become ventures, how encounters become collaborations, and how the places we create can shape what becomes possible. Mike Alvarez Cohen is UC Berkeley’s Director of Innovation Ecosystem Development, where he builds partnerships and supports entrepreneurship across campus. He has worked with hundreds of startups and spearheaded the licensing of more than 100 innovations. He is the principal author of Startup Campus, which explores Berkeley’s rise as a global center for entrepreneurship and innovation. Darren Cooke is UC Berkeley’s Chief Innovation & Entrepreneurship Officer, Executive Director of the Life Sciences Entrepreneurship Center, and a faculty member at Haas. An investor, attorney, and former engineer, he has held leadership roles at Berkeley SkyDeck and Life Science Angels and taught entrepreneurship through NIH and NSF programs. Laura Hassner is Strategic Advisor to UC Berkeley Chancellor Richard K. Lyons, Executive Director of the Office of Innovation & Entrepreneurship, and a faculty member at Haas. She co-created and co-leads Berkeley Changemaker®, an academic program helping students discover their passions, develop their identities, and create meaningful change. Missy Martin is the founder of Cat Eye Collective and a recent UC Berkeley Haas MBA graduate, where she earned the inaugural AI for Business certificate and two fellowships. Her background spans early-stage startups, community building, and venture capital, including experience at Precursor Ventures, where she evaluated more than 1,100 startups. She is passionate about bringing people and ideas together across entrepreneurship, technology, sustainability, and sports. Cat Eye Collective brings people across the startup ecosystem together through experiences designed around curiosity and deep human connection. Inspired by the symbolism of a cat’s eye, the community is rooted in noticing what others overlook, asking better questions, and creating space for conversations that might not otherwise happen.

e31b6379-b415-434d-a1e6-329d10466d99: We are delighted to welcome Fiona McPhillips, Irish journalist, screenwriter, and author of When We Were Silent , to Bookshop West Portal on November 10th! We will be celebrating her new book, The Party in the Woods , an addictive, thrilling whodunit, set in the Dublin mountains. McPhillips will be joined in conversation by Sommer Schafer , Senior Editor of The Forge Literary Magazine and the author of The Women and Hope. This event is FREE to attend. Seating is first-come, first-served. (RSVPs are optional, but encouraged for our planning purposes.) About the Book: From the much-praised author Fiona McPhillips ("Excruciating suspense" -- Stephen King; "Shocking" -- NYTBR ), a novel of murder and betrayal, pulse-pounding music, and all the lives we leave behind Annie Fagan, one of Ireland's first female electronic DJs and producers, spent her early twenties hosting and playing illegal raves across Ireland. Part of a legendary free party crew, she was surrounded by loud music, beautiful people, and the alluring chaos of the dance floor. But after one of their huge parties in the woods, Annie's friend Seán disappeared without a trace, and Annie gave up that part of herself for good. Years later, when Seán's body is discovered in the Dublin mountains and new information about his disappearance comes to light, Annie reunites with her old group of friends--led by Fran Baker, the man she once believed she was destined to end up with--and feels inexplicably drawn back into the scene. Annie--and the police--starts to realize that, far from a tragic accident or random misadventure, Seán's death must have been caused by someone who was at their party. Someone who had a motive. One of her friends. As Annie investigates, her new and old worlds clash, another old friend is silenced, and she realizes that some people may not want the mystery of Seán's death to be solved. In fact, they might do anything to stop her from discovering what happened that night, when the party truly ended. About the Author: Fiona McPhillips is an Irish journalist, author and screenwriter, and an editor at The Forge literary magazine. Fiona's debut novel, When We Were Silent , was shortlisted for the Irish Book Awards, runner-up for the Crime Writers' Association Debut Dagger and named as one of the Irish Times' crime books of the year. The Party in the Woods is her second novel. About the Conversation Partner: Sommer Schafer is Senior Editor of The Forge Literary Magazine and widely published, including a Distinguished Story in Best American Short Stories 2019. She is the author of two books of fiction, The Women and Hope , both released by Unsolicited Press. She lives on Coast Miwok land with her family, a rescue dove, and a bearded dragon.

Erin-Kate has supplied her voice for hundreds of radio and industrial jobs, and has appeared in TV and film for the past 35 years. Erin-Kate is a proud member and former Board Member of Northern California’s SAG-AFTRA, where she continues to serve both as an advisor, and on various committees. She is also a member of AEA (Actors Equity Association) and AGVA (American Guild of Variety Artists). EK is a fourth generation San Franciscan, and raised her sons, the fifth generation, in San Francisco with her wife, Michele. Francine Torres (Director) is a recent transplant from New York, where she served as Head of Acting at New Studio on Broadway. Presently, she serves on faculty at Foothill College. Francine began her career under the tutelage of Luis Valdez, founder of the iconic El Teatro Campesino. Steeped in the Teatro lifestyle of performing and touring, she began work with El Teatro de la Esperanza, and played the protagonist, Ana, in the inaugural production of Real Women Have Curves . Since then, she has been committed to educating, performing, and directing theatre exploring the Chicanx experience. She has mentored and taught underrepresented students of color at historically classical theatres such as the American Conservatory Theatre, the American Repertory Theatre, and the La Jolla Playhouse. Her work also includes nearly twenty years at the American Conservatory Theatre, teaching acting, improvisation, and clown work and transitions seamlessly between street and classical theatre. As a professional actor, she has created many indelible characters during her time at El Teatro Campesino and the American Repertory Theatre, has performed in repertory houses including Berkeley Rep, ACT, Dallas Theatre Center, La Jolla Playhouse, Theatresports, Killing My Lobster, and has toured the country and overseas. Francine’s most passionate interest is the intersection of diversity in theatre – gender, sexuality, color, neurodiversity and physical differences, and her experiences are published in the anthology Gravity Pulls You In . She plays the titular role in BITTEN (Bad Dog Productions), currently winning independent film festival awards across the country. ff498187-2091-4f15-88c4-01a7bf9ce7bd: A group meditation/authentic relating practice that explores what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to each other Welcome to a twice-monthly drop-in Relatefulness practice with Josh Rosenberg and Daniel Ricciardelli. Relatefulness is an exploration of what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to the others in the group. It is a close friend of relational practices like Circling™, Authentic Relating, and T-Group, with slightly more emphasis on group interaction and flexibility in how to express what is arising in the present moment. This is a mixed-levels event. Beginners are welcome and will be supported with tools to aid their exploration. Advanced practitioners will be challenged to find the next edge of their practice. We cap attendance for the event at 15 people. If you want to be sure to be able to join, purchase your ticket in advance! What We’ll Explore Through paired, small group, and full group processes, we will practice: Noticing and naming the content of our experience, including: our emotions, body sensations, and present moment reactions to others in the group. Noticing and naming the context of our experience, including: our assumptions, the norms of the group, and projections onto one another and society. Revealing our experience to one another to help all of us see each other and our broader social reality more clearly. Leading the group in the direction we want to go. This is a practice where all participants are invited to notice their desires for the group and to practice directing the group by embodying the kinds of expression they want to see more of. Why Come? You may be looking to: Cultivate more authentic, nourishing relationships, where you can be yourself and stay connected. Take your insights about personal growth and explore them in an interpersonal context. Set clear, compassionate boundaries instead of repeating painful patterns This practice helps to develop skills that support all of the above. Also, it's fun! What Not to Expect This is not a therapy session or group healing experience, although healing can occur. It’s a group exploration of what is arising in the present moment. This naturally tends to bring out more truth and love in the group, but there is not a particular goal or endpoint we are trying to reach. Here’s what NOT to expect: A space free of conflict or triggers. When people are open about what's coming up in their experience, things can get edgy sometimes! We don’t view being triggered as inherently negative, but rather a natural part of the human experience that can be rich to explore. We aim for a space where safety grows from honesty and genuine care, not from avoiding interpersonal conflict. To support this, we will establish some boundaries up front, such as asking for explicit consent before making physical contact with others. No enforced hierarchy of emotions. Beauty, awkwardness, boredom, anger, and joy are all welcome. Each experience has worth, and none automatically justify themselves as more important. Expression without attunement. We value honest expression, and we also stay attentive to its impact on others. This is a space for mindful connection, not expression at any cost. Facilitators may pause or redirect moments that move away from relational presence. Other logistics and notes Participants enter the space at 6:30 and we close the doors for the event at 6:35. Please arrive on time! We hope to see you at a future event! Feel free to reach out to jhrosenberg [at] gmail [dot] com or dbricciardelli [at] gmail [dot] com if you have questions about whether this event is a fit for you. More about the facilitators Josh Rosenberg (he/him) is a certified facilitator through the Relateful Company training program. He has hosted and facilitated weekly relatefulness sessions for small groups for several years while continuing to grow his practice through retreats and regularly engaging other facilitators. Josh loves exploring what's honestly coming up in the present moment in a group of people, and the novelty and relief it tends to bring. When he's not leading relatefulness sessions or at work, you may find him loving the heck out of music, movies, and comedy, participating in Michael Taft's meditation courses, or passionately following the New York Jets football team despite its many flaws. In his day job, Josh is CEO at the Forecasting Research Institute, a nonprofit aiming to advance the science of forecasting and increase its policy-relevance. Daniel Ricciardelli (he/him) has hundreds of hours in relational awareness practices of various forms, and is a certified Relatefulness practitioner through the Relateful Company. He draws from a decade of experience guiding men’s circles, performance dance teams, applied AI research, and meditation. Some recent inspirations of his are Ego Development Theory, madhyamaka philosophy, and Brazilian zouk. He is known for his steady, compassionate presence and calibrated relational risk-taking. He works full-time at the intersection of mental health and AI as a machine learning researcher.

a4a8e4c8-3f38-4382-844c-b32ec523d592: What would make you believe the impossible? · What happens when the desire to know becomes inseparable from the desire for something to be true? Their conversation will move between psychology, science, faith, mythology, and the impossible to ask what makes a belief reasonable, where skepticism becomes its own kind of certainty, and whether emotion distorts inquiry or gives it urgency. At stake is a deeply human question: when ordinary explanations fail us, what are we willing to believe in order to keep making sense of the world? Scott Lambridis writes literary speculative fiction about the stories people rely on to make sense of the world. His fiction explores belief, consciousness, trauma, and the strange places where psychology, folklore, and love begin to overlap. Before publishing his debut novel, St. Ulphia’s Dead, Scott toured with a progressive rock band, founded an independent press and literary performance series, tended a forty-acre olive farm, and read a book from every country in the world. 4062dd46-ca7d-47af-b089-284e2b45f3fd: One of today’s premier jazz drummers · "The Groove Master", Herlin Riley is widely considered one of the best drummers in any genre of music performing today. The longtime drummer for the legendary Ahmad Jamal and the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra now leads two groups, his quintet and the New Orleans Groove Masters featuring himself, Jason Marsalis, and Shannon Powell. Herlin’s most recent album, Perpetual Optimism, reunites the quintet of rising stars that Riley assembled for his Mack Avenue Records debut, New Direction. Since the release of that acclaimed album, all four of Riley’s bandmates – trumpeter Bruce Harris, saxophonist Godwin Louis, pianist Emmet Cohen, and bassist Russell Hall – have been making major waves across the modern jazz scene, attesting to the master drummer’s Art Blakey-like ear for talent and sage musical guidance. Herlin Riley's source of strength comes from his faith in God, his wife of four decades, and his family of five children and 10 grandchildren; his lifelong home in New Orleans, the creative community that surrounds it, and his positive approach to life and music. His roots in the church are also vital, shining through in the congregational claps that help establish the celebratory spirit that is showcased in the album opener “Rush Hour.” He also relies on his musical family, including his long-established ties with Wynton Marsalis and the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra. Riley’s connection to the Marsalis dynasty traces back a generation earlier, to family patriarch and fellow lifelong New Orleanian Ellis Marsalis. It was while performing with Ellis at the annual New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival in a trio with bassist Reginald Veal that Riley first caught the ear of Wynton, who invited both members of his father’s rhythm section to join him, launching a vital relationship that’s now lasted more than three decades. Riley pays homage to his mentor on the closing track of Perpetual Optimism, the funky arrangement of Ellis Marsalis’ composition “Twelve’s It.” In the quintet’s lively rendition, the tune is not just a cover but a tribute, as Riley intones a short ode to passing the torch that refers to the elder Marsalis as “a great musician who taught a whole lot of fellows.” Another Crescent City icon, the late singer, pianist, songwriter, and producer Allen Toussaint, was the motivator behind Riley’s other vocal turn on the album, a gritty take on Willie Dixon’s blues classic “Wang Dang Doodle.” Toussaint stopped in to hear Riley play at a New Orleans club and heard the drummer’s 5/4 arrangement of the familiar standard. “He was really impressed,” Riley recalls. “He said, ‘Wow, man, I’ve heard ‘Wang Dang Doodle’ a thousand times, but I’ve never heard it performed in 5 before. You should record that.’ A few months later, he passed away, so I recorded the tune to pay homage to the wishes of the great Allen Toussaint.” Though he conveys vivid emotion in his voice, Riley stops short of calling himself a singer. His willingness to step to the mic comes from advice he was given by New Orleans vocal great Germaine Bazzle. “She’s a very elegant and regal lady, but when she’s performing, she scats, rolls her shoulders, dances, and really engages in the music with honesty and passion,” says Riley. When he asked her how she reconciled those two extremes, Bazzle told him, “’ You have to allow yourself to become emotionally naked when you’re on the bandstand.’ When she said that, a light bulb went off in my head. I’m not a singer, but I just do what I do, and I have the audacity to be uninhibited.” The same can be said for Riley’s work behind the kit, where he leads his stellar band with infectious enthusiasm and bristling swing. His “Be There When I Get There” captures the anticipation and excitement of rushing to an eagerly awaited appointment, whether a romantic rendezvous, a gathering of friends, or a night of music. The brisk “Borders Without Lines” comes from the pen of Riley’s Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra bandmate Victor Goines, while the classic “You Don’t Know What Love Is” becomes a sultry simmer, highlighted by Harris’ mournful, muted trumpet. The title track is the rare Riley original composed in a major key, and its sunny disposition perfectly communicates his unflagging hopefulness. The lovely “Touched,” featuring Louis’ achingly lyrical alto, recalls a tender moment with the drummer’s mother before she passed away. “I was in her room in her last days, and she rubbed my head. I’m a grown man, but I felt like an innocent child. There’s a special love wrapped in the touch of a mother of every living creature. That special euphoria only comes from her.” The bittersweet “Wings and Roots” looks to the next generation, referring to Riley’s philosophy of raising children: “You have to root them in good values and fundamental characteristics, but once they get to be a certain age, you have to give them the wings to be free, to go out and be themselves.” Finally, “Stella By Starlight” is another nod to the American Songbook, taken at a graceful midtempo pace with Cohen’s deft touch over Riley’s sensitive brushwork. In the end, Riley hopes that the music of Perpetual Optimism helps spread the upbeat manifesto that he’s chosen to live by. “I always look forward, no matter what happens in life. If you’re grieving or faced with an emotional challenge, keep in mind: If you’re still breathing, there’s a chance that you can overcome and thrive. Commit yourself to PERPETUAL OPTIMISM!”

62f99c79-993d-43c5-bb57-55a12f511478: Embodiment Practices is an invitation to practice giving ourselves permission to arrive fully to where we are, and gently explore movement and stillness to care for our bodies and ourselves. This event happens each week at the Alembic. As an element of self attunement, we will practice making intuitive choices through a lens of self love, meaning that we are each making choices that are nourishing and responsive to ourselves as individuals in that moment. Part of this practice includes being very intentional and explicit about what kinds of choices we might consider, and being curious about how it feels to try them. There will be many options provided throughout, with guidance around how to navigate choice making, including if this is new to you or you are navigating a limitation or injury. There will be a corner of the room set aside in case you’d like to opt out of the facilitated structure and take a moment for yourself to rest. Opening Circle: We'll ground and check-in with whatever feels present for each of us. We get to welcome ourselves to come as we are. Warm Up: We'll do a guided, full-bodied warm up, tuning the instruments of our bodies and attention, giving ourselves time to shake it out, stretch, wiggle, and move through whatever feels stuck. Movements will be simple enough to follow along, giving us a chance to get out of our heads and drop into our bodies, regulating our nervous system. Drawing on contemporary dance and yoga, there will be flow, rhythm, and music. Movement Explorations: We'll explore movements that deepen our connection with our bodies and our intuition, focusing on concepts and areas of the body that can help us settle and release. Meditation: Finally, we'll settle into meditation and rest. Finding stillness might be sitting/standing/lying down and might include cozy props, having eyes open or closed, and suggestions to make yourself comfortable, including allowing some body movement within that quiet space. Please bring clothes you feel comfortable to move in. It’s recommended to bring long sleeves, long pants and socks with you, in case we are moving on the floor. Bring a journal if you’d like. About Suzanne (Zan): With three decades of contemporary/modern dance experience and 15 years of teaching, Suzanne Beahrs guides students in exploring movement as a pathway to deeper connection—with ourselves, our surroundings, and each other. Her classes blend technical training, creative expression, and guidance on being intentional with how we are each practicing. Her movement style was described by The New York Times as “grounded, silken.” In addition to contemporary dance, she is currently heavily influenced by house dance, contact improvisation, and mindfulness practices. She is currently on faculty at Shawl-Anderson Dance Center and teaches around the Bay Area, including ODC, the Berkeley Alembic, and Finnish Hall. Zan has previously taught extensively at Gibney, Elon University, ADF studios, and many more. She has shown her choreography in NY, NC, CA, AZ, MA, and MO, and performed in works by Ishika Seth, Mo Miner, and others. Beyond the studio, Suzanne is a facilitator and has worked as a DEI consultant. She also enjoys exploring writing, visual art, nature, music, and belonging. Education: MFA in Dance, NYU Tisch School of the Arts; BA in Geology, UC Berkeley Learn more about Suzanne, upcoming classes/workshops (contemporary, embodiment, improvisation, contact improvisation and private lessons): IG @suzannebeahrs suzannebeahrs.com

7bec954a-e2f6-4b53-bc73-956ed8deccff: Points Of Departure Fall 2026 Presented by Fort Mason Art Points Of Departure is a new series of immersive live events celebrating the spectrum of Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture (FMCAC) as a place for innovation and discovery, a personal port of embarkation for its community, and a window on the world. Each program celebrates the vibrant past, present, and future of FMCAC as it charts a course toward its 50th anniversary in 2027. Points Of Departure is curated by Brad Rosenstein, Associate Curator of Public Programs. Two Points Of Departure Fall 2026 Events Happen in The Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor Program 2 CIRCUS BY THE BAY Panel conversation and live performances Tuesday, October 13, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Cowell Theater, Pier 2/Gateway Pavilion, FMCAC , RESERVE SPACE Pickle Family Circus at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture Lively Arts Festival 1978. Photo: Terry Lorant In the 1970s, San Francisco became an epicenter of the emerging new American circus – an intimate one-ring model that spurned animal acts and focused on traditional skills of juggling, clowning, acrobatics, and aerial work, all filtered through a countercultural vaudevillian sensibility. This “not-so-big-top” was pioneered by such local companies as the Pickle Family Circus and its later incarnation, the New Pickle Circus, which performed annually at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture, and longtime FMCAC residents Make*A*Circus. This movement spawned a stream of Bay Area talents that spread their influence from Cirque du Soleil and Broadway to movies, and TV, an impact which resonates to this day. Join us for a magical evening celebrating this uniquely San Francisco history through a conversation with some of its leading lights, all veterans of Pickle Family Circus and the New Pickle Circus: performer/writer/director Gypsy Snider , trapeze artist/choreographer/director Shana Carroll , clown/writer/teacher Jeff Raz , and artistic director/choreographer Tandy Beal . The program includes rare archival photos and video, and live performances by Unique Derique ( Prescott Circus ), Chloe Somers Walier ( Dear San Francisco ), Elise Hing ( Circus Bella ), and performers from San Francisco Youth Circus ( SFYC ), Circus Center ’s pre-professional youth program. SFYC is led by Performance Coach Dominic Cruz , a 7 Fingers/ Dear San Francisco alum. (performers subject to change). Program 3 LIFE ON THE WATER: A REUNION Panel conversation and rare performance video Thursday, November 12, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor, Fort Mason Center or Arts & Culture , RESERVE SPACE LEFT TO RIGHT: LIFE ON THE WATER’s Bill Talen , Ellen Sebastian , Leonard Pitt , and Joe Lambert with a model of the Bayfront Theatre remodel 1987. LIFE ON THE WATER (LOTW) was an extraordinary presenting and producing organization based at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture for seven seasons between 1986-1993. Centered in its own custom-designed space (now the Bayfront Theatre), the company was dedicated to presenting artists who originated their own work and committed to a blend of experimental and traditional stage forms, political statement, and cultural diversity. It became nationally renowned for its pioneering showcases of solo theater work by such luminaries as Spalding Gray and Karen Finley as well as co-producing the annual Solo Mio Festival. LOTW’s presentations also ranged from music, dance, screenings, and workshops to ongoing programs such as Latino Theatre Project, Earth Drama Lab, and AsianImprov aRts (AIR). This special evening reunites LOTW’s founding directors Ellen Sebastian Chang , Bill Talen , Leonard Pitt , and Joe Lambert on their former stage for a sparkling conversation about the company’s groundbreaking work, which includes their own creations ranging from Pitt’s “avant mime” theater Not for Real and Sebastian’s epic The Sanctified Church to Talen’s biting satires such as Political Wife . The program includes never-before-seen archival video of some of LOTW’s most celebrated productions. Past Programs Program 1 TELL THEM WE WERE HERE Film screening and panel conversation Thursday, September 24, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor, Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture (FMCAC) , RESERVE SPACE TELL THEM WE WERE HERE Artist Alicia McCarthy Tell Them We Were Here (2021), a film by Griff Williams and Keelan Williams , chronicles visual/multidisciplinary artists currently living and working in the San Francisco Bay Area and how they extend the historical legacy of Bay Area creativity, activism, and community. Reflecting the spirit of FMCAC and its vibrant connection to local art and artists, the film centers the idea of art as a reflection of the place from which it emerges and helps to define the unique character of the Bay Area scene over the past 25 years. The film follows the work of Sadie Barnette , Amy Franceschini ( Futurefarmers ), Jim Goldberg , Tucker Nichols , Lynn Hershman Leeson , Alicia McCarthy , Nigel Poor ( Ear Hustle ), and M ichael Swaine , a select group of artists who have chosen a less-worn path. It touches on the disappearance of cultural communities due to gentrification and economic instability, while reminding us of art’s power to transform and how vital creative communities are to healthy societies and political change. The screening is followed by a panel discussion with director Griff Williams , artists Amy Franceschini and Tucker Nichols , and curator René de Guzman (all featured in the film), exploring how the local art scene has continued to evolve in the five years since the film’s premiere. All Fort Mason Art programs are generously supported by San Francisco Grants for The Arts, the FMCAC Board of Directors, and individual contributions to the Fort Mason Fund. PANELISTS & PERFORMERS PANELISTS TELL THEM WE WERE HERE : Griff Williams is an American painter, publisher and gallerist. In 1993 he founded Gallery 16 and the pioneering fine art printmaking workshop Urban Digital Color in San Francisco. The exhibition and publishing program has worked with hundreds of artists including Lynn Hershman Leeson, William Kentridge, Deborah Oropallo, Jim Isermann, bell hooks, Rex Ray, Margaret Kilgallen, Mark Grotjahn, Paul Sietsema, Arturo Herrera, Michelle Grabner, and Ari Marcopoulos. Williams has also designed and published dozens of acclaimed books with the Gallery 16 Editions imprint. His paintings have been exhibited in galleries and museums including the San Diego Museum of Art, the Crocker Art Museum in Sacramento, and the San Jose Museum of Art . His work has been reviewed in Art in America , Flash Art , and ARTnews . He co-directed Tell Them We Were Here with his son, Keelan Williams , a filmmaker based in Los Angeles. René de Guzman is a longtime Bay Area curator, artist, and arts consultant. He was one of the founding curators at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts as Visual Arts Curator and Director of Visual Arts, serving from 1993-2007, and subsequently served as the Senior Curator of Art and Director of Exhibition Strategy at the Oakland Museum of California from 2007-21. He also served as Deputy Director for Programs and Engagement at Headlands Center for the Arts , overseeing artist residencies and public programs. For more than three decades, he has developed innovative and popular exhibitions for a wide public and is currently Co-Director of Art + Water in San Francisco. Amy Franceschini is an artist whose work facilitates encounter, exchange, and tactile forms of inquiry by calling into question the “certainties” of a given time or place where a work is situated. In 1995, Franceschini founded Futurefarmers as a collaborative platform to consider the social, political, and environmental organization of space. Futurefarmers use various media to deconstruct systems to visualize and understand their intrinsic logics; food systems, public transportation, education … Through this disassembly they find new narratives and reconfigurations that form alternatives to the principles that once dominated these systems. Franceschini received her BFA in Photography from San Francisco State University and an MFA from Stanford University. She has taught in the visual arts graduate programs at California College of the Arts in San Francisco and Stanford University and in the Master of Eco-Social Design at the Free University in Bolzano, Italy. She is a 2009 Guggenheim Fellow, a 2019 Rome Prize Fellow and a 2017 recipient of the Herb Alpert Award for Visual Arts. Tucker Nichols is an artist based in Northern California. His work has been featured at the Drawing Center in New York, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the Denver Art Museum, Den Frie Museum in Copenhagen, and the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. A show of his sculpture, Almost Everything On The Table , was recently on view at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum. His drawings have been published in McSweeney’s , The Thing Quarterly , The New Yorker , and the Op-Ed pages of The New York Times . He is co-author of the books, Crabtree (with Jon Nichols) and This Bridge Will Not Be Gray (with Dave Eggers). Flowers for Sick People , his ongoing multimedia project, was featured on the PBS Newshour and the subject of an exhibition at SFMOMA, Close to Home: Creativity in Crisis , is an exhibition highlighting seven local artists’ responses to the pandemic. He is represented by ZieherSmith in New York and Gallery 16 in San Francisco. CIRCUS BY THE BAY : Gypsy Snider is co-artistic director of Dear San Francisco , now celebrating its fifth anniversary at the city’s historic Club Fugazi. As co-founding artistic director of The 7 Fingers , she wrote and directed SisterS , Réversible, Intersection , Amuse , Un D i a , Traces , and Loft . She has choreographed televised feature performances for America’s Got Talent and Her Majesty’s Royal Variety Performance . In 2013, working with director Diane Paulus on a new vision of Pippin , she created choreography and wove circus into the revival of the Broadway musical, earning her a Drama Desk Award and an Outer Critics Circle Award. Snider began her circus career at the age of four when her parents founded The Pickle Family Circus. She grew up touring the West Coast with the company. In 2002, while in her hometown of San Francisco, she wrote and directed for The New Pickle Circus a show entitled Circumstance , which premiered at FMCAC’s Cowell Theater. Snider is also a guest teacher and guest director at the National Circus School of Montreal. Shana Carroll is co-artistic director of Dear San Francisco , and co-founding artistic director of The 7 Fingers . Since the latter’s inception in 2002, Shana has directed, written, and created choreography for a dozen or so of their touring and/or resident shows, including Passagers , Cuisine & Confessions , Séquence 8 , and Traces . in 2024 Carroll was co-choreographer and Circus Designer for Water For Elephants on Broadway, for which she received the Chita Rivera Award for Best Choreography, as well as Tony, Drama Desk, and Outer Critics Circles nominations in the same category. Carroll has frequently collaborated with Cirque du Soleil , most recently as co-director of their first show on ice, Crystal , and previously as acrobatic designer and choreographer of Paramour (Broadway) and Iris (Los Angeles), and as director/choreographer of their performance at the 2012 Academy Awards. Originally from Berkeley, CA, and daughter of beloved San Francisco columnist Jon Carroll, Shana began her career as a trapeze artist with San Francisco’s Pickle Family Circus and went on to a 20-year career in the air with Cirque du Soleil and many others before co-founding The 7 Fingers. Jeff Raz has performed nationally and internationally for decades, starring in the Pickle Family Circus, Cirque du Soleil’s Corteo , Make*A*Circus, and many other circuses and theaters. Jeff is also a playwright, director, teacher, producer and has authored four books inspired by his career. Over the years he has also co-founded six arts organizations and worked globally as a communications and leadership consultant. Tandy Beal is a performer, director, choreographer, writer, teacher, and … dreamer. An off-the-map career includes: directing Pickle Family Circus for 10 years; touring four continents with Tandy Beal & Co.; writing/directing VIVA for the Moscow Circus in Japan; a show for NASA’s SETI project with Carl Sagan; projects with Lou Harrison, Frank Zappa, John Adams, and decades of projects with Bobby McFerrin, Art Lande, and Jon Scoville; choreographing opera, MTV, ballet; corporate shows (LucasFilms, SF 49ers, MCI, Coca-Cola, Pixar, Oracle+); acting off-Broadway; dancing for the Shah of Iran with Alwin Nikolais in Tehran; guest performances with Atlanta Ballet, Momix, Remy Charlip and in Europe, with Carolyn Carlson; creating what Dance Magazine said was the first contemporary dance/circus Nutcracker . Her life and work are featured in two books, The Pickle Clowns and Living Happily Ever After . She has received awards from AFI, CAC, NEA, Packard, and Hewlett +. Her natural habitat is the Santa Cruz mountains where she lives with longtime co-conspirator, Jon Scoville. PANELISTS LIFE ON THE WATER: A REUNION : Ellen Sebastian Chang is a distinguished multidisciplinary director, dramaturge, writer, and arts educator with a career spanning 50 years, dedicated to advocating for human rights and understanding through the creative arts. She has collaborated with a diverse array of artists and art forms: theater, opera, dance, radio, film and installation. Sebastian Chang commenced her career as a lighting technician and designer before making her debut as a director and writer in 1982 with Your Place Is No Longer With Us , an immersive play staged in private homes about a biracial girl. She co-founded LIFE ON THE WATER (LOTW), a notable producing organization in San Francisco, and served as its co-artistic director. During her time at LOTW she created The Sanctified Church with Luisah Teisch, later renamed Sanctified with Esther Scott, No Trace of the Blonde with Holly Hughes, and Janie Geiser, FACE with Bob Ernst, Artis Fountaine, NAO, and Debora Iyall. She has been the creative director and teaching artist for The World As It Could Be Human Rights Education Program, utilizing the arts to deepen understanding of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and inspire activism across generations. Beyond her work in theater, she co-owned the award-winning FuseBOX restaurant in West Oakland created with Chef Sunhui Chang. She has received numerous grants and fellowships from prestigious arts foundations such as Creative Capital, Kenneth Rainin Foundation, MAP Fund, National Endowment for the Arts, and Ruth Arts Fellowship. Her current focus is rewilding six acres of land in the Pacific Northwest planting 1,350 native trees with foresters Boots on the Ground. William Talen grew up in small towns throughout Minnesota, South Dakota, and Wisconsin, and came west in the 70s, joining the poetry community in Bolinas, CA before moving to North Beach. Exploring storytelling techniques with solo shows in the Eureka Theater and Intersection, he studied with Spalding Gray and Sidney Lanier. Talen then partnered with Ellen Sebastian, and in 1984 they dreamed of a radical kind of theater, inspired by the stage sets of restaurants and the parties of Anon Salon, eventually lifting “Life on the Water” from a billboard in front of a yuppie apartment complex in Richmond, CA. Gathering with Joe Lambert and Leonard Pitt, LOTW kicked off with six weeks of Gray in the fall of ’86. After seven years, Talen departed for New York, leaving the Solo Mio Festival to Marcia Crosby, Joegh Bullock, and Kate Boyd. In New York and Europe, his character “Reverend Billy” caught a wave of post-religious spiritual hunger, inventing the movement against Consumerism by the time of 9/11. With director and life partner Savitri D, daughter Lena Nightstar, and a revolving troupe of 30 singers, the “Church of Stop Shopping” staged earth services at a series of NYC “art churches” and toured shows on five continents, always returning to justice campaigns in New York. In 2016, Neil Young and Daryl Hannah proposed that Talen preach his “Earthalujah” gospel at the opening of each show, which kicked off a 10-year collaboration, performing in 35 amphitheaters and reaching about 650,000 in Young’s rock audiences. Currently, the Stop Shopping Church has settled in the 500-seat Quaker Meetinghouse in Manhattan, the anti-consumerism of its early days now centered on the Earth’s crisis. Talen’s books include The Earth Wants You from City Lights, and now his fifth book, Earthalujah! , being published in November by Autonomedia Press. Leonard Pitt studied mime in Paris with Etienne Decroux for four years, becoming his assistant and performing in his company. On his return to the U.S., Pitt settled in Berkeley, CA, where he opened a school of physical theater, attracting students from around the world. Pitt’s one-man shows have received critical acclaim. He has performed and taught at theaters and festivals throughout the U.S., Europe, Brazil, New Zealand, and Australia. He was also a member of George Coates Performance Works and traveled widely with the company. In Bali he studied mask theatre and performed extensively with his teacher. In 1986, he co-founded LOTW, where his projects included the “avant-mime” production Not for Real (created with Rinde Eckert), Spleenix , The Art of Face , and performing David Barth’s solo play, Ned . In 1991, Leonard created Eco-Rap, an environmental education program combining ecology and rap music as a way to educate inner city youth about urgent social issues. He has written and published seven books, including three books on Paris and a memoir, and created numerous videos on Paris, all viewable on YouTube ( Leonard Pitt Paris ). He continues to live in Berkeley and create and is currently working on two new books. Joe Lambert is the founder of StoryCenter and the originator of the digital storytelling movement, a participatory media methodology used by 100,000s of people all over the world. The work has taken him and his organization to all 50 U.S. states, and more than 90 countries. Earlier in his career, he served as Executive Director of the People’s Theater Coalition and LOTW, where he executive-produced more than 500 performances, festivals, conferences, and national gatherings. Highlights include the first San Francisco Jazz Tap Festival, collaborations with artists like Guillermo Gomez Peña, the Blue Man Group, Marty Pottenger, and Dana Atchley. During that time, he held leadership roles in national initiatives including the Alliance for Cultural Democracy and the National Performance Network, and served as a panelist and principal consultant for numerous public agencies and private foundations. As an author and curriculum developer, he has written numerous articles. For projToday, based in Santa Fe, NM, he continues this work through StoryHost LLC, teaching workshops, hosting the Elderware podcast, and exploring the intersections of story, aging, and meaning-making. PERFORMERS CIRCUS BY THE BAY : Unique Derique , an internationally acclaimed entertainer, is a cornerstone of the Bay Area circus and performing arts scene. He honed his physical comedy with premier troupes including Circus A La Mode, Make*A*Circus, and the historic Pickle Family Circus. Dedicated to community arts education, Derique has spent nearly three decades as an Artist-in Residence at West Oakland’s Prescott Circus Theater, teaching youth the art and history of Hambone body percussion. His versatile talent has graced international television and stages worldwide, opening for legends like Lou Rawls, Sammy Davis Jr., and The Temptations. Annually, his holiday show Fool La La: Whimsical brings joy to all ages at The Marsh Berkeley. Elise Hing , born and raised in Santa Cruz, CA, discovered her natural flexibility at age 12 and quickly developed a passion for contortion. For the past five years she has performed with Circus Bella doing free shows in the park during the summer and under the big top in the winter for their holiday spectacular. In this immersive workshop, you'll learn the foundations of somatic healing and nervous system regulation, and why working with your body is often the missing piece when it comes to creating meaningful, sustainable change. You'll leave with: A clear understanding of what somatic healing is and how it works Practical tools you can immediately integrate into daily life to finally feel more calm and present Greater awareness of your nervous system and stress responses Simple ways to deepen your connection to your body, emotions, and intuition A new approach to personal growth that feels supportive, sustainable, and effective Whether you're completely new to somatics or looking to deepen your understanding of holistic healing, this workshop will give you a strong foundation and simple practices you can return to anytime! 97fb1247-6163-464b-8682-ab331b91d115: As workers and as parents, we all care deeply about how we must prepare ourselves and our children for fulfilling careers at a time when the changing nature of labor is opaque. In this interactive book talk, co-author Illah Nourbakhsh will share brief remarks regarding our voyage in researching and writing a book about careers, AI and the future of education. We will be joined by two special pioneers who will make brief remarks from the audience: Alan Eustace and Professor Michael Genesereth. Alan Eustace served as senior vice president at Google and has witnessed the digital and AI technology revolutions firsthand. Michael Genesereth is faculty at Stanford University and charted the course of artificial intelligence research as one of its founding scholars. Both Alan and Michael care deeply about the next generation, and the ways in which careers will evolve as AI changes the shape of work. We look forward to a dynamic conversation with the audience. Featuring curated essays from leaders in tech and education, Crunch Time empowers parents, educators, students, and professionals to get informed and access their agency in the AI age. The AI revolution is underway, and none of us are fully prepared. In Crunch Time , education and AI experts Illah Nourbakhsh and Michael Druckman confront one of the central questions of our time: How will artificial intelligence reshape careers, education, and opportunity, and what should we do about it now? Rather than predicting a single future, Crunch Time presents AI as a dynamic, uncertain force that demands informed participation. Originally conceived for educators and parents, the book expands its lens to include students, alumni, mid-career professionals, employers, policymakers, and anyone navigating work and learning in the age of AI. Crunch Time weaves together perspectives from AI inventors, business leaders, educators, technologists, and community leaders, featuring more than forty contributors including AI experts Daniela Rus, Hoda Heidari, Michael Genesereth, Sanjay Sarma, university presidents Nancy Cantor, Lisa Ryerson, Laura Walker, Juan Salgado; business leaders David Siegel, Steve Malony, Dan Draper; visionaries Dame Diane Coyle, William Haseltine, Paul LeBlanc; and leading K to 12 educators. Readers will encounter competing viewpoints, practical guidance, and concrete steps for action. Crunch Time is an invitation to understand, to prepare, and to actively shape a more equitable and human-centered AI future. This timely and empowering book is essential reading for students, parents, educators and leaders who wish to shape an AI future that expands opportunity and strengthens our shared humanity. — Farnam Jahanian, President, Carnegie Mellon University For a book about artificial intelligence, this is brimming with human intelligence. You'll find thoughtful, nuanced, and provocative strategies for growing up and thriving in the age of AI. This book challenges us to redesign the connection between education and employment with intention and courage. This is a powerful call to ensure the AI age expands opportunity and strengthens pathways to meaningful work for all. — Lisa Marsh Ryerson, President, Southern New Hampshire University Our youth are growing up in the middle of a massive transition into the age of AI. Smart guides are critical to navigating this rough terrain, and this book is one of those guides. It elevates the power of human intellect and creativity, providing much-needed guidance on how to harness new technologies for the good of society and humanity. — Lisa Guernsey, Senior Director of Birth-12th Grade Policy, New America Illah R. Nourbakhsh is Kavcic-Moura Professor of Robotics at Carnegie Mellon University, inaugural Executive Director of the Center for Shared Prosperity, and co-director of the Community Robotics, Education and Technology Empowerment Lab. He was the Inaugural K&L Gates Professor of Ethics and Computational Technologies. He obtained his PhD in Computer Science from Stanford University. In 2009 the National Academy of Sciences named him a Kavli Fellow. In 2013 he was inducted into the June Harless West Virginia Hall of Fame. He was previously Robotics Group Lead for NASA/Ames. In 2019 he was named a Hastings Fellow. He has co-authored textbooks and popular literature, including Turn Left , AI and Humanity , Robot Futures , and Parenting for Technology Futures . He has authored articles for The New Yorker and Foreign Affairs, in addition to academic journals and book chapters. He is a trustee of the Claude Worthington Benedum Foundation, Winchester Thurston School and the Southwestern Pennsylvania Environmental Health Project. He currently is a Fellow of the Leadership and Society Initiative at the University of Chicago. Michael established the “Senator Robert F. Kennedy Education Awards” in partnership with Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights in 2014 to recognize K to 12 school leaders, teachers and students for moral courage and the “Schools That Can Leaders That Can Awards” in 2017 to recognize leaders giving back to our society’s well-being in service of our youth. Michael chaired the Trey Whitfield School board in East New York, Brooklyn for many years, served on the Portal Learning board in Los Angeles, acted as an advisor to many K-12 schools over the last twenty years and was recognized as Founding Chairman Emeritus of the NYU Center for Global Affairs where he served as Co-Chairman for fourteen years. 3987f64f-0b81-4532-a1f3-a44a9f3cd912: An inspiring guide that reimagines the stages of grief into five healing actions, Reimagining Grief offers light and a new way forward in the midst of darkness. This is the book Kate wishes she'd had, and she wrote it for you. Kate will be joined in conversation by Myra Sacks, the author of award-winning memoir, " Fifty-Seven Fridays: Losing Our Daughter Finding Our Way ," and founder of E-Motion, Inc. There is no way to spin grief. It's hard. It's messy. It's destabilizing. And every single one of us has to go through it. Author and grief coach Kate Doerge knows this too well. Over six years, she lost her father to heart failure and her mother in a car accident five days before Christmas. She also faced the hardest challenge for any parent, losing her sixteen-year-old daughter, Penny, to complications from a rare genetic condition. After Penny's death, Kate knew she had a choice, she could lose herself to a grief so powerful she might not come back from it—or she could find another way through. Reimagining Grief is the result of that search. Drawing from her own experience, the latest research, and conversations with others who have faced devastating loss, Kate offers five actions that can help ground you when you feel out of control, lift you when you're depleted, and help you process the pain of loss. In this book, you'll learn: Why There Isn’t One Right Way to Grieve — and How to Find Your Own Path An Approach to Saying Goodbye That Honors Both You and Your Loved One The 5 Actions Through Grief — and How to Use Them to Heal What Post-Traumatic Growth Really Looks Like How to Find Joy Again Turning Pain into Purpose These actions won’t make grief vanish or disappear; everyone has to go through the difficult path that you are put on after losing someone you loved deeply. However, Reimagining Grief offers some light and healing in the midst of darkness and a different way forward. This is the book Kate wishes she'd had. She wrote it for you. Kate Doerge is a USA TODAY bestselling author, motivational speaker, certified grief coach, and founder of Penny’s Flight Foundation. Through heartfelt storytelling, research-backed insights, and practical strategies, Kate inspires audiences to navigate change, embrace resilience, and lead lives filled with greater purpose and connection. Myra Sack is the author of award-winning memoir, " Fifty-Seven Fridays: Losing Our Daughter Finding Our Way ," and founder of E-Motion, Inc. a nonprofit organization created to support community, movement and ritual to enhance coping and resilience. Myra's life changed when her older daughter, Havi, died in January 2021. Blending Myra's lived experience and knowledge as a certified Compassionate Bereavement Care provider with her lifelong identity as an athlete and career in social impact, E-Motion evolved out of a new way of living with the most difficult reality. Myra holds an MBA in Social Impact from Boston University, and graduated with a B.A. cum laude from Dartmouth College, where she captained the women's soccer team and earned All-America honors. Myra serves on the Board of the Courageous Parents Network. adf26ce2-c44b-4c7a-a37e-010d2aa33aa4: Matt shares his dramatic tale of gentlemen-explorers of the 1930s racing to find and harvest a poisonous Amazon vine. Join us at Mrs. Dalloway's Bookstore on Thursday, November 12 at 7:00 PM when Matt O'Hara comes to the store to present his new book The Flying Death: Poison, Plunder, and the Quest for a Miracle Medicine in the Amazon . Matt will be joined by Rebecca Herman for the conversation and will sign copies of his book after the presentation. In the fall of 1938, a young, frail American explorer set off down a river in the western Amazon in search of curare, a poison he thought might save his life. Richard Gill had learned that local tribes used curare-laced blow darts to kill animals, but it was also potentially a cure for many ailments, including his own. He also thought he could make a fortune by connecting the knowledge of two worlds. Obsessed with curare, he raced to make deals with Indigenous poison masters in the Amazon and pharmaceutical companies back home, even as his Russian-born rival Boris Krukoff sought to do the same. In The Flying Death , the historian Matt O'Hara asks who and what we are willing to sacrifice in the name of discovery and profit. O'Hara brings to life Gill's epic quest, a stranger-than-fiction true story that moves from unexplored territory in the Amazon to rogue medical trials and cutthroat corporate boardrooms in the United States. Navigating treacherous terrain and politics, Gill and Krukoff successfully created a veritable curare–industrial complex, as the plant became a key element in shock therapy, transformed surgery in the United States and across the globe, and eventually led to a Nobel Prize. The Flying Death offers a thrilling ride across Indigenous knowledge, scientific exploration, and exploitation, unearthing a story of discovery that poses searching questions about the price of progress, who pays it, and who gets credit. MATT O'HARA is a professor of history at the University of California, Santa Cruz. He is the award-winning author of many journal articles and two books, The History of the Future in Colonial Mexico and A Flock Divided: Race, Religion, and Politics in Mexico, 1749–1857. REBECCA HERMAN is Associate Professor of History at UC Berkeley, where she teaches about environmental politics, US-Latin American relations, and modern Latin America. She is the author of Cooperating with the Colossus: A Social and Political History of US Military Bases in World War II Latin America and is currently at work on a book about anti-extractivism in Antarctica. Her first novel, The Outposters , will be published next summer by Cardinal.

eb700ee2-4f20-4efc-ac01-8755d2bde6b2: Join us on Thursday, November 12 at 7pm for Weird Science, Strange Beliefs, and the Impossible, an evening with authors Scott Lambridis, Martha Conway, and Yance Wyatt at 9th Ave! Free to Attend, Please RSVP Or Watch on YouTube Live/Link Available Soon About the Event Weird Science, Strange Beliefs, and the Impossible In celebration of the release of their new books, three novelists discuss the pleasures and perils of making the impossible believable. From alternate histories and afterlives to strange science, mythology, and dark humor, Scott Lambridis (St. Ulphia’s Dead), Martha Conway (We Meet Apart), and Yance Wyatt (The Watersmith) explore how fiction destabilizes what we think we know—and what becomes possible when writers allow uncertainty to remain unresolved—in a conversation moderated by writer and critic Olga Zilberbourg. The authors will share brief passages from their new work that speak to the evening’s theme, then dig into genre, research, belief, and the craft of making an impossible premise reveal something emotionally true. About the Authors Martha Conway is the author of several award-winning novels including The Underground River, which was a New York Times Book Editor’ s Choice and published in seven languages. Her short fiction has appeared in The Iowa Review, The Missouri Review, Folio, and other journals. Martha was awarded a California Arts Council Fellowship for Creative Writing, and she teaches creative writing for Stanford University’ s Continuing Studies. She lives with her family in San Francisco. Born and raised in New York, Scott Lambridis earned a degree in neurobiology from the University of Virginia. He’ s toured the Midwest with a progressive rock band, founded an indie press and performance series, earned an MFA from San Francisco State University, tended a 40-acre olive farm, and read a book from every country of the world. He wrote St. Ulphia’ s Dead during his daughter’ s naps during a year in France, and finally settled with his wife and child in Bellingham, Washington, “ the city of subdued excitement.” This is his first novel. Yance Wyatt is from Nashville, Tennessee, or thereabouts. He studied fiction at the University of Southern California, where he now teaches writing. His stories have appeared in dozens of nationally circulated literary journals and received multiple Pushcart Prize nominations. He lives with his wife and son in the foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains. The Watersmith is his first novel.
06b8ff04-ab15-4e66-a82c-89c13ed77627: Contemporary saxophonist, author, and music producer Jackiem Joyner is set to release his 7th album, Touch, worldwide this fall, 2019. After more than 12 years as a recording artist, Jackiem continues to stand out with electrifying live performances and brilliant music productions. As a performer, he has toured over 30 countries and performed with the likes of the late George Duke, Marcus Miller, Keiko Matsui, Donnie McClurkin, Angela Bofill, Najee, Kirk Whalum, Peter White, and many, many more. Joyner’s radio success is widely known within the industry. Joyner has two number-one hit songs, five top 10 Billboard singles, and a number-one debut album under his belt. In addition, he published the highly acclaimed science fiction novel Zarya , which received high praise and a five-star rating on Amazon. “This album is about romance,” Joyner explains of Touch . “I wanted to give everyone something hip, smooth, and sexy at the same time.” The record has an urban feel, laced with the hottest downtempo vibes. The album shares similar textures to the music of artists Tank and Trey Songz. Joyner’s soprano sax leads the charge through most of the album. “My approach to performing on this record was to be melodic and dynamic with my horn”. Peter White joins Jackiem on the first single, “Last Dance”. The combination of soprano sax and nylon guitar pulls you in with its romantic and catchy melody. Najee serves up the flute on a dreamy urban song called “Fairytales”. The unique mix of flute and soprano sax on this vibey tune forms one of Joyner’s best performances and productions. The song was written together with Tim Bailey, aka Twizzboy. Born to a Vietnam War veteran father and a dedicated mother in Norfolk, VA, growing up wasn’t easy for Jackiem. He set his sights high from a young age; he always dreamed of being a performing artist, as unlikely as it was, given his humble upbringing. Even as a child, he loved the attention he received from his family when he danced to Michael Jackson songs. Now, Jackiem is proud to stand front and center on the main stage most weekends around the country. A quick glance at Joyner’s track record makes it clear that he continues to beat the odds in a tough and competitive music industry. “I love what I do, and I have passion”, Jackiem says. “I don’t care how hard things get, it’ll never stop me from doing what I love: playing the sax, writing music and stories, and performing live.” His love of writing novels came as a surprise to many of his fans. “I’m very excited to release my second novel soon after my album release,” Joyner says. “Writing stories is now a big part of my creative journey.” The first single from Joyner’s last album, Main Street Beat (2017), was named for his daughter, Trinity. Joyner’s adoration for his little girl is clearly expressed through the live, pop-influenced song, driven by Steve Oliver’s guitar. The song was an instant hit. Reaching no. 2 on the Billboard. We’re all dying to see if she follows in dad’s footsteps with her own stage career someday! With the creation of his company, JOYNER MEDIA COMPANY L.L.C., Joyner hopes to inspire other creators to follow their dreams and realize their true potential in art and multimedia. When Jackiem is not touring the world, he spends time giving lectures to students across the country. He also enjoys talking to band classes, helping them with practice, and offering insight on how to pursue a career in the performing arts. Currently, Joyner is on a US tour in support of his new album, Touch . He will be touring Los Angeles, CA – Washington, DC – Hampton, VA – Melbourne, FL – Detroit, MI – Chicago, IL – Charleston, SC – Houston, TX – Rehoboth Beach, DE – Mazlatan, Mexico – Syracuse, NY – Tampa, FL – Atlanta, GA, and many more cities.

540d7871-e687-4aab-aa9f-d474db637e81: Throwin’ Bo’s presents: School Fair School Fair (Findlay Buchanan, Semisi Ma’ia’i, Hamish Morgan, De Stevens and Rose Pickernell) make music embedded in the human experience. It’s a product of the band’s native New Zealand, a place that remains intimate and remote, where emotion is magnified over both distance and familiarity. The five band members began the project renting out a factory-sized, sub-zero degree Celsius room normally operated by construction workers in the industrial area of Ōtepoti, Dunedin, New Zealand in 2021, recording music on the 4-track tape recorder that would become debut Gorse on a Hill . The album remained the only trace of the band online for a few years, an artifact for those who know where to look. School Fair’s music has this sense of self-discovery when you find it, a sound that feels both recognizable and like the vacant expanse of a country whirring by on a train. Still with little to no self-promotion, the appearance of sophomore effort Bird the Kid online in early 2025 was a new portal to their world of melodic and intricate indie music that retains a kind of atmospheric beauty. Unexpected Violence (Mutual, 2026) is the first record made between geographical places, with the band now split in between London and New Zealand. You can hear this fragmented approach in the patchwork quality and inherent connective tissue of the album. Recorded initially in a studio in East London, it was the first time the band brought in an outside engineer (Syd Kemp?), as opposed to the band’s prior live recordings, where the tendency was to “feed back off each other in quite a messy abstract and complicated way that works for us but isn’t typically structured.” The band then took these recordings and evolved them back home in Dunedin, with the addition of vocals on some tracks by Pickernell adding to the cohesive energy and collective, dialed-in synergy of the quintet. School Fair is built upon the many eclectic mediums from which the band members individually create: time spent repairing old machines, making short films, metalworking and jewelry-making, writing and engineering. All these counterparts bring a kind of industrial electricity to the music where each part feels necessary and agile, as well as perfectly in conjunction. It’s these points beneath the surface where the songs really bloom. The moody transference of guitar lick to guttural vocal and back again, where melody conjoins with surprising inflection and sharp-hued ambiance, littered with both poetic spoken-word and a self-referentiality of clues and repetition that rewards close listening yet remains accessible and immediate. Transportive lyrics shine with the lore and mythology of a world that is both deeply specific and transcendent in its curiosity toward the surrounding environment. Unexpected Violence is filled with resounding descriptors: from “cat runs blind in the smoke / birds slap their wings away / trees thrash and crash / each lonely in their chosen way” (the meandering “Angelika”) or the consequently spellbinding phrasing of “come out to your dead animal river gushing hard / come out to your heart split open and lit up with stars” of “In Boredom You Shoot Your Gun”. It’s a starkly poetic snapshot into the band’s own universe and a showcase in the thoroughfare of language, where the specificity of one person’s memory counteracts with a landscape that blurs and unravels with the passage of time. Unexpected Violence a record that could only be made in a place like New Zealand, yet its vantage point expands far beyond to the vast unwieldiness of human sentiment. “There’s a sense of remoteness to the record, both emotionally but also in the sense of place, broken farms, cast iron beaches, blank midday fires, lost friends.” Or as the band recites in the austere glimmer of “Spirally Staircase Memory”: “memories are just stories that can’t be found.” But School Fair reaches some sort of access point, a way for them to live on. The name Unexpected Violence was born out of Buchanan and Ma’ia’i coming across the genre title in a bookstore in Berlin, and is a fitting discernment of the heartbreak that often comes with the realities of existence. In album highlight “Gussied Up,” the band intones: “I never never never ever / wanna hear you / see you, feel you or touch you.” It’s a harsh statement that feels swept up in the parallel admission that these are relationships you may never fully escape; they have left their mark. We still pass the places they inhabit, and feel the uncanny emptiness even after moving on. It’s fitting that the record ends on a similar contradiction. Just discernable above spirals of drummed up, ambient noise: “I miss you now you’re gone.” For all things can be true at once. This practice strengthens the immune system, supports the body’s natural capacity to heal, and cultivates mental clarity and emotional steadiness. Through simple, time-honored movements, the nervous system unwinds, the mind becomes more spacious, and the heart opens. Hiromi will be in Japan February 1-21 but will resume classes when she gets back Hiromi Vardy is a certified Zen Shiatsu, Yang style Tai Chi, and Zhineng Qigong healer and practitioner. She first encountered Tai Chi in 1973 while studying theater design and performance art in London. Initially drawn to the beauty of the movements, she soon discovered that the practice had a profound effect on her consciousness, awakening a deep interest in the healing arts. While collaborating on stage with dancers in London, Hiromi began treating injuries in overworked bodies. In 1976, after a serious accident that resulted in loss of circulation in her leg and concern about possible amputation, she turned to daily Tai Chi practice, self-massage, and treatment from a Japanese acupuncturist. This experience became a turning point in her healing journey and led her back to Japan, where she studied Shiatsu at the Namikoshi School and trained at the Zen Shiatsu Center under Shizuto Masunaga. After moving to the United States with her family in 1987, Hiromi continued deepening her practice and teaching. During a period of significant stress later in her life, she encountered Master Ming Tong Gu and began studying Zhineng (wisdom healing) Qigong under his guidance, eventually becoming licensed to teach. The healing shift she experienced through this practice was profound and continues to inform her teaching today. Since 2013, Hiromi has been dedicated to teaching Zhineng Qigong, expanding her offerings to include online classes in 2020. Her work invites students to explore the foundations of Qigong and Tai Chi as embodied, healing practices that cultivate awareness, vitality, and resilience.

Surrounded by hills, buried in green, Eden is a forgotten town full of ordinary lives. Underneath the threat of marital infidelity, financial ruin, and life-changing illness is always the same question: To stay, or to go? If you choose to stay, is it ever a permanent choice? Can you be sure you’ll choose it again tomorrow? After attending New World School of the Arts High School, she earned her BFA in Illustration Design from ArtCenter College of Design in Pasadena, California. Byrne creates expressive watercolor paintings inspired by plants and flowers, balancing recognizable forms with abstraction, gestural brushwork, and bold color. Her process embraces the unpredictability of watercolor, allowing each painting to unfold organically through movement, experimentation, and intuition. She now lives and works in San Francisco’s Outer Sunset neighborhood. About the show: A flower brought home, a plant tended over time, photos taken during my travels— each offers a starting point for these abstract floral paintings. I aim to transform botanical forms into something entirely my own. Working intuitively with watercolor, I allow the paint to move and interact in unexpected ways, following the work wherever it leads. The result exists somewhere between observation and abstraction, where the original subject may emerge or dissolve into color and form. As I continue to understand and experiment with my art practice, I find myself wanting to put the work out into the world as a way of understanding it better. Showing the work publicly is part of the process for me — a chance to step outside of the studio, look at what I’ve made, and see what it has to say back. Please feel free to reach out to me if you have any questions or comments – sarang@sarangbyrne.com Thank you for being here and taking the time to view my work, I truly appreciate it! Sarang
